119:
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Abhinavaṭīkā
## Introduction to the Text (Ganthārambhakathā)

I pay homage to the Buddha, who is the ornament of the three worlds, the source of pure and fresh virtues, whose heart is cooled by compassion, and who is the source of noble prosperity worthy of worship.

I also pay homage to that Sublime Dhamma, which was worshipped by the King of Dhamma himself—the unique teacher in the world of beings—which is profound, supreme, and capable of dispelling the darkness of ignorance.

I always pay homage to that Saṅgha, which is like a pond of white lilies (or the source of virtues in which the virtuous delight), having been awakened by the stainless rays of the Dhamma of the Moon of Sages.

The elder named Buddhaghosa, who possessed a firm mind, wrote the beautiful commentary on the Mātikā named Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, in the ocean of all scriptures which is profound in methods and difficult to cross in every way.

Requested respectfully by the wise elder named Sumedha—who is endowed with a multitude of firm virtues, is an expert in the Vinaya, possesses good conduct, is a son of the Sage (a monk), and desires the longevity of the Vinaya Piṭaka—I shall explain that commentary on the Mātikā so that it is extremely pure and free from confusion. May the virtuous listen to my words attentively.

## Explanation of the Introduction to the Text (Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā)

Wishing to provide the explanation of the meaning of the extremely profound Pātimokkha, which is the chief of all wholesome states and brings great and noble distinction of qualities, this teacher first purifies his own mental continuum by paying homage to the Triple Gem with the words beginning with "Buddhaṃ Dhammaṃ". Indeed, wisdom based on a pure mental continuum is capable of reaching the end of the intended commentary by attaining sharpness and clarity.

Alternatively, by paying homage to the Triple Gem, unwholesome states in the mental continuum are removed, and obstructive kamma accumulated in other lives cannot cause obstacles to the intended explanation of the meaning due to the lack of conditions. For this reason also, the teacher pays homage to the Triple Gem.
120:
In other words, by paying homage to the Triple Gem, all unwholesome states in the mental continuum are dispelled, and even the obstructive kamma accumulated in other lives are unable to cause obstacles to the intended explanation of the meaning due to the deficiency of conditions. Therefore, the teacher performs the homage to the Triple Gem.

Among those, the meaning of the word 'Buddha' should be understood according to the method of explanation in texts such as the Mahāniddesa: 'He is the Buddha because he has realized the Truths; he is the Buddha because he makes the generation of beings realize them.' Alternatively, he is called 'Buddha' in the sense of awakening and blossoming, because of the absolute departure from the sleep of ignorance along with its latent tendencies (vāsanā), or because of the blossomed state of his wisdom. Or else, because there is no knowable thing (ñeyyadhamma) that is not understood, and because the specific knowable is not taken as the object (kamma), the word is used in the sense of understanding as an agent (kattā), thus 'He has understood, therefore he is the Buddha,' just as one says 'The initiated one does not give.' In terms of meaning, however, the 'Buddha' is the continuum of aggregates (khandha-santāna) which is the basis of immeasurable qualities such as Great Compassion and Omniscience, being free from all defilements along with latent tendencies through the self-enlightened knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa) nurtured by the perfections (pāramī). As it is said:

'The Buddha is that Blessed One who, being self-enlightened and without a teacher, realized the Truths by himself among teachings not heard before, and attained omniscience therein, and attained mastery over the powers.'

To that Buddha (I pay homage).

'He is called Dhamma because he upholds (dhāreti).' This Dhamma upholds the person who practices according to the instruction so that they do not fall into the suffering of the four lower realms and the suffering of the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra). Here, 'upholding' means the destruction of the defilements that produce that suffering. In this way, both the Noble Path (ariya-magga) and Nibbāna—as the cause of the success of that Path's purpose—are called Dhamma in the primary sense (nippariyāya) because they uphold. The Noble Fruit (ariya-phala) is called Dhamma in a figurative sense (pariyāya) because it is the pacification of the defilements completely eradicated by that Path and is thus consistent with it; and the Scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-dhamma) is also called Dhamma figuratively because it is the cause for attaining that Path. To that Dhamma (I pay homage). The word 'ca' (and) has the sense of conjunction. By that, in saying 'having worshipped the aforementioned Buddha and this Dhamma,' it joins the Dhamma-gem with the act of worship along with the Buddha-gem.

Not only these two, he said 'and the Saṅgha' (saṅghañca). It is called 'Saṅgha' because it is joined and united by the commonality of noble view and virtue. It is the group of the eight noble persons (ariya-puggala).
121:
It is called the Sangha because the distress of defilements has been well-slain (destroyed) by means of the absolute cutting off and the tranquilizing of those defilements through various Paths and Fruits. The worldling Sangha (puthujjanika-sangha) should also be understood as being included only within this group of eight Noble Persons, because they stand in the practice that is the preliminary part of the Path, just as the preliminary intention is included in the act of giving. Although that worldling Sangha is not yet united with the Noble Ones (Ariyas) through the commonality of view and virtue, they are indeed the Sangha worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇā) and respect, being united by the commonality of view and virtue of worldlings who are on the side of liberation. Therefore, [I worship] that Sangha. The meaning of the word 'ca' (and) should also be understood here in the same manner as previously stated.

In what way are the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha distinguished when being worshipped? It is said: "the vessel of salutation, reverence, worship, and honor." This qualification should be applied to each: "the Buddha, who is the vessel of salutation, reverence, worship, and honor... and the Sangha, who is the vessel of salutation, reverence, worship, and honor." In that context, 'vandanā' (salutation) is the act of homage performed by the world including the devas due to the excellence of qualities such as Arahantship. 'Māna' (reverence) is proper respect. 'Pūjā' (worship) is the offering made with scents, flowers, and so on. 'Sakkāra' (honor) is the giving of specially prepared requisites. Salutation, reverence, worship, and honor are called 'vandanā-māna-pūjā-sakkāra.' They are called 'vandanā-māna-pūjā-sakkāra-bhājana' because they make such acts highly fruitful and because they are the vessel or support for them. By this term, the incomparable nature of the Triple Gem through qualities such as Arahantship is shown. It should be understood that such a demonstration is for the purpose of showing the capability of accomplishing the desired explanation of the meaning, by means of purifying one's own mental continuum through the act of humble respect performed towards the Triple Gem.

"Having worshipped with a clear mind" means having worshipped with a mind that is exceptionally clear through the power of repeatedly recollecting various special qualities such as Arahantship, together with the body and speech which serve as the instruments. It means having paid homage through the three doors. This worship is of three kinds: worship by body, speech, and mind. Among these, when any wholesome sense-sphere intention (kāmāvacara-kusala-cetana) or functional intention (kiriya-cetana) that takes the qualities of the Buddha and so on as its object produces bodily or vocal intimation (viññatti), the worship arising by means of the bodily door or vocal door is called 'bodily worship' or 'vocal worship.' However, the worship arising by means of the mind-door without producing the two types of intimation is called 'mental worship.' This word 'vanditvā' (having worshipped) is connected with the phrase 'vaṇṇanaṃ vaṇဏယိဿာမိ' (I shall describe the commentary).

Having thus shown the homage to the Triple Gem, the author now says "theravaṃsappadīpānaṃ" and so on, wishing to show homage to the teachers of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā-ācariya) who are his own support. In that verse, it is connected as: "having paid homage to the lion-like former teachers with joined palms." He is called 'katañjalī' because the palms (añjali) have been joined by him. Here, for the sake of protecting the meter...
122:
It means having raised the hands in salutation (añjali). The great elders, the ancient commentators of the island of Tambapaṇṇi, are called 'Lion-like Former Teachers' (Pubbācariyasīha) because they are like lions in their ability to endure dangers, suppress opposing defilements, and remain unassailable by the proponents of other views. (I pay homage) to those Lion-like Former Teachers. To explain what kind of persons these Lion-like Former Teachers are, he said "Theravaṃsappadīpānaṃ" and so on. In that phrase, "Theravaṃsappadīpānaṃ" means: the lineage of the noble ones such as the Venerable Mahākassapa, who are called 'Theras' (Elders) because they are firm in the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) and so forth, is called 'Theravaṃsa' (the lineage of the Elders). By this, he rejects the lineages of the seventeen sects with divergent views, such as the Mahāsaṃghikas. (I pay homage) to the Lion-like Former Teachers called 'Lamps of the Lineage of the Elders' (Theravaṃsappadīpa) because, being included in that lineage of the Elders and being endowed with the scriptures (āgama) and realization (adhigama), they illuminate that lineage of the Elders with the lamp of wisdom. They are called 'Thira' because they are firm and unshakeable. The word "Vinayakkame" (in the sequence of the Vinaya) is a term appropriate for the beginning of the work; however, those teachers are also firm in the Suttas and Abhidhamma.

Having thus shown the salutation to the teachers of the commentaries, he now says "Pāmokkhaṃ" and so forth, wishing to show the name and benefits of the special Dhamma to be explained, as well as the excellence of the teacher who taught it. In this context, it should be connected as: "Mahesinā yaṃ pātimokkhaṃ pakāsitaṃ" (The Pātimokkha which was proclaimed by the Great Seer). Therein, "Mahesi" (Great Seer) refers to the Fully Enlightened Buddha, who is called 'Mahesi' either because He sought the five noble aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue, or because He is sought by noble persons, or because He is a seer (isi) who is superior to worldlings (puthujjana), learners (sekha), and non-learners (asekha). "Pātimokkha" refers to either the virtue of the training rules (sikkhāpada-sīla), which is the restraint regarding the seven groups of offenses (āpattikkhandha), or the text of the Pātimokkha (gantha-pātimokkha) known as the Twofold Vibhaṅga (Ubhatovibhaṅga), because it explains that virtue. To explain what kind of Pātimokkha it is, he said "Pāmokkhaṃ" and so forth. It is called 'Pamokkha' because it is good in the beginning; 'Pamokkha' itself is 'Pāmokkha'. It is called 'Pāmokkha' because it is the beginning and the foundation of wholesome states (kusala dhamma)—sensuous-sphere (kāmāvacara), lofty (mahaggata), and supramundane (lokuttara)—known as concentration and wisdom, which are faultless as they are the opposite of faults. For has it not been said: "A wise man, established in virtue, should develop the mind and wisdom"? It is called 'Mukha' (mouth/entrance) because it is like a mouth. Just as for beings, the four types of nutriment—hard food, soft food, lickable food, and drinkable food—enter through the mouth and spread to the limbs and organs, so too for the yogi, wholesome states occurring in the four planes enter through the mouth of virtue and accomplish the desired benefit. Therefore, it is called 'Mukha' because it is like a mouth. Alternatively, it means 'Mukha' because it is the door for entering Nibbāna and for the realization of Nibbāna. Indeed, the Blessed One has said in the Nikāyas: "Ānanda, wholesome virtues have non-remorse (avippaṭisāra) as their purpose and benefit," and so on; non-remorse leads to joy (pāmojja), joy leads to rapture (pīti), rapture leads to tranquility (passaddhi), tranquility leads to happiness (sukha), happiness leads to concentration (samādhi), concentration leads to the knowledge and vision of things as they really are (yathābhūta-ñāṇadassana), the knowledge and vision of things as they really are leads to disenchantment (nibbidā), disenchantment leads to dispassion (virāga), dispassion leads to liberation (vimutti), liberation leads to the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana), and the knowledge and vision of liberation leads to final Nibbāna without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna).

Having thus shown the name and benefit of the special Dhamma to be explained, he now speaks the fourth verse beginning with "Suratena" in order to state the reason for composing the commentary (the requester). In that verse, the meaning along with the word-analysis should be understood thus: "Surata" means one who delights in good deeds...
123:
“Ānanda, wholesome virtues (kusalāni sīlāni) indeed have non-remorse (avippaṭisāra) as their purpose and benefit,” thus it was taught (in the Aṅguttara Nikāya). Furthermore, it was taught (in the Parivāra): “Non-remorse is for the sake of joy (pāmojja); joy is for the sake of rapture (pīti); rapture is for the sake of tranquility (passaddhi); tranquility is for the sake of happiness (sukha); happiness is for the sake of concentration (samādhi); concentration is for the sake of knowledge and vision of things as they truly are (yathābhūtañāṇadassana); knowledge and vision of things as they truly are is for the sake of disenchantment (nibbidā); disenchantment is for the sake of dispassion (virāga); dispassion is for the sake of liberation (vimutti); liberation is for the sake of knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana); and knowledge and vision of liberation is for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna).”

Having thus shown the name and benefits of the sublime Dhamma to be commented upon, the author now speaks the fourth verse beginning with “Suratena” to show the reason (the requester) for the commentary. In that verse, “Suratena” means one who delights in what is beautiful, hence “surata”; (in the grammatical analysis) the vowel ‘u’ is lengthened; by that term “suratena,” it means a person who is gentle because of delighting in beautiful bodily and verbal actions; it means one who is well-trained (vinīta).

“Nivātena” means one who has a humble conduct. “Sucisallekhavuttinā” means one whose conduct is pure and capable of scraping away defilements; it means one who is endowed with the pure practice of fewness of wishes. “Vinayācārayuttena” means one who is endowed with the virtue of restraint (vāritta-sīla) and the virtue of performance (cāritta-sīla). Alternatively, “vinaya” here refers to the discipline of restraint (saṃvara-vinaya) consisting of the Pātimokkha restraint and so forth. “Ācāra” refers to the conduct suitable for monks as mentioned in the description of conduct and resort (ācāra-gocara-niddesa).

In the phrase “Soṇattherena,” “Soṇa” is the name of that Elder. He is called “Thera” (Elder) because he is endowed with firm qualities such as the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). “Yācito” means being specially requested. Indeed, the Elder Soṇa, knowing the depth and difficulty of penetrating the Pātimokkha, and knowing the teacher’s ability to comment upon it, made the request with respect, seeing the benefits: “Venerable Sir, you should provide an explanation of the meaning of the Pātimokkha. Only in this way will the Dispensation (Sāsana) endure for a long time.” The author said “yācito” (requested) to show that the Elder’s request was the cause for his commentary.

Furthermore, by the word “suratena,” the Elder’s gentleness (soracca) is expressed. By the word “nivātena,” his humble mind and humble conduct are expressed; a person endowed with such humble conduct is one who has destroyed conceit and pride, being like a foot-wiping cloth, like a bull with broken horns, and like a snake with its fangs extracted, thus being mild and gentle.
124:
(That Elder Soṇa) is one who is pleasant to live with. It should be understood that by the term “sucisallekhavuttinā,” the author refers to the virtue of sense-restraint (indriya-saṃvara), the virtue of livelihood purification (ājīva-pārisuddhi), and the virtue related to the use of requisites (paccayasannissita-sīla). By the term “vinayācārayuttena,” it should be understood that the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla) is expressed. Praising that Elder Soṇa with such numerous qualities is intended to show that the request and urging of a fellow-monk (sabrahmacārī) endowed with such qualities cannot be refused; thus, this commentary on the meaning of the extremely profound Pātimokkha is undertaken.

Furthermore, it should be understood that an explanation of meaning undertaken based on the urging of such a fellow-monk will reach completion before long due to the influence of his urging and the excellence of my own effort.

Having thus shown the reason for the commentary, the author now speaks two verses beginning with “Tattha” to inspire respect in the listeners by showing the benefits, the method of writing, the source, and the name of this commentary. In those verses, “tattha” means in that Pātimokkha, which was referred to as “the Pātimokkha proclaimed by the Great Sage.” “Sañjātakankhānaṃ” means for those who have developed doubts by way of determining the words and their meanings. “Kankhāvitaraṇatthāya” means for the purpose of overcoming the aforementioned doubts. “Tassa” means of the Pātimokkha. “Vaṇṇanā” refers to the commentary (Atthakathā), so called because the meaning is described or spoken by it. This is to be connected with the word “vaṇṇayissāmi” (I shall comment).

To describe what kind of commentary it is, he said “paripuṇṇavinicchayaṃ” and so forth. “Paripuṇṇavinicchayaṃ” means a commentary with complete decisions, because it clarifies specific decisions by way of the Khandhaka, Parivāra, and Padabhājanī, as well as decisions common to all training rules in seventeen categories by way of the origin (nidāna) and so forth.

“Mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ”: the monastery situated in the area of the Mahāmeghavana park is the Mahāvihāra, which is adorned by the Teacher’s Great Bodhi tree; those who dwell there by virtue of their conduct are the Dwellers of the Mahāvihāra (Mahāvihāravāsī); it means for those Dwellers of the Mahāvihāra. “Vācanāmagganissitaṃ” means depending on the path of instruction, which means depending on the commentaries; it means that here, the method of the Sinhalese commentaries (Sīhalaṭṭhakathā) of the Dwellers of the Mahāvihāra is relied upon. “Vaṇṇayissāmi” means I shall proceed (I shall comment). “Nāmena” means by its own title of quality. “Kankhāvitaraṇī”: it is called Kankhāvitaraṇī because one can overcome doubts by means of this work; (I shall comment on) that Kankhāvitaraṇī. “Subhaṃ” means beautiful because it is endowed with excellence in meaning and phrasing; it is pure because it is beautiful in terms of grammatical characteristics, beautiful in its decisions, and beautiful in being easily understood. Here, by the word “kankhāvitaraṇatthāya,” the purpose is shown. By the word “paripuṇṇavinicchayaṃ”...
125:
By this manner of explanation, with the words "dependent on the path of instruction of those residing in the Mahāvihāra," it should be understood that the purity of the basis of the commentary is shown by avoiding the fault of mixing with the views of other sects; and with the words "I shall explain," he shows his own intention. There is also a reading "I shall proceed" (vattayissāmi).

## The explanation of the introduction to the book is finished.

## Explanation of the Prologue

Having thus shown the name and so forth along with the salutation to the Triple Gem, now, because it was said, "I shall explain the commentary on the Pātimokkha," the following passage beginning with "Tattha pātimokkhaṃ" is undertaken to show that this commentary will proceed according to the order of the recitations, having defined the Pātimokkha first by way of word-meaning (vacanattha), by way of its nature (sarūpa), by way of the text (gantha), by way of the division of recitations (uddesa-vibhāga), and by way of the delimitation of recitations (uddesa-pariccheda).

In that sentence, "tattha" means in that verse-word. "Pa-atimokkhaṃ" means that which is the foremost and chief among the virtues (sīla) in various ways. "Atipamokkha" says the same word by transposition of the prefixes (upasagga). Or, "pa ati mokkha" is the word-analysis, and the meaning of that word with transposed prefixes is stated as "atipamokkha." Having thus explained the word by way of its parts, he states the literal meaning: "it has the meaning of being most noble, most excellent." Here, it should be understood that the Pātimokkha as virtue (sīla-pātimokkha) is noble because it is the root of all good qualities, while the Pātimokkha as text (gantha-pātimokkha) is noble because it is associated with noble qualities. In the word "excellent" (uttama), the method is the same.

"Iti" means "thus" (the aforementioned meaning). By this word "iti," he points out the aforementioned word-meaning. This word "iti" has the sense of pointing out, as in the Saṃyutta Nikāya passages: "'Everything exists,' Kaccāna, this is one extreme; 'everything does not exist,' Kaccāna, this is the second extreme." "Iminā" (by this) is a term indicating what is near and present, because it refers to the word-meaning just pointed out by the word "iti," which has entered the process of auditory consciousness (sotaviññāṇa-vīthi) of the listeners. Or, "iminā" is a term that makes the aforementioned word-meaning present and immediate. "Vacanatthena" means by the literal meaning of "most noble" (atiseṭṭha). "Ekavidhampi" means even though it is of a single part. "Sīlaganthabhedato duvidhaṃ hoti" means that by the division into virtue and text, there are two kinds: the Pātimokkha as virtue and the Pātimokkha as text.
126:
Now, to show that both of these appear in the Sutta texts, the passage beginning with "Tathā hi" is stated. In that passage, it is "pāti" because it protects (pāti); it is "pātimokkha" because it releases (mokkheti) that person who protects it from sufferings such as those of the woeful states. Restraint is "saṃvara"; it is the non-transgression by way of body and speech. Since the Pātimokkha itself is restraint, it is called "pātimokkha-saṃvara." Being endowed with the restraint of the Pātimokkha is called "pātimokkha-saṃvara-saṃvuto." "Viharati" means he dwells (exists).

"Ādimetaṃ" means this virtue of the training rules is the "ādi" (beginning) in the sense of being the first to arise. It is also said: "Therefore, Uttiya, you should first purify the very beginning of wholesome states. And what is the beginning of wholesome states? Virtue that is well-purified and a view that is straight." (SN 5.382).

Just as a city architect wishing to build a city first clears the site for the city, and thereafter builds the city by dividing it into sections such as main roads, crossroads, and junctions; or just as a washerman first washes the cloth with three kinds of alkaline salts and then applies the desired dye to the clean cloth; or just as a skilled painter wishing to paint a figure first prepares the wall and thereafter produces the figure; even so, a practitioner (yogāvacara) first purifies virtue and thereafter realizes states such as serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). Therefore, virtue is called the "beginning" (ādi). The words "mukhametaṃ" and so forth have the meanings already stated. By the word "ādi," the Pali passage beginning with "Pātimokkhe ca saṃvaro" is included.

Virtue (sīla) refers to the virtue of the training rules included in the Vinaya Piṭaka, which is of two kinds: performance (cāritta) and avoidance (vāritta). In terms of its ultimate nature (dhammato), virtue should be understood as the states such as volition (cetanā) of one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth, or of one who fulfills the major and minor duties. For it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "What is virtue? Volition is virtue, mental factor (cetasika) is virtue, restraint (saṃvara) is virtue, non-transgression (avītikkama) is virtue." "Ubhayāni kho panassa pātimokkhāni" means both Pātimokkhas by way of the Bhikkhu-pātimokkha and Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha; the meaning is the two Mātikās. "Assa" (of him) refers to the monk who exhorts the nuns. "Vitthārena" (in detail) means together with both Vibhaṅgas. "Svāgatāni" means well-handed down (well-recited). By the word "ādi," the Pali passage beginning with "Pātimokkhaṃ uddiseyya" is included. "Tattha" means in those [two], the text of virtue and the Pātimokkha.
127:
## 
'Yo' is an indefinite designation meaning 'any person.' 'Naṃ' refers to the virtue (sīla) included in the Vinaya Piṭaka. 'Rakkhati' means protecting by undertaking and not violating. Because he protects, he is called 'pātī'; one who stands in the Pātimokkha virtue is called 'mokkha' because it causes release (from suffering) as a result of being a cause with beneficial effects. Suffering in the lower realms is called 'āpāyika-dukkha,' and that suffering etc. is 'āpāyikādīni.' By the word 'ādi,' all other sufferings of the round of rebirth (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa) are included. 'Attānuvādādīhi' refers to dangers such as self-reproach. By the word 'ādi,' the danger of reproach by others (parānuvāda-bhaya), the danger of punishment (daṇḍa-bhaya), and the danger of rebirth in an unhappy destination (duggati-bhaya) are included. 'Tassa pātimokkhassa jotakattā' means because it illuminates that Pātimokkha of virtue. The word-meaning (vacanattha) mentioned at the beginning is the meaning starting with 'atiseṭṭhaṃ' (most excellent). It is common to both: Sīla Pātimokkha is excellent because it is the root of all virtues; Gantha Pātimokkha (the text) is excellent because it is associated with excellent qualities.

Between Sīla Pātimokkha and Gantha Pātimokkha, 'ayaṃ vaṇṇanā' refers to the explanation to be given later. If it is asked: 'While the explanation of Gantha Pātimokkha is appropriate, how is the explanation of Sīla Pātimokkha appropriate?' the answer is given starting with 'ganthe hi.' The word 'hi' is a particle indicating a reason. The meaning of that text, which is virtue, is already explained. By means of explaining the text, the meaning is also explained. The intention is: since explaining the text also explains the meaning inseparable from that text, it is also appropriate for Sīla Pātimokkha.

Having thus defined by nature, now to define by text, he says 'taṃ panetaṃ' etc. Between the two, Bhikkhu Pātimokkha and Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha, they are called 'uddesapariccheda' (divisions of recitation) because the recitations are divided by the sequences of words to be mentioned later. They exist without confusion through those divisions of recitation.

Having thus defined by text, now to define by recitation (uddesa), he says 'tattha' etc. Here, it is called 'uddesa' because it is recited in its own form, or because it is spoken by this sequence of words. Because it is the recitation of the introduction (nidāna), it is called 'nidānuddesa.' The same method applies to the remaining terms. Because the detailed version itself is the recitation, it is called 'vitthāruddesa' (detailed recitation).

Now, to show the limits of Nidānuddesa etc., he begins with 'tattha nidānuddeso.' Among those five recitations, Nidānuddesa is...
128:
## 
'Uddiṭṭho hoti' (is recited) is the connection [with the preceding]. In this context, the author of the Saṅgaha, wishing to show the limit of the Nidānuddesa, shows the Nidāna-pāḷi found in this Bhikkhu Pātimokkha: 'Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho... āvikatā hissa phāsu hoti.' Without making the connection for the passage 'Uddiṭṭhaṃ kho āyasmanto nidānaṃ,' which is to be recited at the time of the Pātimokkha recitation (uddesa) immediately after that Pāḷi, he shows it by connecting only the announcement (anusāvanā) etc., starting with 'Tatthāyasmante pucchāmi.' It should be understood that showing the announcement etc. in this way is for the purpose of showing the limit of the Nidānuddesa preceded by the showing of an incomplete Nidāna-pāḷi. Alternatively, it should be understood that the connection for that passage was not made because it is clear by way of a small elision (peyyāla). However, at the time of the Pātimokkha recitation (uddesa), it must be recited with the connection.

For the Saṅgaha teacher will say later: 'That passage appears at the end of the Pārājikas etc., not at the end of the Nidāna. Although it does not appear [there], at the time of recitation, after saying "āvikatā hissa phāsu hoti," it must certainly be said in the manner starting with "Uddiṭṭhaṃ kho āyasmanto nidānaṃ, tatthāyasmante pucchāmi"' etc. 'Avasese sutena sāvite' means when the remaining four groups starting with Pārājikuddesa have been made known by way of hearing (suta), thus: 'Sutā kho panāyasmantehi cattāro pārājikā dhammā... avivadamānehi sikkhitabbaṃ.'

To show that the limits of the remaining three Pātimokkha recitations should be known by this same method, he says 'pārājikuddesādīnaṃ' etc. The connection is: 'the limits of Pārājikuddesa etc. should be connected.' 'Starting from the beginning of the Nidāna and concluding with the Pārājikas etc.' means having recited in order the Nidāna, the Pārājika, both of those with the Saṅghādisesa, and those three with the Aniyata, thus concluding with the Pārājikas etc. 'Should be connected' means they should be connected in the manner: 'Avasese sutena sāvite uddiṭṭho hoti pārājikuddeso' (When the rest has been made known by hearing, the Pārājika recitation is [considered] recited). 'Because of the words "the rest should be made known by hearing"' refers to the Uposathakkhandhaka:

'Monks, there are these five recitations of the Pātimokkha: having recited the Nidāna, the rest should be made known by hearing; this is the first Pātimokkha recitation. Having recited the Nidāna and having recited the four Pārājikas, the rest should be made known by hearing; this is the second Pātimokkha recitation,' etc.

This is because it was so stated. 'Yasmiṃ vippakate' means when a certain recitation is not yet finished. 'Antarāyo uppajjati' means if any one of the ten obstacles arises.
129:
Obstacles may arise. The ten obstacles are: the obstacle of kings, the obstacle of thieves, the obstacle of fire, the obstacle of water, the obstacle of humans, the obstacle of non-humans, the obstacle of wild beasts, the obstacle of reptiles, the obstacle to life, and the obstacle to the holy life.

Among these ten obstacles, if while the monks are sitting with the intention, "We shall perform the Uposatha" (Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā, 150), a king arrives, this is the obstacle of kings. If thieves arrive, this is the obstacle of thieves. If a forest fire breaks out or a fire starts in the monastery, this is the obstacle of fire. If there is heavy rain or a flood comes, this is the obstacle of water. If many people arrive, this is the obstacle of humans. If a yakkha seizes a monk, this is the obstacle of non-humans. If fierce wild beasts such as tigers arrive, this is the obstacle of wild beasts. If reptiles such as snakes bite a monk, this is the obstacle of reptiles. If a monk becomes ill, or passes away, or if enemies seize him wishing to kill him, this is the obstacle to life. If people seize one or many monks wishing to make them fall away from the holy life, this is the obstacle to the holy life. Thus, the meaning of the statement, "An obstacle arises; any one of the ten obstacles arises," has been clarified.

"Tena saddhiṃ" means together with the unfinished recitation. The remaining recitation should be made known through hearing (suta), because the remaining words depend on the recitation already shown. This is as stated: "Having recited the Nidāna..." (Mahāvagga, 150). Therefore, it is said: "But in the recitation of the Nidāna..." and so on. What is meant by "should be made known through hearing" is that it occurs only when there is an obstacle to the Uposatha. "Aniyatuddeso parihāyati" (the recitation of the indefinite rules is omitted) is because there is no prescription of indefinite (aniyata) training rules for bhikkhunīs. It should be understood that this absence is because "this very characteristic follows in that Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga as well." "Sesaṃ" (the rest) refers to showing the extent of the remaining recitation. It should be connected as "of these two Pātimokkhas." "Tāva" means first. "Idaṃ" is a general indication of the words that are now to be spoken and are present in the mind; it means this speech, which is fixed and composed of syllables and words, is spoken. To the question "What is that?", it says: "Suṇātu me" and so on.

In that context, "Suṇātu me" and so on refers to the sutta passages found in the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha, such as: "Listen to me, venerable sirs, the Saṅgha; today is the Uposatha day," and so forth.
130:
"Atthanicchaya" means the determination and definition of both the literal meaning (abhidheyyattha) and the intended meaning (adhippāyattha). This is because in this commentary, the literal and intended meanings of those sutta passages are defined in various ways. Alternatively, "nicchaya" is so called because it is determined. It refers to speech that cuts through doubt, occurring in a manner that crushes the "stake" of uncertainty in difficult places. "Atthanicchaya" is the combination of meaning (attha) and determination (nicchaya). It means "the meaning and determination that I shall speak."

"Sīlasampannā" means "sampanna" because virtue is reached or fulfilled from all sides. Because these monks have fulfilled virtue, they are "sīlasampannā," meaning those with perfect virtue. Alternatively, "sampanna" means well-attained or approached. Being endowed with virtue, they are "sīlasampannā," meaning those endowed with the Pātimokkha restraint.

The three trainings known as higher virtue (adhisīla), higher mind (adhicitta), and higher wisdom (adhipaññā) are called "sikkhā" because they are to be trained in. Because they desire those trainings, they are "sikkhākāmā." "Suṇantu me" means "let all those monks listen to me." By this, he enjoins them to listen respectfully to his own commentary. This is because all success in the Dispensation (sāsana) is dependent on respectful listening. Here, only those monks who are endowed with virtue and desirous of the training should be taken. This is because others are not suitable recipients for this commentary. They will not consider that the Vinaya should be heard and practiced.

"Ettha" means in this verse-line, or among the words such as "Suṇātu me" included in the verse. It is called "savanāṇattivacana" because it is a speech commanding one to listen. Although it is a speech commanding one to listen, it is the command of the Blessed One, not of the reciter, because the Blessed One stated that it should be spoken thus by the reciter of the Pātimokkha. Therefore, even a more junior monk may say this, as it is a respectful and deferential speech accompanied by reverence and great esteem for the Saṅgha. For the Saṅgha, being endowed with special qualities such as being well-practiced (suppaṭipannatā), is the highest object of reverence and respectful listening.

To answer the question of who said all this, where, and when, he said: "Sabbam eva cetaṃ" and so on. By way of allowing the recitation of the Pātimokkha:
"I allow you, monks, to recite the Pātimokkha. And thus, monks, should it be recited: a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha: 'Listen to me, venerable sirs, the Saṅgha...'" (Mahāvagga, 133-134).
131:
The Buddha, who allows in this way and so forth. Rājagaha is a city of that name. It is called 'Rājagaha' because it was taken and demarcated by King Mandhātu, the Brahmin Mahāgovinda, and others. This city is inhabited by people only during the time of Buddhas and Cakkavatti Kings; at other times, it is empty of humans and remains as a dwelling place for Yakkhas. 'Tasmā' (Therefore) means because this statement, beginning with 'Suṇātu me bhante,' is to be spoken by the one reciting the Pātimokkha. Do both of those monks recite the Pātimokkha? Why is it said in this way? Thus, it is said, 'Saṅghatthero vā hi,' etc. 'Therādhika' means relating to the Elder or following the will of the Elder. There is also a variant reading 'Therādheyya,' which has the same meaning. It occurs in that assembly. 'Byatta' (competent) means endowed with mature wisdom, one who has memorized the Mātikā. 'Paṭibala' (capable) means able to recite, meaning one who is fearless.

Here, although a young competent monk is also allowed to recite the Pātimokkha, the meaning is this: if the Elder does not know the five, four, or three types of Pātimokkha by heart, but can recite even two types clearly and without interruption, then the recitation of the Pātimokkha is the responsibility of the Elder alone. Only if he is unable to recite even that much clearly is it the responsibility of the competent monk. Now, since 'Saṅgha' is mentioned generally without specification, to distinguish the intended Saṅgha here, it says 'Saṅghoti iminā pana padena,' etc. The particle 'kiñcāpi' is used in the sense of concession and means 'yadi nāma' (if indeed). Because beings prosper through desired wealth because of this gift, it is called 'dakkhiṇā.' It also refers to a gift given with faith in the next world. Because he is worthy of receiving that gift, or because he purifies it to make it of great fruit, he is called 'dakkhiṇeyya.' Because of the gathering of those with similar views and virtue, it is called 'Saṅgha.' Since that Saṅgha is both worthy of offerings and a community, it is called 'dakkhiṇeyyasaṅgha.'

A Saṅgha established by the designation of the Vinaya rules, such as a group of four, is called 'sammutisaṅgha' (conventional Saṅgha). To speak without specification means generally, without distinguishing between Noble Ones (Ariyas) or worldlings (Puthujjanas). Here, it is the Saṅgha intended for performing the Uposatha rite. Is it not true that the conventional Saṅgha is of five types? Regarding the question of which Saṅgha is intended among those five, it says 'So panesa,' etc. There are five types by way of Vinaya actions. Teachers explain that the words vidha, yutta, gata, and pakāra have the same meaning.
132:
A collection or group of four monks is called 'catuvagga' (a group of four). Or, a group endowed with the measure of four is 'catuvagga.' In this way, 'pañcavagga' (a group of five) and so forth should also be understood. Now, to specifically show the actions by which this conventional Saṅgha becomes fivefold, the words beginning with 'Tattha' are said. That word 'tattha' refers to the five types of Saṅgha (among the group of four, etc.). Because the ordination rite (upasampadākamma) must be performed by a group of ten monks in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa), it is said, 'thapetvā... pe... upasampadañca.' By this word 'tathā,' it indicates the meaning that it is not that no Saṅgha action is improper to perform (i.e., it is proper).

If it is proper in that way, for what purpose is a group of more than twenty mentioned? To answer this, it says 'So pana,' etc. 'Atirekatarena' means that an action to be performed by a group of four can also be performed by a group of five or more, and an action to be performed by a group of ten can be performed by a group of eleven or more; this is for the purpose of making it known (ñāpanattha). Because of the reason that 'this group of four, etc., should perform only this action,' it is said 'kammavasena pañcavidho' (fivefold by way of action). If there is uncertainty (aniyama) regarding the action, the objection 'how can this statement be appropriate?' should be regarded as having no grounds. In this context, 'attha' refers to the Uposatha.

This word 'Uposatha' occurs in the senses of Pātimokkha recitation, virtue (sīla), observance (upavāsa), designation (paññatti), and day (divasa). This is so because: in statements such as 'Come, friend Kappina, let us go to the Uposatha (Pātimokkha recitation),' it appears in the sense of Pātimokkha recitation. In statements such as 'Visākhā, when the Uposatha (virtue) endowed with eight factors is observed,' it appears in the sense of virtue. In statements such as 'For the pure one, it is always the Phaggu month; for the pure one, it is always Uposatha (observance),' it appears in the sense of observance (upavāsa). In statements such as 'The elephant king named Uposatha,' it appears in the sense of designation (paññatti). In statements such as 'Monks, one should not leave a monastery where there are monks on that Uposatha day,' it appears in the sense of a day (divasa). Since here too it is intended only in the sense of a day, it says 'Today is the Uposatha day,' etc. It is called 'Uposatha' because one dwells fully (with virtue) on that day. 'Upavasanti' means they dwell being endowed with virtue, or by fasting which is the non-eating of all food, or by taking only milk, honey-drinks, and so forth.

Since all sentences are accompanied by the meaning of the particle 'eva,' in this word 'Uposatho,' the meaning 'Uposatho eva' (only the Uposatha day) is obtained. Therefore, it is said, 'By this statement, the non-Uposatha day is excluded.' This restriction (avadhāraṇa) shows what is excluded. Alternatively, because a word expresses its meaning by way of excluding the meaning of other words (apohana), the meaning of this word 'Uposatho' is 'it is not a non-Uposatha day.' Therefore, it is said, 'By this statement, the non-Uposatha day is excluded.' By this statement 'Esa nayo pannaraso,' another...
133:
In this context, "He rejects the Uposatha day," "eteṇa" means "by this word Uposatha." It is called Pannarasa (the fifteenth) by virtue of completing fifteen lunar days. To explain in detail the meaning briefly stated by the word "Pannarasa" regarding the rejection of other Uposatha days, the author of the Saṅgaha said "Divasavasena hi," and so on. An Uposatha associated with the fourteenth day is called Cātuddasika Uposatha. Similarly, an Uposatha associated with the fifteenth day is called Pannarasika Uposatha. An Uposatha performed on a day when the Saṅgha achieves harmony is called Sāmaggī Uposatha.

Among the three seasons—Hemanta, Gimha, and Vassāna—the Hemanta season consists of the four months starting from the first day of the waning moon of the later Kattika and ending on the full moon day of Phagguna. The Gimha season consists of the four months starting from the first day of the waning moon of Phagguna and ending on the full moon day of Āsāḷha. The Vassāna season consists of the four months starting from the first day of the waning moon of Āsāḷha and ending on the full moon day of the later Kattika. By performing it twice in the third and seventh fortnights (pakkha), there are six Cātuddasika Uposathas. This means that just as there are two Cātuddasika Uposathas in the third and seventh fortnights of the Hemanta season, it is the same for the other seasons, resulting in six Cātuddasika Uposathas. The remaining fortnights are Pannarasika Uposathas, and these remaining Uposathas are eighteen in number. Regarding this, there are these verses:

"From the waning of Kattika until the full moon of Phagguna,
It should be known as the Hemanta period; in that period, there are eight Uposathas.
From the waning of Phagguna until the full moon of Āsāḷha,
It should be known as the Gimha period; in that period, there are eight Uposathas.
From the waning of Āsāḷha until the full moon of Kattika,
It should be known as the Vassa period; in that period, there are eight Uposathas.
But in the third and seventh fortnights of the three seasons,
Those who know the method recite the Pātimokkha as the fourteenth-day Uposatha."

The practice performed due to reasons such as the resident monks not being numerous is called "Pakati-cāritta" (normal conduct). However, if there are reasons such as a large number of resident monks, it is also proper to perform the Uposatha on other fourteenth days. Therefore, he said "Sakiṃ," and so on. "Sakiṃ" means "at one time." "Āvāsikānaṃ anuvattitabbaṃ" means that while the resident monks are performing the preliminary duties (pubbakicca) saying "Today is the fourteenth-day Uposatha," the visiting monks must follow them and not object. By the word "ādi," it indicates the statement "The resident monks must follow the visitors" and the words "Monks, I allow..." and so on.
134:
It also includes the statement: "For those monks to perform two or three 14-day or 15-day Uposathas, how can we perform Pavāraṇā before those monks?" (Mahāva. 240). Here, it should be understood that the Suttas beginning with "by incoming monks" (āgantukehi) are shown because the meaning can also be established by way of normal custom (pakati-cāritta), stating that the Pātimokkha should be recited once on the 14th day of the third and seventh fortnights of each season of the first Sutta, or on the 15th day of the remaining fortnights.

"When there is such a cause" means when there is a suitable cause to perform the Uposatha on another 14th day, such as "the resident monks are more numerous." "On another 14th day" refers to a 14th day other than the 14th day of the third and seventh fortnights of the three seasons.

Stating that they are not only Uposatha days, it says, "But for those monks who have emerged from the first rains..." (purimavassaṃvuṭṭhānaṃ pana), and so on. "Mā" refers to the moon, because days are measured by its movement. That moon is called "Puṇṇamā" (Full Moon) because it is full with all its parts on this day. The full moon of Thadingyut is called "Pubbakattika-puṇṇamā" or "Assayuja-puṇṇamā." This is said to prevent the Pavāraṇā from reaching the later Kattika full moon. "Only of them" means only of the monks who have emerged from the first rains. "Bhaṇḍanakāraka" refers to those who cause quarrels. "Paccukkaḍḍhanti" means to pull up or postpone. It means that due to disputes with quarrelsome monks, they give up the Assayuja full moon and postpone the Pavāraṇā to the waning fortnight or the waxing fortnight. This means they postpone the Pavāraṇā by a formal motion (ñatti) such as: "Listen to me, venerable residents, if it is suitable to the venerable ones, let us perform the Uposatha now, let us recite the Pātimokkha, and let us perform Pavāraṇā in the coming waning fortnight," or "Listen to me, venerable residents, if it is suitable to the venerable ones, let us perform the Uposatha now, let us recite the Pātimokkha, and let us perform Pavāraṇā in the coming waxing fortnight."

"Atha" is a particle used in the sense of "thereafter." The 14th day is called the "Cātuddasa" day. If they have established a motion intending to "perform Pavāraṇā in the coming waxing fortnight," then they must certainly perform Pavāraṇā on that coming waxing fortnight, which is the Komudī full moon of Kattika when the water lilies bloom. It is not permissible to perform Pavāraṇā beyond that day. For this was said by the Blessed One:

"Monks, if those monks who are quarrelsome, contentious, disputatious, talkative, and who cause legal issues in the Saṅgha, should stay together until that waxing moon (the Kattika full moon), then, monks, all those monks..."
135:
## 
"When the full moon of Kārttika comes, which is the end of the four months of the rainy season and the time when the white lilies bloom, one must truly invite (perform Pavāraṇā) even if one is unwilling," it is stated (in the Mahāvagga, 240). For that very reason, (the author of the Saṅgaha) said, "The end of the latter rainy season is also the latter full moon day of Kārttika."

If one performs the invitation after that (full moon of Kārttika) day has passed, one incurs a dukkaṭa offense. "Monks, one should not invite on a day that is not for Pavāraṇā, except for the harmony of the Saṅgha," is it not so stated (in the Mahāvagga, 233)? Because it is associated with a pure Pavāraṇā, they are Pavāraṇā days. By the word 'pi' (also), it is shown that not only are they Pavāraṇā days, but in fact, they are also Uposatha days.

Now, regarding the aforementioned Sāmaggī-uposatha day, and in connection with that, wishing to show the Sāmaggī-pavāraṇā day, he said the words beginning with "Yadā pana." "When that monk has been reinstated" means when an expelled (ukkhittaka) monk has been reinstated; it means that after taking that monk, going to the sīmā, having him confess his offense, he is reinstated by means of the formal act for the suppression of the legal act (kammapappaṭipassaddhi) through kammavācā. "Of that matter" means of that legal issue (adhikaraṇa). At that time, having set aside... it should be connected as "it is called an Uposatha day."

If one asks for what reason, he said the words beginning with "Tāvad-eva." In that statement, "tāvad-eva" means only on that very day. "Vacanato" is because it was stated in the Kosambakakkhandhaka (Mahāvagga, 475). In a monastery where monks, while disputing over minor matters such as bowls and robes, suspend the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā, they do not get the opportunity to perform a Sāmaggī-uposatha in the interval after that legal issue has been settled, saying "We have become harmonious." Those monks who do so are said to have performed Uposatha on a non-Uposatha day.

In the phrase "Kattikamāsabbhantare," the month of Kārttika (Kattikamāsa) refers to the twenty-nine days and nights starting from the first day of the waning moon of the former Kārttika until the full moon of the latter Kārttika; it must be performed only within that period, and it is not allowable before or after that. This refers to any day (within that period). Here too, harmony (sāmaggī) should be understood as being similar to the harmony mentioned in the Kosambakakkhandhaka.

If some monks, having suspended Pavāraṇā due to some minor reason, become harmonious, they must perform Pavāraṇā only on the Pavāraṇā day; it should not be performed on the very day they become harmonious. Those monks who do so are said to have performed Pavāraṇā on a non-Pavāraṇā day. "It should not be performed at all" shows that if one performs it forcibly, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. For performing Uposatha on a non-Uposatha day, a dukkaṭa offense occurs. "Monks, one should not perform Uposatha on a non-Uposatha day except for the harmony of the Saṅgha," is it not so stated (in the Mahāvagga, 183)?
136:
## 
By the words "Pattakālam-eva pattakallaṃ," the author of the Saṅgaha shows that the bhāva suffix is used in the sense of sak-attha. By the negative statement "they do not exist," he strengthens the meaning already stated affirmatively by way of negation.

"Anurūpā" means they are worthy of that Uposatha act, suitable, or authoritative. "Sabbantimena" means by the lowest limit, four monks; without these four pakatatta monks, that Uposatha act cannot be performed, and the consent (chanda) or purity (pārisuddhi) of those four monks does not suffice (if they are absent). As for the remaining monks, even if there are as many as a thousand, if they are of the same communion (samānasaṃvāsaka), then all those monks are entitled to give consent; whether they come after giving their consent and purity or not, the formal act is not invalidated. "Pakatatta" refers to monks who have not been expelled and have not committed a pārājika offense. Hatthapāsa is a place measuring one and a half cubits.

Aiming at the question, "What is that sīmā where monks standing without leaving the hatthapāsa are called 'reached the act' (kammapatta)?", the commentator, wishing to show the sīmā, said the words beginning with "Sīmā ca nāmesa," because the clarification of the nature of various boundaries is primarily through detailed classification. "Sambhindentena" means by mixing. "Ajjhottharantena" means by treading upon, or by including within. "These boundaries are called defective boundaries (vipatti-sīmā)" is how it should be connected. If one asks why they are called defective boundaries, he said the words beginning with "Ekādasahi." "Ākārehi" means by reasons. "Vacanato" is because it was taught in the Kammavagga.

This formal act of the Saṅgha has its limit as an act to be performed by a group of twenty; therefore, he said, "In which sīmā twenty-one monks are unable to sit." In a sīmā where, at the minimum limit, twenty-one monks including the one entitled to perform the act are unable to sit in a circular manner, this is called an extremely small boundary (atikhuddaka). Such a boundary, even if designated, is not considered designated; it is just like village land, and an act performed in that boundary is invalid. This method applies to the remaining boundaries as well.

"Sammatā" means a boundary that is bound, meaning it has a kammavācā that has been recited. Indeed, the recitation of the kammavācā is called the binding (bandhana). Because it does not reach the status of a mark (nimitta), it is called "animittupaga"; that animittupaga means a place not suitable to be a mark. "Tacasārarukkha" (trees with essence in the bark) refers to palm trees, coconut trees, and so on. "Paṃsupuñjavāluka-puñjānaṃ" means in the middle of piles of earth or piles of sand. Here, the genitive case is in the sense of selection (niddhāraṇa). In some palm-leaf manuscripts, however, the reading "paṃsupuñjaṃ vā vāluka-puñjaṃ vā aññataraṃ" is seen, but that is an incorrect reading (apāṭha). This is because that reading does not agree with the word "aññataraṃ." "Antarā" means in between the marks that are suitable to be marks.
137:
In this designation of a boundary (sīmā), when it is bound with three marks, if one mark is established between trees that possess only bark and heartwood and do not qualify as proper marks, that boundary is called a khaṇḍanimittā boundary. However, when it is bound with four, five, or more marks, if one mark is established between such trees, it should be understood that it is not called a khaṇḍanimittā boundary, because there are three distinct marks that do qualify as marks. In the Commentaries, this is stated without distinction; therefore, it should be accepted after careful investigation. 'Sabbena sabbaṃ' means in every way. 'Standing outside the marks' (nimittānaṃ bahi ṭhitena) means the formal act (kammavācā) is recited by the Saṅgha standing outside those marks. As for the marks, it is permissible to recite them while standing either inside or outside.

'Even thus designated' (evaṃ sammatāpi) refers to being designated by the formal act after announcing the marks; this should be understood in connection with the phrase 'it is simply not designated' (asammatāva hoti). 'Monks, every river is a non-boundary' means that even if one announces marks on a river that has the characteristics of a river and says, 'We make this a bound boundary (baddhasīmā)', it does not become a bound boundary. However, by its own nature, that river is similar to a bound boundary, and it is permissible to perform formal acts of the Saṅgha (Saṅghakamma) in all parts of it. The same principle applies to oceans and large lakes. The phrase 'with intertwined branches' (saṃsaṭṭhaviṭapā) indicates the proximity of one tree to another. The phrase 'it is bound' (baddhā hoti) is said with reference to the boundary in the final direction.

'Its region' (tassā padesaṃ) refers to a portion of another's [old] boundary. It means a portion where monks are able to perform a formal act while standing there. If monks bind a boundary by including a place where they cannot perform a formal act, they are said to 'break' (sambhindana) the boundary with another boundary, but not 'overlap' (ajjhottharaṇa) it. In the Gaṇṭhipada texts, 'breaking' (sambhindana) is defined as binding by announcing one or two marks within another's boundary and taking only a mere line. 'Overlapping' (ajjhottharaṇa) is defined as binding by announcing marks in another's boundary, including the whole or a part of it within, and then announcing marks in one or two directions outside that boundary.

The perfection of marks such as mountains is called 'perfection of marks' (nimittasampatti). A mountain itself is a mark, hence 'mountain-mark' (pabbatanimitta); the same applies to the rest. 'When these are spoken' (evaṃ vuttesu) refers to the marks spoken of by the Blessed One in the designation of boundaries in the Uposathakkhandhaka. It is permissible to designate a boundary with these eight marks, whether unmixed or mixed with one another. Therefore, the author of the Saṅgaha said: 'In various directions, whatever marks that qualify as marks are obtained.' However, it is not permissible to designate a boundary with only one or two marks.
138:
It is not permissible to designate a boundary with one or two marks. Starting from three, it is permissible to designate a boundary even with a hundred marks of the types mentioned. The Vinaya expert (Vinayadhara) should ask: 'What is the mark in the eastern direction?' When it is answered: 'A mountain, venerable sir,' the Vinaya expert himself should announce the mark thus: 'This mountain is the mark.' However, it is not permissible to announce it as: 'We make this mountain the mark,' 'We will make it the mark,' 'The mark is made,' 'Let it be the mark,' 'It is,' or 'It will be.' The same applies to stones and other marks. Therefore, it is said: 'What is the mark in the eastern direction?' and so on. Whether an ordained monk or an unordained person (layperson or novice) says, 'A mountain, venerable sir,' or 'Water, venerable sir,' it is permissible.

By the word 'and so on' (ādi), it includes the following: 'What is the mark in the south-eastern intermediate direction? A stone, venerable sir. This stone is the mark. What is the mark in the southern direction, the south-western intermediate direction, the western direction, the north-western intermediate direction, the northern direction, and the north-eastern intermediate direction? Water, venerable sir. This water is the mark.' Here, without stopping at the north-eastern intermediate direction, one must again announce the first announced mark: 'What is the mark in the eastern direction? A mountain, venerable sir. This mountain is the mark,' and only then stop. Only in this way are mark and mark connected. 'Having announced well' means announcing according to the method mentioned, without confusing the names of the marks or using names of things that are not marks. 'Designated' (sammatā) refers to a boundary bound by a pure formal act consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiyakammavācā) as described in the Uposathakkhandhaka, starting with 'Venerable sir, let the Saṅgha listen to me.' In that case, even if the marks are announced only once, they are considered announced. In the Andhaka Commentary, however, it is stated that the marks should be announced three times while connecting the boundary circuit.

'Therein' (tatra) refers to those eight types of marks. 'Qualifying as a mark' (nimittūpagatā) means suitability to be a mark. According to the statement 'starting from the size of an elephant,' a stone the size of an elephant is suitable as a mark. An elephant is seven or seven and a half cubits in height. 'Smaller than that' means a size significantly smaller than the size of an elephant. If there are four or three mountains in the four directions, it is permissible to designate the boundary with those four or three mountain-marks. However, it is not permissible to designate it with only two marks or one. The same principle applies to stone-marks and others remaining after the mountain-mark. Therefore, one who wishes to make a mountain a mark should ask: 'Is it one continuous piece or not?'
139:
If the mountain is continuous (ekābaddha), it should not be designated as a marker. This is because even if one proclaims it in four or eight directions, it is considered as proclaiming only a single marker. Therefore, if a mountain exists surrounding a monastery in a circular fashion, one should proclaim that mountain in one direction, and for the remaining directions, one should place that mountain on the outside and proclaim other markers located within.

If one wishes to include one-third or one-half of a mountain within the Sīmā, one should not proclaim the mountain itself as the marker; instead, for whatever extent one wishes to include within, one should proclaim one of the markers such as a tree or an anthill growing upon that very mountain beyond that area. If one wishes to include an entire mountain measuring one or two yojanas within, one should proclaim markers such as trees or anthills growing on the ground outside the mountain.

"Saṅkhaṃ gacchati" means it arrives at the reckoning or designation. "The size of a ball of molasses weighing 32 palas" should be understood by its bulk, not by its actual weighed weight. In this regard, they say, "One pala is ten kalañjas." Even if a brick is large, it is not suitable as a marker. Likewise, a pile of stones that does not qualify as a marker, or a pile of earth or sand, are even more unsuitable. A flat rock (piṭṭhipāsāṇa) that is level with the ground like a threshing floor, or a stone protruding from the ground like a stump, is suitable if it meets the required size. It is stated, "A flat rock, even if very large, only reaches the designation of a stone," starting with "Piṭṭhipāsāṇa pana." Therefore, if one wishes to include a portion of a large flat rock within the Sīmā, one should not proclaim that flat rock but should proclaim another stone situated upon it. If a monastery is built upon a flat rock and that rock passes through the middle of the monastery, such a flat rock is not suitable. For if one proclaims it, the monastery would be situated above the marker; since a marker must always be outside the Sīmā, the monastery would also end up outside the Sīmā. However, a flat rock that surrounds a monastery should be proclaimed in one place and must not be proclaimed in another.

Regarding forest markers (vananimitta), it is stated starting with "Antosārehi" that a grass forest or a forest of trees with only bark-core is not suitable. "Antosāra" (inner-core trees) refers to trees such as mango, rose-apple, jackfruit, and so on. "Antosāramissakehi" means with trees that are mixed with inner-core trees. "Even if only four or five trees" means...
140:
...the minimum limit has been stated. As for the maximum, a forest even a hundred yojanas in size is suitable as a marker. In this context, if it is a forest of only four trees, three must be core-wood trees and one must be a non-core tree. If it is a forest of five trees, it should be understood that three must be core-wood trees and two must be non-core trees. However, if a monastery is built in the middle of a forest, that forest should not be proclaimed as a marker. Those who wish to include a portion of the forest within the Sīmā should not proclaim the forest itself but should proclaim the trees, stones, etc., within that forest. A forest that surrounds a monastery should be proclaimed in one place and must not be proclaimed in another.

Regarding tree markers (rukkhanimitta), it is stated "Antosāro" because a tree with only bark-core is not suitable. The phrase "established in the ground" excludes trees kept in pots or jars. However, if it is removed from those pots, planted in the ground even at the moment of the Sīmā consecration, fenced, and watered, it is suitable to be proclaimed; the emergence of new roots and branches is not a necessary condition. However, in the case of a tree planted by cutting the trunk, this emergence of new roots and branches is appropriate. "The size of a stylus" is said by teachers to be the size of a writing stylus used in the island of Sīhala; it should be understood as being approximately the size of the little finger. A monk proclaiming this tree marker is permitted to say "tree," or "teak tree," or "sal tree." A tree like a well-established banyan that is continuous (ekābaddha) should be proclaimed in one place and must not be proclaimed in another.

Regarding road markers (magganimitta), it is stated starting with "Jaṅghamaggo vā hotu" because roads leading to forests, fields, rivers, or tanks are not suitable. Any footpath that branches off from a cart road and then rejoins the same cart road, or footpaths and cart roads that are not in use, are not suitable. Therefore, it is said, "By foot-travelers and cart-travelers," and so on. In this matter, if the inner wheel track of a cart road is made the marker, the road remains outside the Sīmā. If the outer wheel track is made the marker, only the outer wheel track is outside the Sīmā, and it should be understood that the rest of the inner road falls within the Sīmā. If two roads branch out and later become one like the pole of a cart, they should be proclaimed only once, either at the point of divergence or at the point of convergence; they must not be proclaimed again. This is because it is a continuous marker.

If four roads surround a monastery and go in four directions, after proclaiming one road in the middle, it is not suitable to proclaim another. This is because it is a continuous marker. However, a road that passes through the corner of the monastery compound may be proclaimed on the other side of the crossing.
141:
A path that passes through the center of a monastery should not be proclaimed (as a boundary marker). If it were proclaimed, it would be because the monastery is situated above the marker. A monk proclaiming this path may use any of the ten names mentioned (in the Cūḷaniddesa), such as "Magga, Pajja, Patha," etc. A path that encircles a monastery in the form of a moat should not be proclaimed in one place and then proclaimed again in another place.

In explaining the characteristics of an unfortified boundary (abaddha-sīmā), the statement "I shall speak of the river" was made (by the author of the Saṅgaha) because the characteristics of a river in a water-thrown boundary (udakukkhepa-sīmā) will be discussed with the words "Yassā dhammikānaṃ rājūnaṃ kāle," etc. If a river flows encircling a monastery in the shape of a cart-axle or in the shape of a moat, like a path, it should not be proclaimed in one place and then proclaimed again in another. The same principle applies to a confluence of four rivers that pass through each other in the four directions of a monastery. However, four separate rivers that do not intermingle may be proclaimed (as markers). If one sinks wooden posts as if making a fence and blocks the river's current with vines, straw, etc., but the water still overflows that obstruction and flows as usual, it is proper to use it as a marker. However, if a bridge is constructed in such a way that the water cannot flow, a river that does not flow is not proper to be used as a marker. It is proper to use it as a river-marker in places where water flows, and as a water-marker in places where it does not flow.

A river that does not flow due to lack of water during a drought or in the summer is proper (as a marker). People dig a canal from a large river; that canal, being like a small river, flows constantly, providing for three types of crops. Although it flows constantly, it is not proper to use it as a marker (as it is not a natural river). However, if a canal that originally came from a large river eventually breaks away from the river along its original course and flows by itself, and further along it becomes a river teeming with crocodiles and the like, navigable by boats and ships, then that canal is proper to be used as a marker.

'Asandamānaṃ' means not flowing. 'Sandamānaṃ' refers to water in rivers, torrents, and canals. 'Vuttaparicchedakālaṃ atitthantaṃ' means remaining without exceeding the specified period, which is "remaining until the conclusion of the Kammavācā." 'Bhājanagataṃ' refers to water contained in vessels such as boats, jars, and the like. The statement in the Andhaka Commentary that "water that must be drawn from deep wells and the like should not be used as a marker" is...
142:
...stated incorrectly; it is merely the commentator's own opinion. In fact, even water in a pig's wallow or in a play-pool of village children is valid as a marker, whether it be little or much, provided it remains until the conclusion of the Kammavācā. In such a place, for the purpose of establishing the perception of a marker, a heap of stones, sand, or earth, or a stone pillar or wooden post should be placed.

Having thus shown the endowment with the perfection of markers, the author now says "Parisāsampattiyā yuttā nāmā," etc., to show the factors by which a designated boundary is said to be endowed with the perfection of the assembly. Since this act (kamma) is to be performed by a group of four, it is said "by four monks" (catūhi bhikkhūhi). Monks wishing to bind this boundary should inquire about the boundary limits of the various nearby monasteries. They should leave an inter-boundary space (sīmantarika) for the boundaries of monasteries with fortified boundaries (baddha-sīmā), and a precinct (upacāra) for the boundaries of monasteries with unfortified boundaries (abaddha-sīmā). At a time when traveling monks are not on the move, if they wish to bind a boundary within a single village territory, they should send word to the monks in the monasteries with fortified boundaries there, saying, "We will bind a boundary today; do not go outside your respective boundary limits."

Monks in monasteries with unfortified boundaries should be gathered together in one place, and the consent (chanda) of those entitled to give consent should be brought. Therefore, it is said "Yāvatikā tasmiṃ gāmakhette," etc. "In that village territory" (tasmiṃ gāmakhette) means the village territory where they stand and recite the Kammavācā. The Elder Mahāsumma said, "If they wish to include other village territories within the boundary, the monks residing in those villages must also come; the consent of those who cannot come must be brought." However, the Elder Mahāpaduma said, "Various village territories are like separate fortified boundaries; therefore, consent and purity (chanda-pārisuddhi) do not come from those territories." He further stated, "Only the monks who have entered within the markers must come." He then added, "At the time of designating a Samānasaṃvāsaka boundary, both coming and not coming are allowable. But at the time of designating an Avippavāsa boundary, those who have entered within the markers must come, and the consent of those who cannot come must be brought."

Now, to show the factors by which a designated boundary is said to be endowed with the perfection of the Kammavācā, he says "Kammavācāsampattiyā yuttā nāmā," etc. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), the remainder of the Pali text is included: "If it seems proper to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should designate a boundary of common communion and a single Uposatha with these markers. This is the motion (ñatti). Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. As many markers have been proclaimed in the eight directions around the boundary, the Saṅgha [designates] a common communion with as many markers..."
143:
“May the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. As many marks as have been proclaimed all around, by these marks the Saṅgha authorizes the boundary for common communion and a single Uposatha. If the authorization of the boundary for common communion and a single Uposatha by these marks is pleasing to a certain venerable one, let him remain silent. If it is not pleasing to him, let him speak. The boundary for common communion and a single Uposatha has been authorized by the Saṅgha by these marks. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent. Thus I record this act of the Saṅgha.” This encompasses the remaining Pali text. The word “vuttāya” refers to that which was spoken in the Uposathakkhandhaka (referring to the Kammavācā). “Pure” means (by a Kammavācā) that is free from defects in the motion (ñatti) and the proclamation (anussāvana).

## Khaṇḍasīmā
Khaṇḍasīmā refers to a small boundary. A boundary authorized for the purpose of common communion is called a Samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā. A boundary authorized for the purpose of being able to reside without being separated from one’s robes is called an Avippavāsa-sīmā. Among these three types of boundaries, monks who wish to authorize a boundary should first establish a Khaṇḍasīmā to facilitate Saṅgha acts such as the novice ordination (pabbajjā) and higher ordination (upasampadā). Those who establish that Khaṇḍasīmā must know the proper conduct. If it is established in a monastery where all structures such as the Bodhi tree, the cetiyas, and the refectory have already been built, it should not be established in the center of the monastery where many people gather, but rather in a secluded area at the edge of the monastery. Those who establish it in a place where the monastery has not yet been built should mark the locations for all structures such as the Bodhi tree and cetiyas, so that when the buildings are completed, the boundary will be in a secluded area at the edge of the monastery. That Khaṇḍasīmā is valid if it can accommodate at minimum twenty-one monks. If it accommodates fewer than that, it is not valid. If it accommodates more than a thousand monks, it is also valid. Those who establish that boundary should place stones as marks (nimitta) around the boundary pavilion (sīmā-maṇḍapa). Monks standing within a Khaṇḍasīmā must not establish a Mahāsīmā, and monks standing within a Mahāsīmā must not establish a Khaṇḍasīmā. Only by standing within a Khaṇḍasīmā should a Khaṇḍasīmā be established; only by standing within a Mahāsīmā should a Mahāsīmā be established.

In establishing that boundary, this is the procedure: Having proclaimed the marks all around as “This stone is a mark,” the boundary should be authorized by the Kammavācā. Thereafter, to reinforce that very boundary, the Avippavāsa Kammavācā should be recited. In this way, if the Kammavācā is performed twice, those who come with the intention to “revoke and destroy the boundary” will not be able to revoke it. After authorizing the boundary, stones for the inter-boundary space (sīmantarikā) should be placed outside the boundary. The inter-boundary space is valid even if it is at minimum four finger-breadths in measure. If the monastery is large, two, three, or even more Khaṇḍasīmās may be established.
144:
After authorizing the Khaṇḍasīmā in this manner, when authorizing the Mahāsīmā, the monks who have come out of the Khaṇḍasīmā and are standing in the Mahāsīmā, circling around, should proclaim the inter-boundary stones as marks. Then, having proclaimed the remaining marks, the monks, without leaving the forearm's reach (hatthepāsa), should authorize the Samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā by the Kammavācā, and to reinforce that boundary, the Avippavāsa Kammavācā should also be recited. Only by doing this will monks who come with the intention to “revoke and destroy the boundary” be unable to revoke it. If one proclaims the marks of the Khaṇḍasīmā, then the marks of the inter-boundary space, and then the marks of the Mahāsīmā, and after proclaiming the marks in these three places, whichever boundary they desire first, it is permissible to establish that boundary first. Even so, they should be established starting from the Khaṇḍasīmā according to the method already mentioned.

When the boundaries are established in this way, monks standing in the Khaṇḍasīmā do not invalidate the acts of monks performing a Saṅgha act in the Mahāsīmā; nor do monks standing in the Mahāsīmā invalidate the acts of those performing an act in the Khaṇḍasīmā. Monks standing in the inter-boundary space (sīmantarikā) also do not invalidate the acts of those performing acts in both boundaries. However, monks standing in the inter-boundary space do invalidate the acts of those performing an act while standing in the village territory (gāmakhetta). This is because the inter-boundary space depends on the village territory. When the authorization of the Avippavāsa-sīmā is performed, that boundary is called the Avippavāsa-sīmā. Therefore, it is said, “It is a variety of that very boundary.” “Of that very boundary” means of the established boundary (baddhasīmā).

This is the distinction: Because of the statement “excepting the village and the village precinct (gāmūpacāra),” the Avippavāsa-sīmā does not extend into the village or the village precinct, whereas the Samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā does extend into those places. Among these boundaries, the Samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā extends by its own nature, while the Avippavāsa-sīmā extends only where the Samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā exists. This is because there is no separate proclamation of marks for that Avippavāsa-sīmā. In that place, if a village exists at the time of authorizing the Avippavāsa-sīmā, the Avippavāsa-sīmā does not extend into that village. However, if a village is settled later within the authorized boundary, that village also comes to be reckoned as part of the boundary. Just as a village settled later becomes part of the boundary, so too does an area that expands later from a village settled earlier become part of the boundary. If houses have been built at the time of authorizing the boundary and there is the intention that “we shall dwell there,” but people have not yet entered, or if people have abandoned an old village along with the houses and gone elsewhere, that place is indeed not a village, and the boundary extends into it. If even a single family has entered or remains without leaving, it is indeed a village, and the boundary does not extend into it.
145:
Having thus shown the bound boundary (baddhasīmā), the author now says "Abaddhasīmā pana," etc., wishing to show the unbound boundary (abaddhasīmā). The village itself is the boundary; therefore, it is called a village boundary (gāmasīmā). Here, by the term "village," it should be understood that market towns (nigama) and cities (nagara) are also included. In whatever area the village headmen (gāmabhojaka) receive tribute (bali) for that village, whether that area be small or large, it is called a single village precinct (gāmakkhetta). Even within a single village precinct, if the king demarcates a certain area saying, "Let this be a separate village," and grants it to someone, that area also becomes a separate village boundary (visuṃgāmasīmā). Therefore, both that visuṃgāmasīmā and the other ordinary village boundary (pakatigāmasīmā) are just like a baddhasīmā. However, they do not specifically receive the privilege of being separate from the three robes (ticīvaravippavāsa).

"Agāmake araññe" (in a forest without a village) refers to a forest such as the Vindhya forest.
