Therefore, the author says "Agāmakaṃ nāma," etc. This forest boundary (araññasīmā) also receives the privilege of being separate from the three robes. "Macchabandhānaṃ" means of the fishermen. "Agamanapathesu" refers to paths that are impassable. It means those journeys where it is not possible to go and return on the very same day. On this side of the limit of their journey, however, it falls under the designation of a village boundary (gāmasīmā). In that place, it is not proper to perform a formal act (kamma) without clearing the village boundary. "Mazzhe ṭhitānaṃ sabbadisāsu sattabbhantarā" means seven abbhantaras in all directions from the standing place of the monks situated in the middle. "Tattha" means within those abbhantaras.

"Tasmā" is said because it increases by the power of the assembly. "Upacāratthāya" means for the sake of the boundary's precinct (sīmūpacāra). "Sīmābhāvaṃ paṭikkhipitvā" means by rejecting the state of being a baddhasīmā. Because there is shared communion in this boundary, it is called "samānasāṃvāsa." Because there is a single Uposatha in this boundary, it is called "ekūposatha." Here, because the Uposatha is taken separately, the state of shared communion should be understood by the power of the remaining formal acts. "Vuttā" means what was said in the Uposathakkhandhaka to show the definition of the unbound boundary. The recurring half-month is called "anvaḍḍhamāsaṃ," meaning every half-month. The same should be understood for terms such as "anudasāhaṃ" (every ten days).

"Deve" refers to the rain. The phrase "valāhakesu vigatamattesu" is in the locative case (bhumma) used in the sense of one action marking another action. "Sotaṃ" refers to the current of water. "Descending by a landing place or by a non-landing place" is the remaining text. "Timandalaṃ paṭicchādetvā" means dressing so as to cover the three circles (the knees and the navel). "Uttarantiyā" refers to one who crosses at any given place. In the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga, because the characteristic of a river appears in the Pāḷi by the power of a nun, it is said "bhikkhuniyā" (by a nun), but not because of any special existence.
146:
"Not made by someone digging" (natural) means, at the very least, not even made by an animal digging. "Breaking a river or the ocean" means breaking the riverbank or the sea-shore (to let water flow). "This is the characteristic" refers to the characteristic stated in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-aṭṭhakathā Nidānavannanā: "In which river water remains during the described rainy season." A salt-water lake also falls under the designation of a natural lake (jātassara). In a jātassara, if there is no water for drinking or for washing hands and feet as soon as the rain stops during the described rainy season, and it dries up, that jātassara falls only under the designation of a village precinct (gāmakkhetta).

In the word "udakukkhepa," the author of the Saṅgaha says "udakukkhepena" (by a water-splash) because the ablative case (nissakkavacana) is used in the instrumental sense (karaṇattha). Regarding the question of how the water should be thrown, the author says "Tattha," etc. "By a man of average stature" means a man of average strength. "This is called udakukkhepa" means this area is called a boundary defined by a water-splash. As much as the assembly increases, so much does this boundary increase. From the edge of the assembly, the water-splash itself is the measure. If, however, the river is not very long and the Saṅgha sits everywhere from the source to the mouth, there is no need for the water-splash boundary act. The entire river is sufficient for those monks.

"Pakativassakāle" (during the normal rainy season) means the rainy season of the nature previously described. "In the four months" means in the four months of the rainy season. An area covered by a flood during a time of excessive rain should not be taken as the boundary. This is because such an area falls only under the designation of a village boundary (gāmasīmā). This same decision should be understood regarding stone slabs, rocks, and small islands that emerge within a river or a natural lake. If the river is full to the brim, the formal act of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma) should be performed within the river itself, even while wearing a water-robe (udakasāṭika). If it cannot be performed in the river, it should be performed while standing on a boat. However, it is not proper to perform it on a moving boat. Why? Because the measure of the water-splash alone is the boundary, and the boat quickly passes that boundary. In such a case, the motion (ñatti) would be in one boundary and the proclamation (anussāvana) would be in another; therefore, the formal act should be performed by stopping the boat with a pole, or by dropping a stone (anchor), or by tying it to a tree growing in the river. It is proper for monks standing on a scaffold (aṭṭaka) built in the river or on a tree growing in the river to perform the formal act.

If, however, a branch of the tree or an aerial root (parāroha) emerging from it rests upon a monastery boundary (vihārasīmā) or a village boundary (gāmasīmā) on the riverbank, then either by clearing the boundary or...
147:
One should perform the act (kamma) even by cutting a branch. It is not allowable to perform the act by tying a boat to a branch or an aerial root of a tree growing outside the riverbank that has entered into the river. Those performing the act must clear the boundary (sīmā), or else they must cut the branch and destroy the part of the tree situated outside the river. It is certainly not allowable to perform the act in a boat tied to a stump driven into the riverbank. 

People build bridges over rivers; if the bridge or the bridge pillars are situated within the river, it is allowable to perform the act while standing on the bridge. However, if the bridge or the bridge pillars are situated outside the bank, it is not allowable to perform the act; one must clear the boundary and then perform the act. If the bridge pillars are within the river but the bridge itself is in the air above both banks, it is allowable. This same method applies to a natural lake (jātassara). 

By the words "in the place where the natural waves overflow and stay," it is shown (in the Mahāvagga Commentary, 147) that it is not allowable to perform the act in a place where overflowing water or natural waves come with force and overflow. If the force of the waves interferes, one should perform it while standing in a boat or on a platform. The decision regarding those boats and platforms should be understood in the same way as mentioned for the river. 

If the ocean overflows and stays over a village boundary (gāmasīmā) or a market-town boundary (nigamasīmā), it becomes the ocean itself. It is allowable to perform the act there. From that point onwards, from the edge of the water that stays overflowing, the inner part is called a river, a natural lake, or the ocean, meaning it is allowable ground (kappiyabhūmi). 

"In the time of drought" refers to the rainy and winter seasons. "Even when dry" means even when there is no water. Just as in the case of digging a tank, when digging wells, ponds, etc., it should be noted that it remains village land (gāmakhetta). "They practice cultivation" means they cultivate gourds, cucumbers, etc. That place is where the tank, etc., was made. Other places, however, are allowable ground (kappiyabhūmi). 

If they fill a natural lake with earth to make dry land, or if they build an embankment on one side and make the whole thing a large tank, it all becomes a non-natural lake (ajātassara). It simply falls under the name of village boundary (gāmasīmā). If they even destroy a river to make a tank, and an embankment is built below so that water comes and fills the tank and stays there, it is not allowable to perform the act here. From the place where the water overflowing from the tank flows into the river in the upper reaches, it is allowable. If a certain river, after a long time, rises and flows overflowing a village or market-town boundary...
148:
...it remains a river, and it is allowable to perform the act. If it overflows a monastery boundary (vihārasīmā), it is known only as "vihārasīmā." This is because the river has entered within. The phrase "a water-splashing limit should be made all around" is said with reference to a place sufficient for such a limit. In cases like small rivers where a water-splashing distance is not possible, the water-splashing limit should be made starting from a sufficient place. "For the sake of upacāra" means for the sake of the boundary's vicinity. 

Why should another sattabbhantara and another udakukkhepa be set aside for the sake of upacāra? It is said, "Ayaṃ hi," etc. The meaning is this: these sattabbhantara-sīmā and udakukkhepa-sīmā are obtained starting from the place where the monks are standing. Those monks are not always the same in number; sometimes they increase, and sometimes they decrease. When the monks increase, boundary overlap (sīmā-saṅkara) can occur. Therefore, another sattabbhantara and another udakukkhepa should be set aside for the sake of upacāra. 

What is said in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, "If it is more than that, it is certainly allowable; if it is less, it is not allowable," is also for this purpose; it should not be taken as meaning that the act performed there is invalid. "One who stands outside the limit without exceeding that much of a limit" means even if one stands outside the limit of their sattabbhantara or udakukkhepa without exceeding that much of a limit of those monks' sattabbhantara or udakukkhepa. How is this known? It is said, "This is the conclusion in all commentaries." This means it is the definition in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, etc., that "it invalidates the act." "Iti imaṃ," etc., is the conclusion of what has been said. There is a verse here: 

"In this Dispensation, Sīmā is of two kinds: Baddha (bound) and Abaddha (unbound). 
The Baddha-sīmā, which is endowed with the three successes (sampatti) and avoids the eleven failures (vipatti), is of three types: Khaṇḍa-sīmā, etc. 
The Abaddha-sīmā, other than the Baddha-sīmā, is also of three types: Gāma-sīmā, etc." 

Sabhāgāpatti (common offense) is of two kinds: vatthu-sabhāga (common in basis) and āpatti-sabhāga (common in offense). Here, vatthu-sabhāga is intended; to show it is not the other, it is said, "Yaṃ sabbo saṅgho vikālabhojanādinā," etc. "Lahukāpatti" (light offenses) refers to the five classes of offenses known as thullaccaya, pācittiya, pāṭidesanīya, dukkaṭa, and dubbhāsita, because they can be purified by a light disciplinary act. Even if there is a saṅghādisesa offense which is vatthu-sabhāga, the Uposatha act is certainly not "pattakalla" (timely and proper).
149:
It is stated in the Commentary: "It is not proper to reveal [that offense] in the presence of a monk who has committed a common (sabhāga) saṅghādisesa offense. If one does reveal it, the offense is indeed revealed, but one is not released from the dukkaṭa offense." This is said because that (saṅghādisesa) offense cannot be purified merely by confession (desanā). Commonality of the basis (vatthusabhāga) means an offense that has a similar portion in terms of the basis, meaning it belongs to the same category. It is not proper to confess this very vatthusabhāga offense because it was said (in the Mahāvagga): "Monks, a common (sabhāga) offense should not be confessed; whoever should confess it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)." However, it is not that one cannot confess a commonality of the offense (āpattisabhāga). Therefore, it is said: "If an offense is committed due to the factor of eating at the wrong time," and so forth. Commonality of the offense (āpattisabhāga) means having a similar portion in terms of the offense.

'Neighboring residences' (sāmantā āvāsā) means a nearby monastery or a residence in the vicinity. 'Immediately' (sajjuka) means for the purpose of returning on that very day. 'Should be sent' (pāhetabbō) means he should be dispatched. "If it is so, it is good" means that obtaining a monk (to settle the offense) in this way is very excellent and is a proper attainment. "If he is not obtained" means if (a monk to settle the offense) is not obtained due to the distance of the monasteries or due to dangers on the road. By the words "he will settle it in the presence of that monk," it is shown that even the revealing (confession) of a common offense cannot be performed. If (a monk) is obtained, one should perform the Uposatha only after revealing the offense. However, if the entire Saṅgha has committed a common saṅghādisesa offense, it is not proper to perform the Uposatha by setting a motion (ñatti); it would only be an obstacle to the Uposatha. Both (the one confessing and the one receiving) incur a dukkaṭa offense because it was said: "Monks, a common offense should not be confessed; for him who confesses it, there is a dukkaṭa. Monks, a common offense should not be accepted; for him who accepts it, there is a dukkaṭa." 'Vimati' means doubt; one who is possessed of that doubt is called 'vemātika'. The statement "When one is again free from doubt, it must certainly be confessed" is found neither in the Pāḷi nor in the Commentary; however, there is no fault in confessing it. In the same manner as already mentioned, such as "Venerable sirs, let the members announce their purity," a monk with an offense who performs the Uposatha incurs the prescribed dukkaṭa offense. As to why only the common offense (sabhāga) is mentioned, it is said: "In these offenses," and so forth. Even if there are uncommon (visabhāga) offenses, the Uposatha is still valid (pattakalla). If there are uncommon offenses, the offense lies only with those individuals and not with the Saṅgha; therefore, the Saṅgha's act is indeed valid.

'One who has committed an ultimate offense' (antimavatthu ajjhāpannaka) refers to one who has committed any one of the four Pārājika offenses. The decision regarding eunuchs (paṇḍaka) and others will be made clear later in the Pārājika section...
150:
Regarding 'animal' (tiracchāna), it should be understood as any being of non-human birth (amanussa), starting from even Sakka, the king of devas, down to young Nāgas and the like; it does not refer to horses, cattle, and so on. Therefore, it is said: "And in this case," and so forth. In that context, "in this case" refers to this discussion on persons to be excluded. As to whose ordination is prohibited: "Monks, an animal is unordained and should not be ordained" (Mahāvagga 111). As stated, the ordination of such animals as Nāgas, Supaṇṇas, etc., is prohibited; such a being is also called an 'animal' in this context. In that statement, starting from even the devas, any being of non-human birth such as a young Nāga is intended by the term 'animal'. For it is said in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary: "Monks, regarding 'animal' in this context, whether it be a Nāga or any one of the young Supaṇṇas, etc., or any being of non-human birth starting from even Sakka, the king of devas—all of them should be understood as 'animal' in this sense" (Mahāvagga Commentary 111). A doctrine is called 'tittha'; those who hold that doctrine are 'titthika'; 'titthika' are the same as 'titthiya', meaning those who hold doctrines other than this Dispensation.

The recitation of the Sutta is called 'suttuddesa'. Since purity itself is the Uposatha, it is called 'pārisuddhi-uposatha'. This same method should be understood for the term 'adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha'. The term 'so' refers to the recitation of the Pātimokkha. Exhortation itself is the Pātimokkha; the recitation of that Pātimokkha in its own form is called 'ovāda-pātimokkhuddesa'. Commanding or prescribing by way of offenses, such as "If one commits this transgression, there is an offense of such a name," is called 'āṇā' (command); the remaining words are the same as what was said immediately before.

"Patience is the highest austerity..." and so forth. The three verses are as follows:

"Patience, which is long-suffering, is the highest austerity;
The Buddhas say Nibbāna is supreme.
One who strikes another is not a renunciant;
One who harms another is not a recluse.

Not doing any evil, the attainment of the wholesome,
And the purification of one's own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas."
151:
“Not reviling, not harming, restraint in the Pātimokkha, moderation in eating, secluded lodgings, and devotion to the higher mind; this is the teaching of the Buddhas.” These are the three verses.

Among those verses, “khantī paramaṃ tapo” means that the patience known as patient endurance (adhivāsana-khantī) is the supreme practice of austerity (tapa). “Titikkhā” is simply a synonym for patience (khantī); the meaning is that patient endurance, called titikkhā, is the most excellent austerity. “Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ vadanti” means the Buddhas declare Nibbāna to be supreme in every way. “Na hi pabbajito parūpaghātī” means that one who, because of lacking patient endurance, harms or oppresses others, is not called a renunciant (pabbajita). The fourth line is a synonym for that same third line. The synonym for the phrase “na hi pabbajito” is “na samaṇo hoti” (he is not a recluse). The synonym for the word “parūpaghātī” is “paraṃ viheṭhayanto” (one who harasses others).

Alternatively, “parūpaghātī” means one who destroys virtue (sīlūpaghātī). Virtue is called “para” (supreme) because of its most excellent nature. If a recluse (samaṇa) harms any other living being and thus destroys his own virtue, he is not called a renunciant (pabbajita).

Alternatively, if a person, due to the absence of patient endurance, harms others and intentionally takes the life of another, even down to a mosquito or a gadfly, he is not a renunciant. Why? Because he has not yet expelled his stains. “One expels one's own stains, therefore one is called a ‘renunciant’ (pabbajita)”—this is the characteristic of a renunciant. Even if one does not kill but still harasses others with sticks, etc., that person who harasses others is not a recluse (samaṇa). Why? Because his harassment has not been calmed. “Because of having calmed all evils, one is called a ‘recluse’ (samaṇa)”—this is the characteristic of a recluse.

In the second verse, “sabbapāpassa” means of all unwholesome states. “Akaraṇaṃ” means not bringing them into existence (not doing). “Kusalassa” means of the wholesome states belonging to the four planes. “Upasampadā” means fulfillment or attainment. “Sacittapariyodapanaṃ” means purifying one's own mind, making it radiant, and cleansing it in every way; that purification of the mind occurs through the Path of Arahantship. Thus, having abandoned all evil through the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara), and having fulfilled the wholesome through mundane and supramundane tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā), one should purify the mind through the Fruit of Arahantship; this is the teaching, the advice, and the instruction of the Buddhas.
152:
In the third verse, “anūpavādo” means not reviling anyone through the door of speech. “Anūpaghāto” means not committing the act of harming or killing anyone through the door of the body. “Pātimokkha” refers to the virtue that is noble in various ways, exceedingly noble, and supreme. Alternatively, it is called “Pātimokkha” because it protects (pāti) from specific bad destinations and liberates (mokkheti) from the fears of woeful states. Or, because that person protects that virtue, and that virtue liberates that person from danger, it is called “Pātimokkha.” In that Pātimokkha. “Saṃvaro” means restraint characterized by the non-transgression of the seven classes of offenses. “Mattaññutā” means knowing the measure in terms of receiving and using the four requisites. “Pantā sayanāsanaṃ” means dwelling in secluded lodgings that are free from the crowding of people and are solitary.

In this verse, it should be understood that by mentioning only the two requisites of alms-food and lodgings, contentment with all four requisites is shown. This is because, by the similarity of contentment with requisites, the other two—robes and medicine—are also illuminated by the method of characteristic-induction (lakkhaṇāhāra-naya). “Adhicitte ca āyogo” means the mind of the eight attainments which is the basis for insight, and even more so, the mind of the Path and Fruit is called “higher mind” (adhicitta); “āyoga” in that aforementioned higher mind means initial application and repeated practice. “Etaṃ buddhāna sāsanaṃ” means that this non-reviling of others, non-harming, restraint in the Pātimokkha, knowing the measure in receiving and using requisites, and dwelling in secluded lodgings for the sake of mastery in the eight attainments, is the teaching, the advice, and the instruction of the Buddhas. It should be understood that these three verses are the verses for the recitation of the Pātimokkha (Pātimokkhuddesa) of all Buddhas. Only the Buddhas recite them, not the disciples.

The recitation spoken of in the manner beginning with “Listen to me, venerable sirs, the Saṅgha” is called the “Pātimokkha of Authority” (āṇā-pātimokkha). Only the disciples perform that Pātimokkha of Authority. The Buddhas do not perform the legal acts of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma), nor are they included within them; therefore, the commentator said, “Only the disciples perform it, not the Buddhas.” “Imasmiṃ atthe” means in this sense of “one should recite the Pātimokkha.”

“Anupagato” refers to one who was ordained right there [during the later rains] or one who did not enter the first rains due to forgetfulness. “Cātumāsiniyaṃ” means on the Cātumāsiya (the full moon day of Kattika). Because that full moon day marks the completion of four months, it is called “Cātumāsī”; that same day is called “Cātumāsinī.” In that Cātumāsinī means on the full moon day of the later Kattika month. “Kāyasamaggi” means unity of the body, which means coming within the reach of the hand (hatthapāsa).

Here is the decision (vinicchaya): If five monks entered the first rains, and five monks also entered the later rains, when the five monks of the first rains have performed the invitation (pavāraṇā) after setting aside the motion (ñatti)...
153:
Monks who entered the later rainy season retreat (pacchimikā vassa) should perform the pārisuddhi-uposatha in the presence of those who entered the earlier rainy season retreat (purimikā vassa). Two motions (ñatti) should not be proposed in a single Uposatha hall. If there are four, three, two, or one monk who entered the later retreat, the same rule applies. If there are four monks in the earlier retreat and four, three, two, or one in the later retreat, the same rule applies. If there are three monks in the earlier retreat and three or two in the later retreat, the same rule applies.

The defining characteristic here is: if the monks who entered the later retreat are fewer than or equal in number to those who entered the earlier retreat and can complete a group (gaṇa) for Saṅgha-pavāraṇā, the monks of the earlier retreat should perform pavāraṇā by proposing a motion for Saṅgha-pavāraṇā. However, if there are three monks from the earlier retreat and one from the later retreat, although they total four, it is not proper to perform pavāraṇā by proposing a Saṅgha-ñatti. But since that monk from the later retreat completes the group for a gaṇa-ñatti, the monks of the earlier retreat should perform pavāraṇā by proposing a motion for a group (gaṇa). The remaining one (from the later retreat) should perform pārisuddhi-uposatha in their presence. If there are two in the earlier retreat and two or one in the later retreat, the same rule applies. If there is one in the earlier retreat and one in the later retreat, one should perform pavāraṇā in the presence of the other, and the other should perform pārisuddhi-uposatha.

If the monks who entered the later retreat outnumber those who entered the earlier retreat by even one, the Pātimokkha should be recited first, and afterwards, those who are fewer in number should perform pavāraṇā in their presence. Regarding the Pavāraṇā on the full moon day of Kattika, if the monks who entered the retreat later are more than or equal in number to those who entered the retreat earlier and have already performed the Mahā-pavāraṇā, they should perform pavāraṇā by proposing a motion. After they have performed pavāraṇā, the remaining monks should perform pārisuddhi-uposatha. If the monks who performed the Mahā-pavāraṇā are many and those who entered the retreat later are few or only one, after the Pātimokkha has been recited, the one who entered the retreat later should perform pavāraṇā in their presence.

'Ekāṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā' means properly arranging the upper robe over one shoulder. 'Añjaliṃ paggahetvā' means raising the joined palms, which shine with the ten fingernails meeting. If there is also a monk undergoing probation (pārivāsika) there, he should sit in the place of the most junior of the Saṅgha and, while sitting there, perform pārisuddhi-uposatha according to his own text (pāḷi). While the Pātimokkha is being recited, however, he should not sit in the row (pāḷi) but should leave the row and sit without leaving the arm's reach (hatthapāsa). The same rule applies during pavāraṇā.
154:
"Sabbaṃ pubbakaraṇīyaṃ" refers to the ninefold preliminary duties (pubbakicca) such as sweeping and so on. Just as when the entire Saṅgha has fallen into a common offense (sabhāgāpatti), they are allowed to perform Uposatha by proposing the motion: "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs... I shall remedy it"; so too in this case, three monks may perform Uposatha by proposing a group motion (gaṇa-ñatti): "Let the venerable ones hear me, these monks have fallen into a common offense; when they see another pure monk who is free from offense, they will remedy that offense in his presence." Two monks may also perform Uposatha by saying: "When we see another pure monk, we will remedy it." Even a single monk may perform Uposatha by resolving: "When I find a pure monk, I will remedy it."

"Tadahu" means on that day, on that Uposatha day. "Nānāsaṃvāsakehi" means by monks of different communions based on their views. An "anāvāsa" is any place such as a temporary work-hall and so on. "Aññatra saṅghena" means without a sufficient number of monks to form a Saṅgha. "Aññatra antarāyā" means except for the ten dangers mentioned previously. In the final limit, one may go with a group of four including oneself, or if there is danger. Just as one should not go to residences and so on, if they perform Uposatha in a monastery, they should not go to a sīmā or a river for the purpose of resolving the Uposatha. However, if there is any monk in that sīmā or river, it is proper to go to him. It is also proper to go from a monastery where the Saṅgha-uposatha has been abandoned. A monk who goes in this way is also allowed to resolve the Uposatha. 

A forest-dwelling monk (āraññaka) should also return to his own monastery after going for alms in the village on the Uposatha day. If he enters another monastery, he must return only after performing Uposatha there; it is not proper to return without performing it. If he knows, "I can go there this very day," he should go to such a residence. By performing Uposatha together with the monks there, this monk will not be one who creates an obstacle to the Uposatha.

"Udakaṃ āsanena ca" means drinking water and water for use along with the preparation of seats. The preliminary action to be done before the Saṅgha assembles is called pubbakaraṇa. Although it is done after the pubbakaraṇa, it is called pubbakicca because it must be done before the Uposatha rite. Since both are to be done before the Uposatha rite, they are referred to here only as "pubbakicca," as it was said: "Thus, the ninefold preliminary duties are shown by these two names." Regarding the question "Has that preliminary duty been done?", the words beginning with "Na hi" were spoken. It is not proper to perform Uposatha without doing those preliminary duties. "Monks, a monk who is not ill and is commanded by an elder..."
155:
## 
“A healthy monk who is ordered by an elder should not remain without sweeping; if a monk does not sweep, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” and so forth. Because of this word (Mahāvagga, 159), it was said, “Therefore, [a monk] ordered by an elder,” and so forth.

If the monk who is ordered does not obtain even a temporary broom, he should make a suitable one from branches and sweep. For a monk who cannot obtain even such branches, whatever he can manage is considered suitable. “Drinking water and usable water should be set out” means that drinking water and water for general use should be prepared for the sake of incoming guests. “Seats should be prepared” means that seats such as benches and planks should be arranged. If there are no seats in the Uposatha hall, they should be brought from the communal quarters, arranged, and then returned again. If there are no seats, it is proper to spread out mats or carpets. If even carpets are not available, branches should be made suitable and spread out. For a monk who does not have a lay attendant (kappiyakāraka) to make them suitable, whatever he can manage is considered suitable.

“A lamp should be made” means it should be lit; it means the act of lighting a lamp should be performed. The elder who gives the order should say, “In such and such a place, there is oil, a wick, or a lamp-bowl; take it and prepare it.” If oil and such are not available, they should be sought. For a monk who searches and does not find them, whatever he can manage is considered suitable. Indeed, even a fire should be lit in a clay pot. The elder who gives the order should not command a monk who is performing some work, or one who always stays alone, or one who is bearing the burdens of the Sangha, or any among the intoners (sarabhāṇaka) and Dhamma-preachers; rather, the remaining monks should be ordered in turn. Therefore, the author of the Compendium (Saṅgaha) said, “The elder, having known what is appropriate, should give the order.”

“One who comes after performing the Uposatha outside” refers to a monk who has performed the Uposatha in a river, a sīmā, or any other place and then arrives; he must give his consent (chanda). The meaning is that he does not have the right to remain without giving consent by thinking, “I have already performed the Uposatha.” “One busy with duties” refers to one busy with duties such as nursing the sick. If a sick monk is unable to give his consent and purity (chandapārisuddhi), he should be brought into the midst of the Sangha by means of a couch or a bench, and the Uposatha should be performed. If the nursing monks think, “If we move this sick person from his place, his illness will increase or he will pass away,” then that sick person should not be moved from his place; the Sangha should go there and perform the Uposatha. The Uposatha should not be performed by a divided (vagga) Sangha. If they do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If there are many such sick monks, the Sangha should stand in order...
156:
...and all must be kept within the forearm’s length (hatthapāsa). If they are very far apart and the Sangha is insufficient [to bridge the gap], the Uposatha should not be performed on that day; the Uposatha must not be performed by a divided (vagga) Sangha. Because the Blessed One said, “I allow, monks, one giving purity on the Uposatha day to also give consent if there is business for the Sangha” (Mahāvagga, 165), one following the command of the Buddha says, “I give my consent.” Because of the words, “Monks, if a carrier of consent, after consent has been given, departs from that very place, the consent should be given to another” (Mahāvagga, 165), one says, “Carry my consent,” in order to remove the fatigue of giving one's own consent. Because it was said, “Monks, if a carrier of consent, having reached the Sangha, intentionally does not report the given consent, the consent is [considered] brought, but there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the carrier of consent” (Mahāvagga, 165), one says, “Report my consent,” to free him from that dukkaṭa offense.

“Should be made known by body, by speech, or by both” means that it should be made known or understood by one who, having intended it in the mind, uses a bodily gesture with any limb, or by one who is able to utter words using speech, or by both body and speech if one is able to do both. Because of the phrase “This is the meaning,” it is proper to make it known in any language. In the giving of purity (pārisuddhi), the decision is the same as what was said regarding the giving of consent. However, one giving that [purity] must first confess any existing offenses. Indeed, one who has an offense is not permitted to say, “I give my purity, carry my purity, report my purity” (Mahāvagga, 164). Although it should be said, “There are (santi) duties of the Sangha,” it was said as “There is (santi) duty of the Sangha” (using a singular noun with a plural verb form) by way of grammatical variation. In the context of “He gives the consent and purity of those [monks] and of himself,” the term “chandapārisuddhi” should be understood by the method of sarūpekasesa (where one term represents both consent and purity). “Itarā” refers to the consent and purity of others. In the phrase “biḷālasaṅkhalikā chandapārisuddhi,” “biḷālasaṅkhalikā” means a cat-chain (cat-shackle). In that shackle, the first link of the chain reaches only the second link, not the third; similarly, this consent and purity does not go anywhere else other than to the person to whom it was given by the donor. Therefore, because it is like a cat-chain, it is called “biḷālasaṅkhalikā.” It should be understood that the mention of “biḷālasaṅkhalikā” here is merely an illustration for any kind of chain link.
157: Utukkhāna means the season is called utu because it brings about various activities; announcing that season is utukkhāna, meaning telling the season. To show the manner of telling the season specifically, it says "of the winter, etc." Gaṇanā means counting. Admonishing the bhikkhunīs with the eight Garudhammas is called Bhikkhunovāda. When it is said, "Tomorrow is the Uposatha day," it means they should come today; in a 15-day Uposatha, they come on the 14th day of the fortnight, and in a 14-day Uposatha, they come on the 13th day (to request). However, in the Mahāpaccari, it is stated: "They should come only on the 13th day of the fortnight and ask, 'Venerable sir, is this Uposatha a 14-day or a 15-day one?'" When asked thus, if the monks perform the Uposatha on the 14th day, they should say, "Sister, it is a 14-day Uposatha." If they perform it on the 15th day, they should say, "Sister, it is a 15-day Uposatha." "Monks, I allow the exhortation to be received by the rest, excluding the foolish, the sick, and those about to travel," because of this statement, it says "excluding those persons," etc. Among them, a monk who does not know the procedure for announcing is called bāla (foolish). A monk who wishes to go on the 14th or 15th Uposatha days, or on the day after the Uposatha, is called gamiya (traveler). However, a monk who goes from the second day of the fortnight onwards is not called a gamiya in this context of receiving the exhortation. A monk who dwells in the forest is called āraññika. Such a forest-dwelling monk also does not have the right to think, "I am a forest-dweller, tomorrow is Uposatha, I do not stay in the monastery," and thus not receive the exhortation. If he does not receive it, he would incur a dukkaṭa offense. For it was said: "Monks, the exhortation must not be unreceived; whoever does not receive it, there is an offense of dukkaṭa." That forest-dwelling monk should make an appointment for the purpose of reporting back. For it was said: "Monks, I allow a forest-dwelling monk to receive the exhortation and to make an appointment, saying 'I will report back here'." Therefore, if a forest-dwelling monk can obtain alms in the village where the bhikkhunīs reside, he should wander for alms in that village, and upon seeing the bhikkhunīs, he should announce the exhortation before leaving. If alms are not easily obtained in that village, he should wander for alms in a nearby village and then come to the bhikkhunīs' village and act in the same manner. If he must go to a distant place, he should make an appointment, saying, "I will come to such-and-such a rest house, or a pavilion, or the foot of a tree at your village gate; come to that place." The bhikkhunīs must go to that place; they do not have the right not to go. For it was said: "Monks, a bhikkhunī..."
158: "...must not fail to go to the appointed place (saṅketa); whichever bhikkhunī does not go, there is an offense of dukkaṭa," thus it was said (in the Cūḷavagga). "In the uposathagga" means in the place where the Uposatha is performed. "With eight factors" means: (1) He must be virtuous, living restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint, possessed of proper conduct and resort (ācāra-gocara), seeing danger in even slight faults, and training himself by undertaking the training rules. (2) He must be one of great learning (bahussuta), a bearer of what he has heard, a storer of what he has heard. He must have heard much, retained in mind, practiced verbally, pondered in the mind, and well-penetrated by view those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, which proclaim the holy life (brahmacariya) with its meaning and phrasing, entirely complete and pure. (3) Both Pātimokkhas (for monks and nuns) must be well-mastered by him in detail, well-analyzed, well-recited, and well-ascertained according to the rules and their parts. (4) He must be of pleasant speech and pleasant delivery. (5) He must be generally liked and dear to the bhikkhunīs, one who gladdens their hearts. (6) He must be capable of exhorting the bhikkhunīs. (7) He must not have previously committed a garudhamma (a saṅghādisesa offense) against a bhikkhunī who has gone forth for the sake of the Blessed One and wears the saffron robe. (8) He must have twenty vassas or more than twenty vassas. He must be endowed with these eight factors. "Pāsādikena" means with bodily, verbal, and mental actions that inspire confidence and are faultless. "Sampādetu" means let him fulfill the three types of training (sikkhā). When those bhikkhunīs, seeing only the recitation of the Pātimokkha, request the exhortation, then the Saṅgha of monks assembled in the Uposatha hall, by way of preliminary duties, should ask: "Are there any bhikkhunīs requesting exhortation?" If so, the Pātimokkha reciter should have someone else say the words he himself should say, and then he himself should say, "Is there any monk in the Saṅgha of monks who is appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs?" etc., and then go himself to inform the bhikkhunīs. Or else, he should have another monk recite the Pātimokkha on that day. The plural word "tāhi" refers to the bhikkhunīs who come together. "Ñattitthapakena vā" means if there is no recitation of the Pātimokkha in a place where three monks reside, the announcement is made by the monk who sets the motion (ñatti). "Itarena vā" means in a place where two monks or one monk reside, the announcement is made by the other monk. If he himself is the one appointed as the exhorter of bhikkhunīs, he should say, "I...". It should be said just as it is said in the Uposatha hall. By the words "anāroceတွာ", the act of staying without informing is prohibited. "Monks, the exhortation must not be ungiven; one must not go without informing; whichever bhikkhunī does not inform, there is an offense of dukkaṭa," thus it was said.
159:
(It) should be said. "Tatheva" means just as it was said in the Uposatha hall (sīmā). By this word "ārocetvāva," the act of not informing is prohibited. Because of the words (from the Cūḷavagga Pali), "Monks, the exhortation (ovāda) should not be left uninformed; should any monk not inform, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa)," it is not proper to remain without informing in the Uposatha hall after having received the exhortation. "Parisuddhabhāvaṃ" means the state of being pure from offenses. "Ārocetha" means "make it manifest." "Ettha siyā" means that in this word "I shall recite the Pātimokkha," there might be the following question. "What word might there be?" (The commentator) says, "The Saṅgha should perform the Uposatha," and so on. "Pubbenāparaṃ sandhiyatī" means the preceding word and the following word reach a connection. "Sāmaggiyā" means due to the harmony of body and mind. "Gaṇassa" refers to the remaining monks in the group of four, excluding the reciter. "Saṅghassa uddiṭṭhaṃ hoti" means it is recited by the Saṅgha. Here, the genitive case "saṅghassa" is used in the sense of the instrumental (karaṇa). "Ettha" means in the recitation of the Pātimokkha. "Lakkhaṇaṃ" means the nature (sabhāva).

In this context of "Therā ca navā ca majjhimā ca," monks with ten years of standing and those with more than ten years are Elders (Theras). Monks with less than five years are New Monks (Navas). Monks with five years and those with more than five years are Middle Monks (Majjhimas). "Aṭṭhiṃ katvā" means making oneself benefit from that Pātimokkha, or paying respect by attending to that Pātimokkha as "This is my Pātimokkha." "Manasi karitvā" means keeping it in the mind. "Sotadvāravasena" means by the power of the impulsion consciousness (javana-viññāṇa) occurring at the ear-door. "Sဗ္ဗစေတသာ သမန္နာဟရာမ" (Sabbacetasā samannāharāma) means reflecting and noting well with the entire mind, not allowing the mind to wander outside even a little. "Manasi karoma" means reflecting and paying attention. Such attention (manasikāra) here is not the attention characterized by providing the object, but rather the attention characterized by establishing the mind preceded by the attention that provides the process (vīthi) and the impulsion (javana). Therefore, it is said, "Being of one-pointed mind, we shall keep it in the mind." "Na sameti" means it does not reach harmony. To the question "Why does it not harmonize?", he says, "For the harmonious Saṅgha..." and so on. To the question "What further reason is there?", he says, "And the reciter of the Pātimokkha..." and so on. "Saṅghapariyāpanno" means included within the Saṅgha, or contained within. Now, to show that manner, it is connected thus. "Āyasmanto" is an address to the assembled monks with endearing words.
160:
"Alajjitā" means due to shamelessness or due to the state of being shameless. In fact, this word "alajjitā" is a word in the nominative case (pathamā-vibhatti) used in the sense of the third case (instrumental/causal). This same method should be understood in words such as "aññāṇatā" (ignorance). "Kukkuccappakatatā" means due to the state of being overcome by remorse (kukkucca). "Satisammosā" means due to the loss or lapse of mindfulness. "Vītikkama" means the transgression of a training rule.

"Sañcicca" means having intentionally endeavored and, while knowing it is unallowable, sending forth the mind that is the cause of transgression. "Parigūhati" means he conceals; he does not report (a light offense) or does not emerge (from a heavy offense). It is shown that a monk who conceals an offense out of shame is not called "shameless" (alajjī). Only one who conceals out of disrespect (anādariya), thinking "What will happen by this offense?", is shameless. "Agatigamanañca gacchati" means he also goes to the wrong paths (agati), such as the wrong path of favoritism (chandāgati), in places like the distribution of goods. "Alajjipuggalo" is a person devoid of shame that arises within oneself. Here also, by the word "sañcicca," it is shown that only those who fall into an offense out of disrespect, those who conceal a committed offense, and those who follow the wrong paths in distributing goods are shameless; others are not.

"Mando" means one with little wisdom; this is a name for one without wisdom. "Momūho" means one who is very deluded. "Virādheti" means he does not accomplish or succeed. "Kukkuce" means in doubt regarding the Vinaya (vinaya-saṃsaya). "If an allowable act is to be done" means after questioning a Vinaya expert, and after that Vinaya expert has examined the basis (vatthu), the matrix (mātikā), the word-by-word analysis (padabhājanī), intermediate offenses, and non-offenses, and has said, "Friend, this act is allowable; do not doubt here," then it should be done.

In this Pali "sahaseyya-cīvaravippavāsādīni," "sahaseyyā" refers to the offense incurred by sleeping together with an unordained person for more than two or three nights. "Vippavāso" refers to being away (from robes) by the power of one night, six nights, etc. By the word "ādi," offenses due to exceeding seven days, etc., are included. "Sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ" refers to the seven classes of offenses known as Pārājika, Saṅghādisesa, Thullaccaya, Pācittiya, Pāṭidesanီya, Dukkhaṭa, and Dubbhāsita.

"Desေတု ဝါ ပကာသေတု ဝါ" means confessing or making manifest (the offense) in the midst of the Saṅgha, or in the midst of a group, or in the presence of a single person. Here, the confession of a Pārājika offense means the relinquishing of the state of a monk. However, emerging (vuṭṭhāna) is also to be understood as "confession" (desanā) because it is a specific type of confession. "Pakāsetu vါ" means to inform.

"Evaṃ anāpannā vါ" means an offense not fallen into by one of these six ways. "Vuṭṭhitā vါ" means an offense from which one has emerged through Vinaya procedures such as parivāsa. "Ārocitā vါ" means...
161:
Or it is made manifest. Let the monk who is informing say, "I manifest an offense in your presence," or "I inform you," or "I notify you," or "Know that I have fallen into an offense," or let him say in such a manner as "I manifest a heavy offense"—by all these modes, it is indeed considered informed. However, if a monk wishing to manifest a heavy offense says in such a manner as "I manifest a light offense," that offense is not considered manifested. Whether he informs of the basis (vatthu) of the offense, or informs of the offense itself, or informs of both—by these three ways, it is indeed considered informed. In the phrase "asantiyā āpattiyā," the locative case is in the sense of "bhāvena bhāva-lakkhaṇa" (a state characterizing another state). In the phrase "tuṇhībhāvenāpi," the meaning of the word "api" should be understood as: not only by saying "Venerable sirs, we are pure," but also by remaining silent, (purity) is to be understood.

What is this "announced up to three times" (yāvatatiyānusāvita), and how does it become "announced up to three times"? To show that meaning based on the differences of opinion among the teachers in this investigation, it is said: "yāvatatiyaṃ anusāvitaṃ hotīti ettha," etc. In that statement, it should be understood as connected: "that which is announced up to three times." "Atthavyañjanabhedato" means: because it is understood (ariyanti), it is called "attha" (meaning), which is the thing to be expressed (abhidheyya). Because it makes the meaning clear, it is called "vyañjana" (phrasing/letter), which is the syllable (akkhara). Meaning and phrasing are called "attha-vyañjana." Their difference is "attha-vyañjanabheda." Therefore, it means because the meaning and the phrasing are not the same.

Now, to clarify that very meaning, it is said: "anusāvanañhi nāma," etc. The word "hi" is a particle in the sense of cause (kāraṇattha). It should be understood as connected with the word "abhinnaṃ." "Tena" means because of being different. "Assa" refers to the group of three statements beginning with "yassa siyā." This point must certainly be accepted in this way; otherwise, to show that there might be the fault of over-extension (atiprasaṅga), it is said: "yadi cetaṃ," etc. "Etaṃ" refers to the three statements beginning with "yassa siyā." Other teachers consider that the word "anusāvitaṃ" does not indicate the past sense but rather the future sense. They reason that in connection with the meaning of the root, a suffix prescribed for another time can also be validly used for another time. Therefore, it is said: "apare anusāvitanti padassa," etc. "Upari uddesāvasāne" means at the end of the recitation of the Pārājika section. "Atthayuttīnaṃ abhāvato" means because of the absence of the future meaning and the causal factors. Now, to clarify that very point, it is said: "idaṃ hi," etc. For the question of how this is known, it is said: "yadi cassa," etc.
162:
This word "ayaṃ" refers to the future tense. "Anusāvitaṃ hessati" (it will have been announced) should be said; that is, the Buddha would have said "anusāvitaṃ hessati" by making the auxiliary verb (anuppayoga) in the future tense. The intention here is: if the "ta" suffix connected with the meaning of the root were used here, then being connected with the root meaning would be the state of qualifier and qualified (visesana-visesya). And that state arises only when there is identity of meaning with the auxiliary verb, not when there is none. Therefore, He would have said the auxiliary verb "hessati," but it was not said. Thus, it does not indicate the future, but only the past tense. This is because of the present tense word "anusāviyamāne."

If so, what is this statement "it is announced up to three times" (yāvatatiyaṃ anusāvitaṃ hoti)? Because of this question, it is said: "yāvatatiyaṃ," etc. What is marked by that statement, by which it would be a mere marking statement (lakkhaṇa-vacana)? Because of this question, it is said: "tena," etc. "Tena" means because of the reason of being a mere marking statement.

"Tadetanti" refers to the Pātimokkha. "Taṃ panetanti" refers to the announcement up to three times (anusāvana) beginning with "tatthāyasmante pucchāmi." "Na dissati" means it is not found (not obtained). "This meaning only" refers to this very meaning stated by us. For if the three statements beginning with "yassa siyā āpatti" were the announcement up to three times, then He would have said that very thing in the Uposathakkhandhaka, but He would not have said "sakimpi anusāvitaṃ hoti," etc. Is it not that this decision does not appear in the Commentaries? If so, from where is it obtained? Because of this question, it is said: "ayameṭṭha," etc. The lineage that makes the various meanings known to the teachers who are experienced in the matters of Vinaya is called "ācariyaparamparā" (teacher lineage). Because it is brought down from that teacher lineage, it is called "ācariyaparamparābhata."

Is it not that in deliberate lying (sampajāna-musāvāda), there should be a pācittiya offense? If so, why is it a dukkaṭa offense? Because of this question, it is said: "sā ca kho na musāvādalakkhaṇena," etc. In the phrase "what happens in deliberate lying," it means: what offense is that lie which is stated as "he has a deliberate lie"? "It is a dukkaṭa" means it is a dukkaṭa offense. "It is an offense arising from non-action (akiriya) at the vocal door (vaci-dvāra)" means: for that monk who sits silently with an improper acknowledgement, there is no offense at the mind door (mano-dvāra). However, because he did not manifest what should have been manifested, it should be understood that an offense occurs for that monk due to non-action at the vocal door.

To show the stated meaning by citing the Pāḷi, it is said: "vuttampi cetaṃ," etc. That statement was made by the Venerable Upāli in the Parivāra Pāḷi, in the Sedamocana verses.

"Without speaking to any person with words" means: intending that others will hear my voice, and thus not letting even a sound out. "He would fall into a vocal offense" means he would fall into an offense produced by speech (vaci-viññatti). In the Pāḷi "this problem should be considered by the wise," it should be understood that the meaning is: this problem should be considered by the wise.
163:
This offense should be understood as arising from the non-performance of what should be done, together with vocal intimation (vacīviññatti) at the vocal door. To prove the meaning already stated with the Pali text, he said "Vuttampi cetaṃ", etc. This is the meaning stated by the Elder Upāli in the Sedamocanagāthā (Sweat-inducing Verses) of the Parivāra: "Vuttampi ca".

"Anālapanto manujena kenaci vācā" means not speaking or talking with any human being. "Giraṃ no ca pare bhaṇeyya" means not even emitting a sound with the intention toward other persons, thinking "These people will hear my words". "Āpajjeyya vācasikaṃ" means one would incur an offense arising from speech (vocal intimation). In the phrase "Pañhāmesa kusalehi cintitā", "Pañhāmesa" is stated with a gender shift (feminine), and it means "this question should be considered by the wise". This question is stated specifically regarding this false speech (musāvāda).

Because it comes into the midst of the continuity of beings by way of obstructing various attainments, the disadvantage such as that pertaining to the present life is called "antarāya" (danger/obstacle). It is called "antarāyika" (obstructive) because it is associated with that danger in the sense of transgression, or because it deserves a result similar to danger, or because it has the habit of creating danger. Therefore, he said "Vippaṭisāravatthutāya", etc. In that phrase, "Vippaṭisāravatthutāya" means: "vippaṭisāra" is the distortion of the mind by way of subsequent regret; it means because of being the cause of that remorse. It means because it assists remorse, which is the opposite of non-remorse (avippaṭisāra), which is the condition for the first jhāna and so on. "Pāmojjādisambhavaṃ": weak or tender rapture (pīti) is called "pāmojja" (joy); the arising or acquisition of those states beginning with joy is called "pāmojjādisambhava". By the word "ādi" (etc.), states such as rapture (pīti) and tranquility (passaddhi) are to be taken. In the phrase "Paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ", by the word "ādi", the inclusion of the second jhāna, etc., should be understood as stated: "It is an obstacle to the attainment of the second jhāna... third jhāna... fourth jhāna... jhānas, deliverances (vimokkha), concentrations (samādhi), attainments (samāpatti), renunciation (nekkhamma), escape (nissaraṇa), seclusion (paviveka), and wholesome states (kusala dhamma)". When "Tasmā" (therefore) is said, because of the invariable connection between the words "yaṃ" and "taṃ", the meaning "Yasmā" (since/because) is already evident; thus he said "Tasmāti yasmā", etc. "Jānantena" means knowingly. By this word "jānantena", he shows the intentionality (sacetanā) of this deliberate lying (sampajāna-musāvāda). "Visuddhiṃ apekkhati" means one who desires purity, thus "Visuddhāpekkho" (one looking for purity).
164:
That monk who looks for purity. Since purity here means Vuṭṭhāna (rising from an offense) and so on, the author of the Saṅgaha said, "desiring to rise from an offense, desiring to be pure." It means desiring to rise from a Saṅghādisesa offense, which is Vuṭṭhānagāminī (leading to rising/rehabilitation), and desiring to be pure from the five groups of lesser offenses, which are Desanāgāminī (leading to purity through confession). "Whether in the midst of the Saṅgha, or in the midst of a group, or to a single individual" means it should be declared in the midst of the Saṅgha by informing the Saṅgha in the Uposatha hall, or in the midst of a group by informing monks sitting in two groups in that same Uposatha hall, or to a single individual by informing the monk immediately nearby.

"Having risen from here" means having left this Uposatha hall. In this regard, when informing a nearby monk, it should only be told to a monk of similar status (sabhāga). This is because if it is told to a monk of dissimilar status (visabhāga), there may be arguments, quarrels, and schisms in the Saṅgha. Therefore, without telling that visabhāga person, one should perform the Uposatha with the intention, "I will leave this Uposatha hall and remedy the offense," as stated in the Andhaka Commentary.

"Karaṇatthe" means in the sense of the instrumental case. This nominative case (paccattavacana) is in the sense of the agent because it depends on the word "phāsu." "Paccattavacana" means the nominative case. For the sake of attaining the first jhāna and so on, comfort (phāsu) arises for that monk. Because restraint (saṃvara) is the cause of the absence of remorse (avippaṭisāra), comfort arises. Therefore, he said, "those which have absence of remorse as their root," and so on. The absence of mental remorse by way of whether one has done or not done evil and meritorious deeds is called "avippaṭisāra." That avippaṭisāra is the root (cause) of those states such as joy, etc.; those states are called "avippaṭisāramūla." "Avippaṭisāramūla" itself is called "avippaṭisāramūlaka." It refers to those states like joy, etc., which have absence of remorse as their cause. "Sukhappaṭipadā sampajjati" means the pleasant practice is fulfilled; the meaning is that the attainment of the first jhāna and so on occurs easily and happily.

The placing of the motion (ñatti) in the introduction (nidāna), the questioning of the preliminary duties,
The procedure in listening to the recitation of the introduction, the procedure in announcing purity,
And the offense for not announcing purity—these five collective meanings should be known.

## Thus ends the Explanation of the Introduction (Nidāna-vaṇṇanā)
## in the Vinayatthamañjūsā Līnatthappakāsanī, the New Sub-commentary
## on the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Pātimokkha Commentary.
165:
## Pārājikakaṇḍa

Now, to explain the meaning of the Pārājikuddesa (Recitation of the Defeats) mentioned immediately after the Nidānuddesa (Recitation of the Introduction), the passage beginning with "Idāni" is commenced. "Nidānānantara" is a neuter abstract designation, meaning "having made the Nidāna immediate." In that Pārājikakaṇḍa, within the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha, the word "cattāro" (four) is a numerical delimitation to prevent deficiency or excess. "Pārājikā" is the specific name for offenses of a similar class, while "āpattiyo" is a general name common to all offenses. That which is recited is called "uddeso" (recitation). This designation of "uddeso" is stated with emphasis on the state (bhāva). Therefore, it is said "uddisitabbataṃ" (the state of being recited).

## 1. Commentary on the First Pārājika

In the phrase "Yo pana," the word "pana" is merely a particle, and "yo" is the substantive word. That word "yo" indicates a person in an indefinite manner. Therefore, to show its meaning, it is said "yo koci" (whosoever). Since any person is inevitably known by one of the characteristics such as liṅga (appearance), yutta (engagement), jāti (birth), nāma (name), gotta (clan), sīla (habit), vihāra (dwelling), gocara (resort), or vaya (age), the passage beginning with "rassadīghādinā" is stated to make that person known through such characteristics. By the word "ādi," new work (navakamma) and so forth should be included. In the phrase "liṅgādibhedena," it is called "liṅga" because one is known or recognized by this appearance. It means by the variety of that appearance and so forth. Here, by the word "ādi," engagement (yutta) and so forth should be included.

The intended meaning is: let a person be such and such by way of appearance (liṅga)—whether tall or short, dark or fair, tawny-skinned (like the back of a bug), thin or fat. Let a person be engaged in this or that by way of application (yoga)—whether engaged in new work, engaged in recitation, or engaged in the burden of insight (vāsadhura). Let a person be of this or that birth by way of caste (jāti)—whether a Khattiya, a Brāhmaṇa, a Vessa, or a Sudda. Let a person be of such and such a name by way of name (nāma)—whether Buddharakkhita, Dhammarakkhita, or Saṅgharakkhita. Let a person be of such and such a clan by way of clan (gotta)—whether Kaccāyana, Vāsiṭṭha, or Kosiya. Let a person be of such and such a habit by way of virtue (sīla)—whether having the habit of new work, the habit of recitation, or the habit of the burden of insight. In dwellings (vihāra) also, let a person be such and such a dweller—whether one who dwells doing new work, one who dwells reciting, or one who dwells practicing insight.
166:
Or in resorts (gocara) also, let a person have such and such a resort—whether new work is the resort, recitation (uddesa) is the resort, or the burden of insight (vāsadhura) is the resort. In ages (vaya) also, let it be this person or that—whether an elder (thera), a new monk (nava), or a middle-standing monk (majjhima); indeed, in this context, everyone is referred to as "yo" (whosoever).

Now, to explain the word "bhikkhū," the passage beginning with "ehibhikkhūpasaṃpadā" is stated. Therein, "ehibhikkhūpasaṃpadā" is the attainment of monkhood merely by the words of the Blessed One, "Come, monk." "Saraṇagamanūpasaṃpadā" is the attainment of monkhood through the three refuges, spoken by breaking the speech into three times in the manner beginning with "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi." "Ovādappaṭiggahanūpasaṃpadā" (ordination by accepting exhortation) is the ordination granted to the Elder Mahākassapa by his acceptance of this exhortation:

"Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: 'A keen sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa) shall be present in me towards the elders, the new monks, and those of middle standing.' Thus, Kassapa, you should train yourself. Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: 'Whatever Dhamma I shall hear that is connected with the wholesome, I will listen to all that Dhamma with respect, attending to it, reflecting on it with my whole mind, and listening with an attentive ear.' Thus, Kassapa, you should train yourself. Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: 'Mindfulness immersed in the body (kāyagatāsati) accompanied by joy shall not leave me.' Thus, Kassapa, you should train yourself."

This ordination by accepting exhortation was granted to the Elder Mahākassapa. "Pañhābyākaraṇūpasaṃpadā" (ordination by answering questions) is the ordination granted to the novice Sopāka. It is said that the Blessed One, while walking up and down behind the novice Sopāka at the Pubbārāma monastery, asked ten questions related to foulness (asubha), such as: "Sopāka, are these things called 'perception of a bloated corpse' (uddhumātakasaññā) and 'perception of form' (rūpasaññā) different in meaning and different in phrasing, or are they the same in meaning and different only in phrasing?" The novice answered those questions. The Blessed One, having given him approval (sādhukāra), asked, "How old are you, Sopāka?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, I am seven years old." The Blessed One, with a satisfied mind, saying, "Sopāka, you have answered the questions in accordance with my Omniscience," granted him ordination. This is called Pañhābyākaraṇūpasaṃpadā.

"Aṭṭhagarudhammapaṭiggahanūpasaṃpadā" (ordination by accepting the eight heavy rules) is the ordination granted to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī by her acceptance of the eight heavy rules.
167:
Ordination by messenger (dūtenūpasampadā) refers to the ordination granted to the courtesan named Aḍḍhakāsī.

Ordination by eight proclamations (aṭṭhavācikūpasampadā) refers to the ordination of a bhikkhunī through two formal acts: a motion and three announcements (ñatticatutthakammavācā) from the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, and a motion and three announcements from the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.

Ordination by a motion and three announcements (ñatticatutthakammūpasampadā) is the ordination currently granted to monks. 'By a motion and three announcements' (ñatticatutthena) means by a formal act consisting of three announcements (anussāvanā) and one motion (ñatti); thus, the motion is the fourth. Although the motion is recited first of all, because the three announcements do not differ in meaning and phrasing, the motion—which does differ in meaning and phrasing—is treated as the fourth in relation to them, and thus it is called 'ñatticatuttha'. 'By an unshakeable act' (akuppena) means by a formal act that has reached a state where it cannot be overturned or criticized. 'By a fit act' (ṭhānārahena) means by a motion and announcements that are appropriate to the cause and suitable for the Teacher’s Dispensation. 'One who is ordained' (upasampanno) means one who has attained the higher state. The state of a monk is indeed the higher state, and since that person has attained that state through the aforementioned formal act, he is called 'upasampanno'.

If it is asked: 'Why is only the one ordained by this motion and three announcements taken here, and not those ordained by other methods?' The answer is: Ordination by 'Come, monk' (ehibhikkhūpasampadā) is only for those in their final existence; ordination by taking the refuges (saraṇagamanūpasampadā) is only for those who are pure; ordination by accepting exhortation (ovādappaṭiggahena) and by answering questions (pañhābyākaraṇa) were granted only to the Venerable Mahākassapa and Sopāka respectively. Furthermore, such persons are incapable of committing offenses that are worldly faults (lokavajja) such as the pārājikas. Ordinations such as the acceptance of the eight heavy rules (aṭṭhagaru-dhamma-ppaṭiggahena) are granted only to bhikkhunīs. Since the 'monk' referred to here is a male monk, it should be understood that only the one ordained by the formal act of ordination with a motion and three announcements is taken, and no others. However, regarding training rules that are faults by regulation (paṇṇattivajja), others such as those ordained by 'Come, monk' are also included. As it will be stated later: 'In training rules that are faults by regulation, others are also included.' Now, in order to explain in detail the meaning briefly stated as 'one ordained by an unshakeable and fit act', the text beginning with 'tassa pana' is spoken.

'Therein' (tattha) means among those five. It is called 'vatthu' (basis/object) because the formal act of ordination resides in this person; it is the support or foundation. Therefore, it is said: 'the person desiring ordination' (upasampadāpekkho puggalo). One who has not yet completed twenty years is 'one under twenty years' (ūnavīsativasso). What should be said here, we shall explain later in the commentary on the training rule concerning one under twenty years in the Sappāṇaka Chapter. 'Among them' (tesu) means among the eleven types of unsuitable persons (abhabba-puggalo) such as the paṇḍaka. Here, the paṇḍaka is of five kinds: the āsitta-paṇḍaka, the usūya-paṇḍaka, the opakkamika-paṇḍaka, the napumsaka-paṇḍaka, and the pakkha-paṇḍaka. Among these, for the āsitta-paṇḍaka...
168:
The going-forth (pabbajjā) of the usūya-paṇḍaka is not prohibited, but the going-forth of the other three types is prohibited. Among those three, the going-forth of the pakkha-paṇḍaka is prohibited only during the half-month (pakkha) in which he is a paṇḍaka. In this context, the three persons—the opakkamika, the napumsaka, and the pakkha-paṇḍaka—are not 'vatthu' (valid objects) because they are unsuitable for going-forth and ordination. Therefore, the words beginning with 'āsittapaṇḍakañca' are spoken.

Among those five types of paṇḍakas, the one whose passion is calmed when he has taken the male organ of others in his mouth and is showered with semen is the āsitta-paṇḍaka. The one whose passion is calmed when envy arises in him while watching the sexual misconduct of others is the usūya-paṇḍaka. The one whose testicles have been removed by surgical effort is the opakkamika-paṇḍaka. The one who is born without sexual characteristics from the very moment of conception is the napumsaka-paṇḍaka. It should be understood that a certain person who, by the power of unwholesome result (akusala-vipāka), becomes a paṇḍaka during the dark half of the month (kāḷapakkha) but whose passion is calmed during the bright half (juṇhapakkha) is a pakkha-paṇḍaka.

Because he lives in communion by means of theft, that person is called a 'communion-thief' (theyyasaṃvāsaka). By 'theyyasaṃvāsaka', it is not intended to mean only one who steals the communion, but rather one who steals the mark (robes), or both. Therefore, the words beginning with 'theyyasaṃvāsako pana tividho' are spoken. 'Does not count the years of a monk' means he does not count the years of seniority by lying, saying, 'I have ten years' or 'I have twenty years'. 'Does not tolerate the homage of senior monks or novices' means he does not accept the homage of senior monks or novices according to the seniority he has falsely shown. 'Does not obstruct with a seat' means he does not obstruct a seat by saying, 'Go away, this seat belongs to me'. 'Does not appear at Uposatha and so on' means he is not seen at the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā ceremonies. In the phrase 'liṅgamattasseva', the word 'eva' excludes communion. 'Being' (samāno) means existing as such. 'Communion suitable to the mark' (liṅgānurūpassa saṃvāsassa) means the social interaction of a novice that is suitable for the mark of a novice.

If one lays down the burden of the robes and, while being a non-monk through sexual intercourse or other such acts, wears the yellow robes either naked or dressed in white, he is a 'thief of the mark' (liṅgatthenaka). If, desiring the state of a layman, he wears the yellow robe by tucking it up or in another manner of lay dress to test, 'Does the layman's mark suit me or not?', he waits for that long. If he accepts that 'it suits me' and then enjoys the mark of a monk again, he is a thief of the mark. The same should be understood regarding testing and accepting while wearing white cloth.
169:
The method is: whether one wears white cloth over the dyed saffron robes to test or to accept, it is considered as guarding (the monk's mark). The phrase "the same method applies to one who has reached the ultimate matter" means that this same method should be understood for a monk who has committed a Pārājika offense. The meaning is this: if a certain monk, while still diligent regarding the robes, wears white cloth and indulges in sexual intercourse, and then wears the robes again and follows all procedures such as counting years of seniority and so forth, this monk is not a 'thief of the mark' (liṅgatthenaka) because he has not abandoned the mark given by the monks. Nor is he a 'thief of communion' (saṃvāsatthenaka) because he accepted the communion appropriate to the mark.

"Videsa" means another region. This word is spoken to show a place where one is able to deceive. If a person does this even in his own region, he is also a 'thief of communion' (saṃvāsatthenaka). By the words "saṃvāsamattasseva," the mark (liṅga) is excluded. If a certain person who ordained late in life (vuddhapabbajita) counts the years of a monk and accepts food offered in large baskets (mahāpeḷā) and so forth, he is also a 'thief of communion' (theyyasaṃvāsaka). If he himself is a novice (sāmaṇera) and takes food by falsely counting years according to the novice's seniority, he is not a 'thief of communion.' However, if a monk takes food by falsely counting years according to the monk's seniority, he should be dealt with according to the value of the goods (bhaṇḍagghena).

If it is asked, "Is not communion (saṃvāsa) defined as having shared legal acts, shared recitation of the Pātimokkha, and shared training?", the words beginning with "bhikkhuvassagaṇanādiko hi" are spoken. By this sentence, it is shown that in this context, not only the specific actions such as shared legal acts are intended as communion, but other things such as counting the years of a monk are also shown as communion. "Imasmiṃ atthe" refers to the subject of the 'thief of communion' (theyyasaṃvāsaka). "Sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya" means having abandoned the training. The meaning is this: if a certain monk abandons the training but does not remove the mark, and whether he performs an immoral act or not, thinks "no one knows me," and follows all the procedures mentioned before, such as counting years of seniority, he is a 'thief of communion' (theyyasaṃvāsaka).

If a king is angry with a certain person, and that person thinks, "In this way, I shall be safe," and takes the mark himself and flees. Seeing him, they report to the king. The king says, "If he is an ordained one, it is not proper to do anything to him," and he lets go of his anger toward him. That person thinks, "My danger from the king has been pacified," and into the midst of the Saṅgha...
170:
A person who comes back taking the lay mark without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha should be ordained. However, if he thinks, "I have obtained my life by depending on the Sasana; now I shall truly ordain," and having developed a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he comes in that same (monk's) mark but does not accept the duties of a guest, and whether questioned by the monks or not, he reveals his true circumstances and requests ordination, he should be ordained after removing the (taken) mark. But if he accepts the duties, or shows the behavior which is the basis of the monk's mark, and follows all the procedures mentioned before, such as counting years of seniority and so forth, this person should not be ordained.

In this Sasana, if a certain person, being unable to survive during a famine, takes the mark himself and eats the food of all sects, and when the danger of famine has passed, he comes back taking the lay mark without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha, everything is just as said before.

Another person desires to cross a great wilderness, and a caravan leader is traveling taking monks with him. That person thinks, "If I do this (take the mark), the caravan leader will take me along," and he takes the mark himself, crosses the wilderness with the caravan leader, and upon reaching a safe place, comes back taking the lay mark without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha; everything is just as said before.

Another person, when the danger of disease arises and he is unable to survive, takes the mark himself and eats the food of all sects, and when the danger of disease has been pacified, he comes back taking the lay mark without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha; everything is just as said before.

Another person has an angry enemy who wanders about seeking to kill him. That person thinks, "In this way (by ordaining), I shall be safe," and he takes the mark himself and flees. The enemy searches, asking "Where is he?" and hearing that "He has fled after ordaining," he lets go of his anger toward him, saying, "If he has ordained, it is no longer possible to do anything to him." That person knows, "My danger from the enemy has been pacified," and if he comes back taking the lay mark without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha, everything is just as said before.

Another person goes to his relatives' house, renounces the training, and becomes a layman. Then he thinks, "These robes will be destroyed here in this house; if I take these robes and go to the monastery, they will catch me on the way, saying 'He is a thief'; it would be better if I go wearing them on my body." Thinking thus, he wears and wraps himself in the robes for the purpose of carrying them and goes to the monastery. Seeing him coming from afar, the novices and young monks go out to meet him...
171:
(Fearing that thieves might seize them, he thinks:) 'These robes will only perish in this house; if I take these robes and go to the monastery, thieves will seize me on the way. It would be better if I wear the robes on my body and go.' Thinking thus, he puts on the robes to carry them and goes to the monastery. Seeing him coming from afar, the novices and junior monks welcome him and perform the duties. That person does not delight [in being a monk] and reveals himself as he truly is. If the monks say, 'Now we cannot let you go,' and wish to ordain him by force, he should be re-ordained after removing the dyed clothes.

In particular, if he thinks, 'These monks do not know that I have disrobed,' and claims the status of a monk, practicing all the details such as the number of years (seniority) mentioned before, he should not be ordained. Therefore, it was said: 'Due to fear of kings, famine, wilderness, disease, or enemies,' etc. Here, the word 'fear' (bhaya) should be applied to each: 'due to fear of kings, due to fear of famine,' etc. 'Liṅgaṃ ādiyati' means taking the guise. 'Idha' means in this Sasana. 'Saṃvāsaṃ nādhivāseti, yāva so suddhamānaso' means that because he has no intention to deceive the monks, as long as he is pure-hearted and does not consent to communion, even if he has a deceptive thought like 'Let laypeople know me as a monk,' since he has no desire to deceive the monks, there is no fault. Thus, the meaning is that he is not called a theyyasaṃvāsaka (one who lives in communion by theft).

One who has gone over and entered among the sectarians is called a titthiyapakkantaka. He does not become a titthiyapakkantaka merely by entering among those sectarians; rather, it is only by accepting their doctrine. Therefore, it was said: 'Whosoever [monk],' etc. By the word 'upasampanno' (ordained), it is shown that a novice (sāmaṇera) who is not fully ordained does not become a titthiyapakkantaka. For it is said in the Kurundī Commentary: 'This titthiyapakkantaka is spoken of regarding a fully ordained monk. Therefore, even if a novice goes to a sectarian place in his own guise, he can still receive the going-forth (pabbajjā) and full ordination (upasampadā) again.' In the word 'kusacīrādikaṃ,' by the word 'etc.' (ādi), pieces of bark, matted hair, etc., are included. Even if he thinks, 'This sectarian going-forth is noble,' and adopts that noble state, he is not released and remains a titthiyapakkantaka. 'Vatāni' refers to practices such as the squatting practice. If he wears grass garments or ties matted hair or carries a yoke for the purpose of testing, thinking, 'Does this sectarian going-forth suit me or not?', as long as he does not accept that doctrine, he still preserves [his status]. The moment he accepts it, he becomes a titthiyapakkantaka. One who wears grass garments because his robes were stolen, or takes the sectarian guise due to fear of kings, etc., does not become a titthiyapakkantaka because of the absence of [accepting] the doctrine.

'Avaseso sabbopi' refers to Nagas, Supannas, Yakkhas, Gandhabbas, etc. What should be said here has already been said below.
172: The act of destroying one of the same species is particularly heavy, but not so for one of a different species; therefore, it is said 'of human species' (manussajātika). The name 'parents' due to the connection with a son, and the term 'son' due to adoption, etc., are well-known in the world. Since these terms are figurative, to show the primary sense, it is said 'janettī' (the mother who gives birth). Janettī means the progenitress, the mother. Just as for one established in the human state, wholesome states can reach sharpness, clarity, and courage—as that [state] led to the fulfillment of the three types of Bodhi for the three Bodhisattvas—so too, for one established in the human state, unwholesome states can reach sharpness, clarity, and courage. Therefore, it is said 'while being human' (manussabhūteneva). Sañcicca (intentionally) means killing by being motivated by the intention to kill along with the perception of 'a living being'. 'This person is a matricide (mātughātaka)' means this person is a matricide due to the act of killing a mother which brings immediate results (ānantariya).
