If one kills a foster mother, an elder mother (aunt), or a younger mother (aunt) who is a human woman but not the biological mother, or if one kills a biological mother who is not a human woman, the going-forth is not prohibited, and it is not an ānantariya act. If one who is himself an animal kills a mother who is a human woman, he also does not commit an ānantariya act. However, because he is an animal, his going-forth is rejected. His act is heavy and stands as if it were an ānantariya act. One who is himself of human species and intentionally deprives a human father of life is a patricide (pitughātaka) due to the ānantariya act of killing a father. To indicate this meaning, it is said: 'The same method applies to a patricide.' Even if he is the son of a prostitute and does not know 'This is my father,' if he kills the one from whose semen he was born, he is simply called a 'patricide' and touches (commits) the ānantariya act. The 'Four Sheep' (eḷakacatukka), 'Four Battles' (saṅgāmacatukka), and 'Four Thieves' (coracatukka) should also be mentioned here. One who, with the intention 'I will kill a sheep,' kills a mother or father who is human and standing in the place of the sheep, commits an ānantariya act because the object of the ānantariya act was destroyed with the intention to kill. One who kills a sheep, thinking it is a sheep or thinking it is a parent, does not commit an ānantariya act because it is not an object of an ānantariya act. One who kills parents with the intention of [killing] parents...
173:
In killing a mother or father, if one kills knowing they are parents, it is an ānantarika-kamma (an action with immediate result). The same applies to the other two sets of four (e.g., killing a parent thinking they are a sheep, etc.). In all cases, the initial perception (abhisandhicitta) is not the criterion; rather, the intent to kill (vadhakacitta) and the life faculty (jīvitindriya) which is the object of that mind are the criteria for whether it constitutes an ānantarika-kamma or not.

One who kills an Arahant should be understood as killing an Arahant of human birth. Therefore, it was said, "even one who stands in the guise of a layperson," and so on. Killing a non-human Arahant, or a Noble Person (ariya) of human birth other than an Arahant, does not constitute an ānantarika-kamma. For such a person, ordination is not prohibited, though the deed is powerful. An animal killing a human Arahant does not commit an ānantarika-kamma, but the deed is grave; this is the decision here. Just as with parents, the sets of four regarding sheep (eḷakacatukka), etc., should be understood in the case of an Arahant as well.

"Pakatattaṃ bhikkhuniṃ" means a nun of pure virtue who has been ordained by both Sanghas. If someone causes the destruction of a nun's virtue through physical contact, his going forth and higher ordination are not prohibited. One who defiles a nun against her will, even after forcing her to wear white clothes, is indeed a "defiler of a nun" (bhikkhunī-dūsaka). However, if she is forced to wear white clothes but consents to the defilement, he is not a "defiler of a nun." Why? Because as soon as she accepts the status of a layperson, she is no longer a nun. Furthermore, defiling a nun who has already lost her virtue, or acting wrongly towards a female trainee (sikkhamānā) or a female novice (sāmaṇerī), does not make one a "defiler of a nun"; such a person can still receive going forth and higher ordination.

"Uddhamma" means that which is apart from the Dhamma. The same applies to the term "ubbinaya." "Catunnaṃ kammānaṃ" refers to the four types of legal acts: apalokana-kamma, ñatti-kamma, ñattidutiya-kamma, and ñatticatuttha-kamma. If one performs any of these Sangha acts separately within a single boundary (sīmā), the Sangha is said to be split. Therefore, it was said, "He splits the Sangha by means of any of the four types of acts."

To clarify the meaning of "with a corrupt mind" (duṭṭhacittena), it was said "with the intent to kill" (vadhakacittena). A mind corrupted by the intention to kill is here called a corrupt mind (duṭṭhacitta). "Causes blood to flow" means causing blood to be produced or clotted within the body. Because the Buddha's body is unbreakable, blood cannot flow out by breaking the skin through another's effort; however, blood collects in one place inside the body. Blood damaged by an assault becomes clotted; it is in reference to this clotting that this was said. If someone, like Jīvaka, performs surgery to cure a disease, removing putrid flesh and clotted blood to provide comfort, he is not a "causer of blood to flow" (lohituppādaka). On the contrary, he generates much merit (puñña).
174:
This statement was made in reference to that blood. Alternatively, if someone, like Jīvaka, performs surgery with a knife to alleviate a disease, removing putrid flesh and clotted blood to provide comfort, he is not a "causer of blood to flow" (lohituppādaka); rather, he generates much merit (puñña).

Both types of organs (duvidhampi byañjanaṃ) refers to both the female organ and the male organ arising from the two aforementioned types of kamma. By this analysis, the compound "ubhatobyañjanaka" is shown to be an asammānādhikaraṇa-bahiratthasamāsa (a possessive compound with members in different cases) and that the case ending of the first member is not dropped. There are two types: the female hermaphrodite and the male hermaphrodite. Among them, in a female hermaphrodite, the female organ is apparent and the male organ is concealed. In a male hermaphrodite, the male organ is apparent and the female organ is concealed. When a female hermaphrodite acts as a male towards women, the female organ becomes concealed and the male organ becomes apparent. When a male hermaphrodite takes the female role towards men, the male organ becomes concealed and the female organ becomes apparent. A female hermaphrodite can both conceive herself and cause another to conceive. A male hermaphrodite, however, cannot conceive himself but can only cause another to conceive. This is the distinction between them.

"Aparāmasanāni" means not taking or not mentioning. Not mentioning the candidate for ordination as "so-and-so" means not mentioning the name of the person being ordained. This refers to not saying "this Dhammarakkhita" when one should say, "Venerable Sir, let the Sangha listen; this Dhammarakkhita is the candidate for ordination of the Venerable Buddharakkhita." Not mentioning the preceptor's name as "the candidate of so-and-so" means saying, "Venerable Sir, let the Sangha listen; this Dhammarakkhita is the candidate for ordination," but omitting the words "of the Venerable Buddharakkhita." Not reciting the motion (ñatti) at all means omitting the motion and performing the act of proclamation by reciting the kammavācā four times. "Sampannaṃ" means a complete (act).

"Hāpanaṃ" means abandoning. If someone omits the single motion and recites the proclamation only once or twice, he also diminishes the proclamation (sāvana). "Duruccāraṇaṃ" (mispronunciation) means saying one syllable/letter when another should be said.
175:
Pronouncing a different letter when another should be pronounced is called bad pronunciation (*duruccāraṇa*). Therefore, a monk who recites the *Kammavācā* should well note these ten varieties of phonetic understanding (*byañjanabuddhi*), as it is said:

“Unaspirated letters, aspirated letters, long letters, short letters,
Heavy letters, light letters, nasal letters,
Connected letters, delimited letters, and released letters—
Thus, there are ten varieties of phonetic understanding.”

Among these ten, *sithila* (unaspirated) refers to the first and third letters in the five groups (*vagga*). *Dhanita* (aspirated) refers to the second and fourth letters in those same groups. *Dīgha* (long) refers to letters like ‘ā’ which are pronounced with a long duration. *Rassa* (short) refers to letters like ‘a’ which are pronounced with half the duration of a long letter. *Garuka* (heavy) refers to the long letters themselves, or letters followed by a conjunct consonant, such as in “āyasmato buddharakkhitattherassa yassa nakkhamatī.” *Lahuka* (light) refers to the short letters themselves, or letters not followed by a conjunct consonant, such as in “āyasmato buddharakkhitattherassa yassa na khamatī.” *Niggahīta* (nasal) refers to letters pronounced with a nasal sound by pressing the vocal organs (*karaṇa*) without releasing them and without opening the mouth. *Sambandha* (connected) refers to instances where a word is joined with the following word, such as pronouncing “tuṇhissā” or “tuṇhassā.” *Vavatthita* (delimited) refers to instances where a word is disconnected from the following word and pronounced separately, such as “tuṇhī assā” or “tuṇha assā.” *Vimutta* (released) refers to letters pronounced without a nasal sound, by releasing the vocal organs and opening the mouth.

Among these letters, pronouncing “suṇāthu me” by changing the letter ‘ta’ to ‘tha’ when “suṇātu me” should be said is called making a *sithila* into a *dhanita*; likewise, saying “patthakallam esā ñattī” instead of “pattakallam esā ñattī” is also making a *sithila* into a *dhanita*. Pronouncing “bante saṃgo” by changing the letters ‘bha’ and ‘gha’ to ‘ba’ and ‘ga’ when “bhante saṃgho” should be said is called making a *dhanita* into a *sithila*. Pronouncing with a nasal sound and a closed mouth as “suṇamtu me” instead of “suṇātu me” with an open mouth, or “esaṃ ñattī” instead of “esā ñattī,” is called making a *vimutta* into a *niggahīta*. Pronouncing “pattakallā” with an open mouth and no nasal sound when “pattakallam” should be said with a closed mouth and a nasal sound is called making a *niggahīta* into a *vimutta*. Thus, these four—making a *dhanita* where a *sithila* should be, a *sithila* where a *dhanita* should be, a *niggahīta* where a *vimutta* should be, and a *vimutta* where a *niggahīta* should be...
176:
...consonants (pronunciation) within the *Kammavācā* can spoil the legal act (*kamma*). For one who recites in this way, if they say one letter instead of another, it is said that they perform a bad recitation (*durutta*).

Regarding the remaining six types of consonants such as *dīgha* and *rassa*, one should perform the *Kammavācā* by pronouncing each letter according to its proper place—*dīgha* where it is *dīgha*, and *rassa* where it is *rassa*—without destroying the traditional lineage of recitation. However, if one does not do this and says *rassa* where *dīgha* should be, or *dīgha* where *rassa* should be; likewise, *lahu* where *garu* should be, or *garu* where *lahu* should be; or *vavatthita* (disconnected) where *sambandha* (connected) should be, or *sambandha* where *vavatthita* should be—even if spoken in this way, the *Kammavācā* is not invalidated. This is because these six types of consonants do not spoil the legal act.

Although the Elders who are experts in the Suttas (*Suttantika*) say, "The letter 'da' becomes 'ta', 'ta' becomes 'da', 'ca' becomes 'ja', 'ja' becomes 'ca', 'ya' becomes 'ka', and 'ka' becomes 'ya'; therefore, pronouncing 'ta' etc. when 'da' etc. should be spoken is not contradictory," this statement is not appropriate when it comes to the *Kammavācā*. Therefore, a master of the Vinaya (*Vinayadhara*) must not change 'da' to 'ta' ...pe... nor 'ka' to 'ya'. One should perform the *Kammavācā* by purifying the linguistics (*nirutti*) in accordance with the Pali text and avoiding the mentioned faults among the ten types of consonants. Otherwise, it is called a failure in the proclamation (*sāvana*). Apart from the motion (*ñatti*), the first performance of the proclamation (*anussāvana*) is connected [to this failure].

"Yāvatikā bhikkhū kammappattā" means the number of monks who are suitable and appropriate for that ordination ceremony (*upasampadā-kamma*). At the very least, these must be five monks of natural status (*pakatatta*) who are within the same boundary (*sīmā*) and have not left the *hatthapāsa* (arm's reach). Without them, that legal act cannot be performed, nor can their consent (*chanda*) be obtained. As for the remaining monks, even if there are a thousand, if they are within the same boundary and the same location and are of the same communion (*samānasaṃvāsaka*), they are all entitled to give consent. Whether they come after giving consent or not, the legal act is not invalidated. "Paṭikkosana" means a protest or prohibition. "Ṭhāna" means cause (*kāraṇa*), because the result resides there depending on it. Here, because it is the cause for performing the ordination ceremony, the word of the Blessed One known as the *Upasampadā-kammavācā* is called "ṭhāna." Therefore, it was said, "Because it is worthy of being a cause and worthy of the Teacher's dispensation." Performing it exactly as instructed by the Blessed One is the fundamental cause of the ordination ceremony.
177:
...because of this, it is called *thānāraha* (suitable for the occasion). Some teachers say that in this word '*thānārahena*', the instruction of the Teacher (the *Sāsana*) such as 'O monks, one with a severed hand should not be ordained' and so forth, is called the cause (*thāna*). 'Herein' refers to this *Pārājika* training rule. Just as in this case, it should be understood that in all *lokavajja* (worldly faults) training rules, this [type of] monk is intended. Therefore, it is said, 'But in the case of *paṇṇattivajja* (prescribed faults)...' and so forth. Why are others, such as *Ehibhikkhu* monks, included in the training rules concerning prescribed faults? Because they are included by way of meaning. This is true; for it is stated generally in the *Parivāra*: 'Two types of persons are not liable to fall into an offense: the Buddhas and the Paccekabuddhas. Two types of persons are liable to fall into an offense: monks and nuns.' It is clear by way of meaning that *Ehibhikkhu* monks and others also fall into *paṇṇattivajja* (prescribed faults) such as *sahasayya* (sleeping together), committed unintentionally, through lack of mindfulness, or without conscious intent.

Now, since the word 'of monks' (*bhikkhūnaṃ*) has no special meaning [here], it is not explained separately. Instead, to show that one is 'endowed with the training and livelihood of monks' because they are possessed of that training and livelihood, it is said: 'endowed with the training and livelihood of monks' and so forth. It is called '*sikkhā*' (training) because it is to be trained in; it is the *Pātimokkhasamvara-sīla* (virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha). It is called '*sājīva*' (livelihood) because they live together in that training; it is the prescription (*paṇṇatti*) consisting of the *Mātikā* and so forth. Both the training and the livelihood are called '*sikkhāsājīva*'. One who has attained both is called '*sikkhāsājīvasamāpanna*'. Therefore, it is said: 'That which for monks...' and so forth. Here, since '*sikkhā*' is associated with '*sājīva*', it is intended as the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*); thus it is said: 'known as higher virtue'. It is called higher virtue (*adhisīla*) because it is an exceeding and noble virtue.

What herein is virtue (*sīla*), and what is higher virtue (*adhisīla*)? To answer—the five precepts and the ten precepts are merely virtue; they are not higher virtue. However, the *Pātimokkhasamvara-sīla* is called 'higher virtue'. Indeed, like the sun among lights and Mount Sineru among mountains, it is superior and supreme among all mundane virtues. It exists only when a Buddha arises; it cannot exist without the arising of a Buddha. No other being is able to set forth that prescription. Only the Buddhas, having completely cut off the flow of transgression in the doors of body and speech in every way, can prescribe the respective restraint of virtue (*sīla-samvara*) suitable for each transgression. Even compared to the *Pātimokkhasamvara-sīla*, the virtue associated with the Paths and Fruits (*Magga-phala*) is the true higher virtue; however, that is not intended here. For one who has attained that [Path and Fruit virtue] does not engage in sexual intercourse.
178:
'*Ete*' (these) refers to monks differentiated by various regions, castes, lineages, and so forth. '*Saha jīvanti*' (they live together) means they exist together by way of having the same recitation of the Pātimokkha (*ekuddesa*) and so forth. Therefore, it is said: 'those who have a single livelihood and similar conduct'.

'Known as the training rule' (*sikkhāpada-saṅkhātaṃ*) means known as the prescription (*paṇṇatti*). For that [prescription] is also called a 'training rule' because it points out [the nature of] abstinence and so forth. This has also been said: 'A training rule is that which is there as a group of names (*nāmakāya*), a group of words (*padakāya*), a group of language (*niruttikāya*), and a group of syllables (*byañjanakāya*)'. 'Therein' (*tattha*) means among those trainings.

'Fulfilling the training' (*sikkhāṃ paripūrento*) means fulfilling the two types of virtue known as *vāritta-sīla* (virtue of avoidance) and *cāritta-sīla* (virtue of performance) by way of avoiding what should not be done and doing what should be done. It means bringing about within oneself the volition associated with abstinence by way of *vāritta-sīla*, and the volition dissociated from abstinence by way of *cāritta-sīla*.

'Not transgressing the livelihood' (*sājīvañca avītikkamanto*) means not trampling upon the training rules. The meaning is that these two—the restraint of virtue and the non-transgression of the livelihood—are what is called 'endowment' (*samāpajjana*) here. Among them, the non-transgression of the livelihood is the cause for the fulfillment of the training. For by not transgressing it, the training is fulfilled up to the Path.

Furthermore, by the phrase 'fulfilling the training', only the time when the restraint of virtue, known as the volition of abstinence, arises in the continuity [of the mind] is specifically taken. By the phrase 'not transgressing', the time when it does not arise is also taken. For a monk who brings it about within himself by way of fulfilling the training, as well as a monk who does not bring it about due to sleep and so forth, are both called 'endowed by way of training' because of the absence of transgression.

Since the meaning of renouncing the training (*sikkhāpaccakkhāna*) is the revealing of a certain weakness, the Buddha, intending to explain the meaning of the phrase 'without renouncing the training' (*sikkhāṃ apaccakkhāya*), said: 'without revealing weakness' (*dubbalyaṃ anāvikattvā*). To show this meaning, [the commentator] said: 'without renouncing the training, without revealing weakness' and so forth.

In that statement, an objection might arise: Since not all revealing of weakness is a renunciation of the training, should one not first say 'without revealing weakness' and then say 'without renouncing the training' to define its meaning? That is not so. Why? Because it would not follow the sequence of the meaning. For it has been stated 'endowed with the training and livelihood'; thus, when it is said 'without renouncing the training' with which one is endowed, and 'without revealing weakness' in the livelihood with which one is endowed, the meaning is stated in the proper sequence, and not otherwise. Therefore, this [phrase] 'without renouncing the training' is stated first.

Now, to make both of them clear, he said 'therein' (*tattha*) and so forth. 'By the absence of that' (*tadabhāvena*) means by the absence of those [states of] mind and so forth. 'With a mind desiring to leave' (*cavitukāmatā-cittena*) means with a mind that wishes to depart from the Sāsana...
179:
(The training should be renounced) with a mind desiring to leave the Dispensation. "Davā" means speaking hastily (suddenly). In fact, if one wishes to say something else but hastily says, "I renounce the Buddha," this person is said to be speaking "davā" (jokingly/inadvertently). "Ravā" means speaking by stumbling or slipping. In fact, if one wishes to say something else but mistakenly says, "I renounce the Buddha," this person is said to be speaking "ravā" (mistakenly).

If it is asked, "What is the difference from the former (davā)?"—the former (davā) is saying something else due to the power of haste, even for a wise person. This (ravā), however, is when a person who stumbles due to dullness or great confusion intends to say something else but says another thing. Some teachers say, "One who is unable to say what should be said due to ignorance of the sequence of letters or lack of proper articulation, and thus says something else, is said to be speaking 'ravā'."

Because he closely observes great and small faults, he is called "Upajjhāya" (Preceptor); it refers to that preceptor. A teacher who teaches conduct and training, such as "This is how it should be recited, this is how one should approach," etc., is called "Ācariya" (Teacher). Because he usually lives nearby, he is called "Antevāsī" (Resident pupil); the case ending is retained without elision, as in the word "vanekaserukā". One who has the same preceptor is called "Samānupajjhāyaka". Likewise, one who has the same teacher is called "Samānācariyaka". "Sabrahmacārī" refers to a monk. Because that monk practices this noble practice together—having the same formal acts, the same recitation of the Pātimokkha, and the same training—he is called "Sabrahmacārī" (Fellow-celibate).

"Those thus mentioned" refers to those terms taught in the Word-for-Word Analysis (Padabhājanīya). Just as in the world, the place where crops grow is called a "field" (khetta), so too these terms such as "Buddha" are called "fields" (khetta) because they are the grounds where the renunciation of the training occurs. Therefore, (the author of the Compendium) says, "of these twenty-two terms of the fields." Since the renunciation of the training can also occur through the synonyms (vevacana) of those field-terms, it is said, "together with the synonyms." Various expressions for a single meaning are called "vivacana"; vivacana itself is called vevacana (synonym); it is also a synonymous name (pariyāyanāma). Because it is together with synonyms, it is called "savevacana"; "of that (term) together with synonyms." Herein, the thousand names found in the Vaṇṇapaṭṭhāna text, the hundred names found in the Upāligāthā, and other names obtained by way of attributes should be known as "Buddha-vevacana" (synonyms of the Buddha). All names of the Dhamma should also be known as "Dhamma-vevacana". This method should be understood in all cases.

"Among those, for one who wishes to say any one thing but says another, there is renunciation of the training" means: for one who wishes to say any one term among those twenty-two field-terms, even if he speaks by uttering any other term, it is renunciation of the training because it is included within the field-terms. This person, intending to say "I renounce the Buddha"...
180:
...it means there is renunciation of the training. This is what is meant: If this person wishes to say "I renounce the Buddha" but says it by reversing the words as "I renounce, the Buddha," or if he says that meaning in another language such as a Milakkha language, or if he wishes to say "I renounce the Buddha" but says out of order "I renounce the Dhamma" or "I renounce the fellow-celibate." For example, in the Uttarimanussadhamma-vibhaṅga, one who intends to say "I attain the first jhāna" says "the second jhāna." If the person to whom he speaks understands even this much—"This monk wishes to give up the state of a monk and is speaking this meaning"—there is no failure; it has entered the field itself, and the training is indeed renounced. Like a being who has passed away from the state of Sakka or Brahma, he has indeed passed away from the Dispensation.

"Alaṃ" means "let it be" or "it is enough." "Kiṃ nu me" means "What business have I? What should be done? What should be accomplished?" "Na mamattho" means "There is no use for me." "Sumuttāhaṃ" means "I am well-freed." "By the fourteen terms mentioned before" means by the fourteen terms starting from "Buddha" and ending with "fellow-celibate" mentioned previously. In the phrase "Yannūna ahaṃ paccakkheyyaṃ," "yannūna" is a particle used to show reflection. This is what is meant: "If I were to renounce the Buddha, it would indeed be good for me." By the word "ādi" (etc.), terms such as "I have renounced," "I will renounce," "I will be," "I am," "I have become," or "I am" are to be taken. If he says, "From today onwards, regard me as a layman (gihi)," or "Know me," or "Recognize me," or "Bear in mind," whether in the Ariyaka language or in a Milakkha language. When such a meaning is spoken, if the person to whom he speaks understands, the training is renounced. This same method should be understood for the remaining seven terms such as "lay follower" (upāsaka). Herein, the Ariyaka language refers to the Māgadha dialect. The Milakkha language refers to non-Aryan languages such as Andhra, Tamil, etc.

"Akkharalikhanaṃ" means the writing of letters for the purpose of showing others, such as "I renounce the Buddha." The movement of the hand, such as bending the fingers, which makes one's intention known, is called "hatthamuddā" (hand gesture). Here, the word "hand" (hattha) should be understood as the fingers, which are a part of the hand, as in the rules such as "I, while eating, will not put the whole hand into the mouth." Therefore, showing the movement of the hand, such as bending the fingers, which makes one's intention known...
181:
## 
In the phrase "hatthamuddādidassanaṃ," the meaning should be understood as follows: the word "ādi" (etc.) includes showing the shaking of the head and so forth.

In the phrase "ummatta-khittacitta-vedanāṭṭānaṃ," "ummatta" refers to one who is insane due to bile. "Khittacitta" refers to one whose mind is scattered by yakkhas (demons), meaning one who is demon-insane. The distinction between these two will be made clear in the section on non-offenses (anāpatti-vāra). "Vedanāṭṭa" refers to one who is overwhelmed and delirious due to being afflicted by intense painful feelings. If such a person renounces the training while talking deliriously, it is considered as not renounced. "Manussajātiko hoti" means any human being who possesses intelligence, whether they are agreeable or disagreeable, a layperson or a monk.

In the phrase "ummattakādīnaṃ," the word "ādi" includes those with scattered minds, those afflicted by pain, deities, and animals. Among those, if one renounces the training in the presence of the insane, the scattered-minded, the pain-afflicted, or animals, it is considered as not renounced because they do not understand. However, in the presence of deities, they can understand very quickly. Deities are of great wisdom, having triple-rooted rebirth (tihetu-paṭisandhi), and thus understand very rapidly. The mind is also something that changes quickly. Therefore, with the intention that "for a person with a quick mind, let there not be a very rapid destruction [of the monkhood] merely by the power of the mind," renouncing the training in the presence of deities was prohibited. Thus, it was said, "he must not be any one of the insane, etc." "Dūtena vā" means by a messenger through a verbal message, saying "Tell them of my renunciation of the training." "Paṇṇena vā" means by sending a letter after writing it on a leaf or paper.

"If they understand the renunciation of the training" is how it should be connected. "Āvajjanasamaye" means at the time of reflecting on the meaning. By this term, it is shown that it is difficult to know [the understanding] at that very moment, neither before nor after. "Vacanānantaram-eva" means immediately after the speech; it has the same meaning as "at the time of reflection." The word "eva" excludes understanding that occurs only after a long time. "Ukkaṇṭhito" refers to one who lives in hardship in this Sasana due to dissatisfaction (anabhirati). Alternatively, it refers to one who is restless and distracted, living with his neck craned (in expectation), thinking, "I will go today, I will go tomorrow, I will go from here, I will go there." This is an indicator (upalakkhaṇa) to make known those who are "dissatisfied, wishing to fall away from the monkhood," and so forth. "Yena kenaci ...pe... jānanti" means if they understand the renunciation of the training through any manner, such as [thinking] "he is weary," or "he longs for the state of a layman," or "he is dissatisfied," or "he wishes to fall away from the monkhood."
182:
The previously mentioned training rules of Abhūtārocana (false claim of superhuman states), Duṭṭhullavācā (lewd speech), Attakāma (desire for self-pleasure), Duṭṭhadosa (malicious accusation), and Bhūtārocana (true claim of superhuman states) also have the same boundaries [regarding comprehension]. If they are understood at the time of reflection, they reach the "head" (the point of an offense). If there is doubt, such as "What is he saying?" and they are understood only after a long time, they do not reach the "head." Therefore, it was said, "Atha aparabhāge" (then at a later time), and so forth.

If, in a place where two people are standing, one says, intending both of them, "I shall inform these people," and if either one of them or both of them understand, the training is renounced. The same should be understood for many people. "Vuttanayena" means by the method stated, such as "immediately after his speech," and so forth. "Yo koci manussajātiko" means any human being, including at the minimum a worker (navakammika).

Regarding this, it is stated in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary: 
"If a monk who is oppressed by dissatisfaction (anabhirati), being suspicious of fellow monks, makes a loud sound intending 'let anyone know,' and says 'I renounce the Buddha,' and if a worker or any other intelligent person standing nearby hears it and understands, 'This monk is weary, he longs for the state of a layman, he has fallen from the Sasana,' then the training is renounced."

If one understands the meaning of the words but does not know "this monk is weary" or "he longs for the state of a layman," the training is not yet renounced. However, if one does not understand the meaning of the words but knows "he is weary" or "he longs for the state of a layman," the training is renounced. "Davāyapi" means even with the desire to play or jest. "Cittādīnaṃ vā vasena" means by the power of the six factors starting with the mind. In this regard:

Mind, field, and time,
Effort, person, and
Understanding;
These are the six factors of renouncing the training.

"Sabbaso vā pana apaccakkhānena" means by not renouncing at all, because not even one of the ways of renouncing the training, such as "I renounce the Buddha," exists. By this, it shows the absence of the arising of thought (cittuppāda) such as "I will make this word heard, I will renounce the training." For whom such an arising of thought does not exist, he is called one who does not renounce in any way. "Sikkhāpaccakkhānassa" refers to the meaning of renouncing the training, such as "I renounce the Buddha." "Atthabhūtaṃ ekaccaṃ dubbalyaṃ" means speaking or making known, "I renounce the Buddha." Monks, such speaking is both the declaration of weakness and the renunciation of the training.
183:
With the words "The training is renounced" etc., as spoken in the Pārajika Pāḷi (page 53), both the renunciation of the training and the declaration of weakness occur. In those words such as "I renounce the Buddha" etc., the renunciation of the training occurs without explicitly declaring the actual state of weakness. In saying "I renounce the Buddha" etc., since the state of weakness in fulfilling the training is also understood, it should be noted that this declaration of weakness is the actual meaning of renouncing the training. Here, by the term "atthabhūta" (the actual meaning), the declaration of weakness such as "What if I were to renounce the Buddha" etc. is excluded. This is because only when both the renunciation of the training and the declaration of weakness occur through a word, that word is the actual meaning of renouncing the training. If only the declaration of weakness occurs through a word and not the renunciation of the training, that word is not the actual meaning of renouncing the training.

Because it is the practice of those who have reached a similar state through the obsession of lust, only the Dhamma called "methuna" (sexual intercourse) is mentioned; thus it is said "rāgapariyuṭṭhānena" etc. In that context, "rāgapariyuṭṭhānena" means by the obsession of lust, by the state of the mind being overwhelmed and enveloped by the arising of sexual lust. "Dhammo" means misconduct (ajjhācāra). In the term "seveyya" (should associate), it means there is no special meaning of the prefix as in terms like "palambate" or "vilambate". "Ajjhāpajjeyya" means should he reach by overwhelming (should he commit). "Sabbantimena" (with the very last) means with the lowest of all females, starting from the goddesses of the Paranimmita-vasavatti heaven down to the goddesses of the Cātumahārājika heaven, human women, female nāgas, female garuḍas, and young women. "Tiracchānagatāya" means with a female born among animals by way of rebirth. Therefore, it is said "paṭisandhivasena" (by way of rebirth). Here, only the female animal that is the basis for a Pārajika offense should be taken as "tiracchānagatā", not all. In this classification, the boundary is: "Among footless creatures, the female snake and female fish; among two-footed creatures, the hen; among four-footed creatures, the female cat—these creatures are the bases for a Pārajika."

In that verse, by the term "ahi" (snake), all long-bodied species (dīghajāti) such as pythons and vipers are included. Therefore, among those long-bodied species, any creature into whose any of the three paths an organ even the size of a sesame seed can be inserted is a basis for a Pārajika. The remaining long-bodied species should be known as bases for a dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) offense. By the term "maccha" (fish), all aquatic species (odakajāti) such as fish, turtles, and frogs are included. Among those aquatic species as well, the basis for a Pārajika and the basis for a dukkaṭa should be known in the same way as mentioned for the long-bodied species. However, there is this distinction: there are frogs called pataṅgamukha; their mouth shape is large, but the opening is small, and it is not sufficient for insertion. However, because the mouth shape is counted as a sore (vaṇa), that frog should be known as a basis for a thullaccaya (grave) offense.
184:
It should be known. By taking the term "hen" (kukkuṭī), all bird species such as crows and pigeons are included. Among those bird species as well, the basis for a Pārajika and the basis for a dukkaṭa should be known by the aforementioned method. By taking the term "cat" (majjārī), all four-footed species such as civets, mongooses, and monitor lizards are included. Among those four-footed species as well, the basis for a Pārajika and the basis for a dukkaṭa should be known by the aforementioned method.

"Pārajiko hoti" means he is defeated, he has encountered defeat. This word "Pārajika" occurs in the senses of the training rule, the offense, and the person. Among them, "It is impossible, Ānanda, there is no occasion, that the Tathāgata would, for the sake of the Vajjis or the Vajjiputtaka monks, abolish the Pārajika training rule that has been laid down"—thus it should be known as occurring in the sense of the training rule. "Monk, you have fallen into a Pārajika offense"—thus it should be known as occurring in the sense of the offense. "We are not Pārajikas; only he who stole is a Pārajika"—thus it should be known as occurring in the sense of the person. In phrases like "one should accuse with a Pārajika Dhamma" etc., they say it occurs in the sense of "Dhamma". However, since "Dhamma" in that context refers to the offense in some places and the training rule in others, it should not be mentioned separately. Therein, the training rule is called "Pārajika" because it defeats the one who transgresses it. The offense is called "Pārajikā" because it defeats the one who commits it. The person is called "Pārajiko" because he has reached defeat, having encountered defeat. Here, however, it is said "Pārajiko hoti" etc. with the intention that the person should be known. By this, it is also shown that: "In the word parājita, the prefix is lengthened (vuddhi), and the letter 'ta' is changed to 'ka', thus it is indicated as Pārajiko hoti."

The four types of Sanghakamma (legal acts of the Sangha) such as apalokana (announcement) are called "ekakamma" (unified act) because they must be performed together by monks of natural status (pakatatta) within a defined boundary (sīmā). By the word "ādi" (etc.), ekuddesa (unified recitation) and samasikkhatā (equality in training) are included. Therein, the five types of Pātimokkha recitation are called "ekuddesa" because they must be recited together. Excluding the training rules allowed specifically for certain individuals, such as those who were formerly barbers, all remaining training rules are called "samasikkhatā" because they must be practiced equally by all conscientious (lajjī) individuals. This is because all conscientious monks...
185:
They live together in these matters such as sharing a single legal act; not even one is seen outside that group. Therefore, taking all those together, the three types of communion (saṃvāsa), such as sharing a single legal act, are so called. It is said: 'That aforementioned type of communion does not exist with that person; for that reason, that person who has fallen into a Pārājika offense is called "one without communion" (asaṃvāsa).' 

Now, since it is not only the organ of a human woman that is the basis (vatthu) for a Pārājika offense, but also the organs of non-human females and female animals; and not only of women, but also of hermaphrodites (ubhatobyañjanaka), eunuchs (paṇḍaka), and men; therefore, to show in detail all those beings, whichever of their organs constitutes the basis, and how one who indulges in those organs becomes a Pārājika, the text says: 'Ayaṃ panettha vinicchayo' (This is the decision herein), and so forth. 

Herein, 'ettha' means in this training rule. 'Tesu' means among the thirty tracts (magga) mentioned. 'Attano vā' (or his own) is said with reference to a monk with a long organ or a monk with a soft back. 'Santhatassa vā' (or one that is covered) refers to an organ that is covered by wrapping it with any cloth, leaf, bark, skin, or sheets of lead or tin, or by inserting it inside. 'Akkhāyitassa vā' (or one not eaten) refers to an organ not eaten by jackals, wild dogs, and so forth. 'Yebhuyyena akkhāyitassa' (mostly not eaten) refers to an organ not eaten for as long as it is not yet called 'half-eaten'. 'Allokāse' means in a wet place. 'Santhataṃ' means covered by any of those cloths and so forth. 

The summary of the meaning here is: there is no exemption from the offense by merely touching inorganic matter (anupādinnaka) with inorganic matter. Rather, whether organic matter (upādinnaka) touches inorganic, or inorganic touches organic, or inorganic touches inorganic, or organic touches organic—if one inserts it with the mind of indulgence (sevanacitta) to the extent stated for a Pārājika to occur, then in all cases, this monk is said to have fallen into a Pārājika offense. 

Having thus shown the offense for a monk who inserts with the mind of indulgence, now, since such insertion can occur not only by one's own effort but also by the effort of another, the text says 'parena vā' (or by another) and so forth, to show that the offense occurs only for the monk who consents (i.e., who possesses the mind of indulgence) and not for the other. In that statement, 'parena' means by any other person, such as an enemy of the monk. In the phrase 'pavesanapaviṭṭhaṭṭhita-uddharaṇesu': insertion from the tip to the base is called 'pavesana' (insertion). Entry of the organ to the full extent capable of entry, without remainder, is called 'paviṭṭha' (inserted).
187:
A regulation laid down later is called a subsequent regulation (anupaññatti). A regulation laid down before an offense has arisen is called a regulation for what has not yet arisen (anuppannapaññatti). A regulation laid down for all regions, both in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa) and in the border regions (paccantima janapada), is called a universal regulation (sabbatthepaññatti). A regulation laid down only in the Middle Country is called a regional regulation (padesapaññatti). A regulation common to both monks and nuns is called a common regulation (sādhāraṇapaññatti). A training rule prescribed only for monks alone or only for nuns alone is called an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇapaññatti). A regulation for both is called a regulation for both (ubhatopaññatti).

'Vinayadharapañcamena' means with a group where the fifth member is a Vinaya-expert (anussāvanakācariya). 'Guṇanguṇūpāhanā' refers to sandals made starting from four layers; it does not refer to sandals of one, two, or three layers. 'Cammattharaṇa' refers to leather that is to be spread out. The regional regulation is said to be of four kinds based on these training rules. Because these four kinds of regulations were laid down only in the Middle Country, they are called regional regulations. Thus it is said, 'Only in the Middle Country...' and so on. This is because an offense occurs if one transgresses the stated matter only in the Middle Country, but not in the border regions; therefore, it is understood as a regional regulation.

'Dhuvannhānaṃ paṭikkhepamattaṃ' means merely the prohibition of constant bathing. Here, by the word 'matta' (merely), three other training rules are excluded. These training rules appear in the Cammakkhandhaka (Leather Chapter) as follows: 'Monks, I allow ordination in all border regions with a group of five including a Vinaya-expert,' and so on. Therefore, it is said, 'Apart from that, there is no such thing as a regional regulation.' 'Sabbāni' refers to all the remaining training rules.

Because the regulation for what has not yet arisen (anuppannapaññatti) comes only for nuns by way of the eight heavy rules (aṭṭhagarudhamma), and because, excluding the prohibition of constant bathing, all training rules in the Pātimokkha are universal regulations (sabbatthepaññatti), and because the pair of common regulations and the pair of individual regulations differ only in phrasing but are identical in meaning, it is called 'sabbattha' (universal). 'Sabbattha' means in all training rules. Here, although it is said 'āpatti' (offense) by dropping the latter word, it refers to the varieties of offenses; thus it is said, 'Āpatti means the varieties of offenses by way of preliminary effort (pubbappayoga) and so on.'

Among the failures in virtue (sīla), conduct (ācāra), view (diṭṭhi), and livelihood (ājīva), the first two groups of offenses are called failure in virtue (sīlavipatti). The remaining five groups of offenses are called failure in conduct (ācāravipatti). Wrong view and the view of extremes (antaggāhikadiṭṭhi) are called failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti). The six training rules prescribed because of livelihood are called failure in livelihood (ājīvavipatti). Thus, it means one of these failures in virtue, conduct, view, or livelihood.

To show that they are not spoken of only in the way already mentioned, it is said, 'They are also called the origins of training rules (sikkhāpadasamuṭṭhāna).' Although these origins are the causes of offenses,
188:
Although these origins (samuṭṭhāna) are only the causes of offenses and not the causes of training rules, they are figuratively called 'origins of training rules' (sikkhāpadasamuṭṭhāna) for the sake of convenience in terminology. 'Tattha' means among those six origins. 'Tesu' means among those with intention (sacittaka) and without intention (acittaka). Because this offense has one origin as its cause of arising, it is called 'single-origin' (ekasamuṭṭhāna). Or, because its origin is by one cause, it is called 'single-origin'. In terms like 'double-origin' (dvisamuṭṭhāna) and so on, the same method should be understood.

'Samuṭṭhānavasena' means by way of taking the origin as the heading. Because it has an origin similar to the first Pārājika, it is called 'having the origin of the first Pārājika' (paṭhamapārājikasamuṭṭhāna). Likewise, in terms like 'having the origin of taking what is not given' (adinnādānasamuṭṭhāna) and so on, it should be understood in the same way.

Because an offense can occur through the body by digging the earth oneself, or through speech by commanding another to dig, it is said, 'as in digging the earth and so on.' By the word 'ādi' (and so on), taking what is not given and others are included. The first Kathina offense occurs to one who does not perform the determination (adhiṭṭhāna) or the assignment (vikappanā) that should be done by body and speech, but not to one who does. Therefore, it is said, 'as in the first Kathina offense.' The offense of receiving a robe from the hand of an unrelated nun arises through action (kiriyā) and non-action (akiriyā) because it occurs through receiving the robe from her hand (action) and through not giving a garment in exchange (non-action). In the phrases 'siyā karontassa' and so on, the word 'siyā' is an indeclinable (nipāta) with the same meaning as 'sometimes' (kadāci), as in the scriptural passages like 'Brahmin, it might sometimes occur to you thus.' The offense of receiving money (rūpiya) occurs sometimes through the action of taking it, and sometimes through the non-action of not refusing it. Therefore, it is said, 'as in the offense of receiving money.' The offense of building a hut (kuṭikāra) occurs sometimes to one who, having had the site pointed out by the Saṅgha, exceeds the measurement. It can also occur to one who exceeds the measurement without having the site pointed out, or to one who builds a hut of proper measurement, or to one who does not build it. Therefore, it is said, 'as in the offense of building a hut.'

Because there is release from the offense due to the absence of perception (saññā), it is called 'release through perception' (saññāvimokkha). This should be understood as a compound where the middle term is elided (majjhepadalopa-samāsa). Therefore, it is said, 'because of the absence of the perception of transgression,' and so on. The 'other' (itarā) refers to an offense from which one is not released even in the absence of the perception of transgression. This is because the word 'itara' refers to the opposite of what has been stated. 'Yā acittakena vā' means that an offense arises sometimes through an origin without intention (acittaka) or sometimes through an origin mixed with intention (sacittakamicchaka). Here, it should be understood that the pair of perceptions is stated by way of non-offense (anāpatti), and the pair of intentions is stated by way of offense (āpatti).
189:
The phrase "in the part where the mind is only unwholesome" means that in an offense that is with intention (sacittaka), the mind is only unwholesome. Even in an offense that is without intention (acittaka), such as drinking intoxicants (surāpāna)—which is described as being both with and without intention—the mind is only unwholesome in the part where it is with intention through the consciousness that recognizes the object; this offense is called a worldly fault (lokavajja). Indeed, the expression "in the part where the mind is with intention" is said with reference to offenses that are both with and without intention. This is because there is no purpose in using the specific qualifier "in the part where the mind is with intention" for an offense that is purely with intention.

In this regard, there is a statement in the Sinhalese Gaṇṭhipada: "In drinking intoxicants, if one drinks knowing it is 'liquor' or knowing 'it is not allowable,' it is only unwholesome." In that statement, the phrase "knowing it is not allowable" is inappropriate, because it would lead to the consequence that a prescribed fault (paṇṇattivajja) would also become a worldly fault (lokavajja). If there is no such restriction as "the mind is only unwholesome in the part where it is with intention," then that offense is called a prescribed fault (paṇṇattivajja); to show this meaning, it is said, "The remaining offenses are prescribed faults."

To clarify, in such an offense, in the part where the mind is with intention through the consciousness that recognizes the object, the mind may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate (abyākata); therefore, there is no restriction that "it is only unwholesome." "To be committed in two doors" means an offense to be committed in both the body-door and the speech-door; such offenses include taking what is not given (adinnādāna) and so forth. The statement "There is no such thing as an offense in the mind-door" is said for the most part, as it should be understood that an offense can occur in cases such as consenting to gold and silver placed nearby.

"One with an unwholesome mind commits an offense" means one reaches an offense with an unwholesome mind in the various types such as Pārājika, Sukkavisaṭṭhi, Kāyasaṃsagga, Duṭṭhulla, Attakāmapāricariya, Duṭṭhadosa, Saṅghabheda, Paharādāna, Talasattika, and so forth. A monk who teaches the Pali Dhamma word-by-word (padasodhamma) to one who is not ordained, or a monk who preaches the Dhamma to a woman—such offenses are reached with a wholesome mind. One reaches offenses such as sleeping in the same place (sahaseyya) unintentionally with an indeterminate mind. Whatever offense an Arahant reaches, he reaches it only with an indeterminate mind. Therefore, it is said, "or one with a wholesome or indeterminate mind."

"Or one endowed with painful feeling" means a monk reaching various offenses such as those involving a corrupt mind (duṭṭhadosa) reaches them while endowed with painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā). However, one reaches various offenses such as sexual intercourse (methunadhamma) while endowed with pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā). A monk who reaches the very same offense that is reached with pleasant feeling, but does so while being neutral, reaches it while endowed with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukha-vedanā). Therefore, it is said, "or one endowed with the other two feelings." These two triads (the wholesome triad and the feeling triad) are also stated only for the most part.
190:
Indeed, one who has lain down and entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is without mind and without feeling, yet he can reach the offense of sleeping in the same place (sahaseyya). Although this is stated without restriction, the phrase "even though this is so" is said to show that there is a distinction here. "Even though this is so" means it is appropriate to acknowledge the reason for stating the distinction. "Three minds by way of all" means the three minds—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—occur in padasodhamma and so forth.

Now, to apply these seventeen types, ending with the triad of feelings and beginning with the aforementioned origin, to this training rule, the phrase "But here in this..." is said. "Here" means in this first Pārājika training rule. "In the city of Vesālī" refers to the city known by this name, used in the feminine gender. That city is called "Vesālī" (The Wide) because it became wide by the expansion of its surrounding walls three times. It should be understood that this city reached full prosperity in every aspect only when the Fully Enlightened One attained Omniscience. The two supplemental regulations (anupaññatti)—"without giving up the training" and "even with a female animal"—were stated by way of the cases of the monkey and the sons of the Vajjis. These two supplemental regulations, "even with a female animal" and "without giving up the training," cause an offense independently from the first regulation.

"As in the Aññavādaka training rule and others" means just as in the Aññavādaka training rule and others, the supplemental regulation beginning with "due to harassing" (vihesaka) causes an offense. By the word "others" (ādi), the Ujjhāpanaka training rule is included. Here, even in the Vihesaka training rule and others, a Pācittiya offense occurs independently from the Aññavādaka rule. As it is said: "A monk who is being questioned in the midst of the Saṅgha regarding a matter or an offense for which a charge of harassing has been brought, and who, desiring not to speak or not to disclose it, remains silent and harasses the Saṅgha, there is an offense of Pācittiya."

Because the intention of enjoying the emission of semen that exists in a dream is negligible (abbohārika), it does not cause an offense; thus it is said, "except in a dream," and so forth. For the mind in a dream is negligible because it is overcome by sloth and torpor (thina-middha); since the mind is negligible, the intention that initiates the effort is also negligible. For it was said: "Monks, that intention exists, but it is negligible." Therefore, this supplemental regulation "except in a dream" results in no offense. By the word "others" (ādi), the phrase "except in the case of overestimation" (adhimāna) and so forth are included.

"As in the Adinnādāna training rule and others" means as in the Adinnādāna training rule and others, the supplemental regulation beginning with "except by theft" is understood. Here, by the word "others" (ādi), the first Pārājika and so forth are included. In this second Pārājika, the Buddha stated the supplemental regulation "except from the forest" and so forth, which serves the purpose of preventing the boastful speech of monks who speak in a clinging manner in the village or in the forest; thus it only serves to support the original offense. Therefore, it is said in the Vibhaṅga: "Friends, is it not so?" "In the manner stated" means it occurs in the three paths (maggas) in the manner stated by way of humans, non-humans, animals, lodgings, and so forth. The connection of this term with the word "magga" should be understood.
191:
In the training rules such as Adinnādāna, the meaning is that it is like the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) beginning with "whether in the forest" (araññā vā). Here, the word "beginning with" (ādi) includes the first Pārājika and others. In this second Pārājika, for the purpose of preventing the excuses of monks who speak evasively in such a manner as "he steals that theft only in the village, not in the forest," the Buddha spoke the supplementary regulation beginning with "whether in the forest," which serves to support the original regulation. For that very reason, it is stated in the Vibhaṅga by the monks: "Is it not so, venerable sirs, that it is just like that?"

"In the tract (magga) of the described variety" refers to the thirty tracts of the described variety by way of humans, non-humans, and animals. This phrase is connected with the word "when severed." "Without leaving the skin and so forth" means without leaving the thin skin and thick skin situated on the outside in the region of the sexual organ. "Only the shape of the sexual organ is apparent" is said because the thin skin and thick skin still exist inside the flesh of the sexual organ. "Cammakhila" means a skin-peg or a piece of skin. They also call that piece of skin a "wart" (unṇigaṇḍa). Since that skin-peg is produced on the sexual organ, it is indeed the sexual organ itself. Therefore, it is said: "If there is a mind wishing to indulge, it is a Pārājika."

"A mind wishing to indulge" means a mind wishing to indulge in sexual intercourse. However, if there is a mind wishing to indulge in physical contact (kāyasaṃsaggā), it is only a Saṅghādisesa offense. "Here, the body-sensitivity (kāyappasāda) is destroyed" means a piece of wart or dry skin where blood does not circulate and the body-sensitivity is destroyed. Since it is stated that a Pārājika offense is incurred even in a corpse that has not been devoured by dogs or crows, or a corpse that has mostly not been devoured, a Pārājika offense is indeed incurred by a monk who inserts his organ into a female organ where the body-sensitivity is destroyed. "Without leaving even the mere shape of the sexual organ" means without leaving even the flesh of the sexual organ, etc., which remains in the form of the sexual organ as described.

"By way of counting as a wound (vaṇa)" means by way of inclusion in the category of wounds. The incurrence of a Thullaccaya offense in a wound should be understood by the power of this sutta: "He inserts a non-tract organ into a non-tract wound; there is an offense of Thullaccaya." In that sutta, it is stated that a Thullaccaya offense is incurred by a monk who, between two joined wounds, inserts into one wound and brings it out through the second. It is also stated in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary: "By the power of suitability for this being, a Thullaccaya offense should be understood in all places counted as wounds." The eyes and so forth of humans are also included in the category of wounds; therefore, wishing to show them by making them of the same division as a wound, he spoke the words beginning with "Likewise." The counting of those as wounds should be understood according to the sequence of suttas such as "The body with nine openings is called a great wound." In that context, "of humans" refers to the four types of humans by way of women, men, eunuchs (paṇḍaka), and hermaphrodites (ubhatobyañjanaka).
192:
"Vatthikosesu" refers to the sheaths of the male organ (prepuce) located at the bladder of men. "Hatthiassādīnañca tiracchānānaṃ" refers to animals such as elephants, horses, cattle, donkeys, camels, and buffaloes. "Tiracchānānaṃ pana" refers to all animals. "Sabbesaṃ" refers to all beings, including the aforementioned humans.

Having thus shown the specific offenses incurred in a living body, he now speaks the words beginning with "matasarīre" (in a dead body) to show the specific offenses incurred in a dead body. Among the four parts of the anus, the urinary tract, and the mouth, when two parts are left and the other two parts are devoured, it is called "half-devoured" (upaddhakkāyita). "Na kuthitaṃ hoti" means it is not yet putrid (boiling/decaying) by way of swelling and so forth, but is still moist. When the body is swollen, putrid, swarming with black flies, infested with worms, and has putrid pus flowing from the nine wound-openings such that one cannot even approach it (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.59-60), at that time it ceases to be a basis for Pārājika or Thullaccaya and becomes only a basis for Dukkaṭa; therefore, he said: "kuthite dukkaṭaṃ" (a Dukkaṭa in the putrid). "Kuthite" means when it has reached the state of being swollen. In such a body, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred by a monk who makes an effort in any place whatsoever. Likewise, it means a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred by a monk who inserts the organ into an open mouth without touching the four sides and the palate (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.73). If he inserts while touching either the bottom, the top, or both sides, a Pārājika offense is incurred. If he inserts without touching the four sides but touches the palate inside, it is indeed a Pārājika. It is connected that a Thullaccaya offense is incurred by a monk who inserts the organ into the tongue protruding outside the mouth or into the teeth. Even in a living body, if he inserts into the tongue protruding outside the mouth, it is only a Thullaccaya. However, if he wraps it with the tongue outside and inserts it into the mouth, it is indeed a Pārājika. If the teeth are firmly closed so there is no space inside the mouth, and the teeth are covered on the outside by the flesh of the lips, a Pārājika offense is indeed incurred by a monk who inserts even as much as a sesame seed into that moist space in the mouth not touched by air. For one who peels back the lip and makes an effort only on the teeth, a Thullaccaya offense is incurred. This same method should be understood for teeth that protrude outside and cannot be covered by the lips.

One who is oppressed by pain is called "vedanāṭṭa." In this section on non-offense (anāpattivāra), "ummattaka" refers to one who is insane due to the disturbance of bile (pittummattaka), as stated by the words beginning with "yo pittavasena."
193:
‘By the power of bile’ means by the power of bound bile (baddha-pitta). Indeed, when that bound bile moves from the gallbladder and comes out, beings become insane; having perverted perception and discarding shame and fear, they behave inappropriately. Even when they are trampling upon and violating minor or major training rules, they do not know. They are also incurable by medical treatment. For such an insane person, there is no offense. Unbound bile (abaddha-pitta), however, is spread throughout the whole body like blood. When that bile is disturbed, beings experience itching, scabies, bodily tremors, and so on. These can be calmed by medical treatment. Therefore, it is said, ‘by the power of bound bile’.

One with a disturbed mind (khittacitta) means one with a distracted mind, referring to one driven mad by a yakkha; thus it is said, ‘one whose mental distraction is caused by yakkhas is called khittacitta’. It is said that yakkhas, by showing terrifying objects, or by inserting their hands into the mouth, or by squeezing the heart-matter, make beings distracted in mind and perverted in perception. For such a person with a disturbed mind, there is no offense.

However, the difference between these two is this: one driven mad by bile is constantly insane and does not regain normal perception. One driven mad by a yakkha, however, regains normal perception from time to time. But in this training rule, whether one is mad due to bile or mad due to a yakkha, if he is completely forgetful, knows nothing, and wanders about trampling on fire, gold, excrement, and sandalwood as if they were all the same, for such a person, there is no offense. But for one who regains normal perception from time to time and performs the act while knowing, there is indeed an offense. Therefore, it is said, ‘and in these two types of persons’, and so on.

‘By excessive pain’ means by painful feeling that is beyond measure. One who is engaged in the first instance of an act is called the first doer (ādikammika). He who is engaged in the first act is the first in that action; thus it is said, ‘he who’, and so on. In this training rule, the Elder Sudinna is the first doer; for him, there is no offense. For the remaining ones, such as the monk with the female monkey and the Vajjiputtaka monks, there is indeed an offense.

Accomplishing is called ‘paṭipādana’. Because only the one who is performing the act reaches that offense, it is called an ‘action’ (kiriya). This statement is made mostly in terms of the fact that when there is the effort of another in the act of sexual intercourse, for one who consents, it is an origin by non-action (akiriya-samuṭṭhāna). Because one is released due to the absence of sensual perception connected with sexual intercourse, it is called ‘release through perception’ (saññā-vimokkha). For it was said, ‘There is no offense for one who does not know, for one who does not consent’. Because one reaches that offense only with the mind of sexual intercourse and not without that mind, it is ‘with intention’ (sacittaka). Because it must be reached only by the power of lust, it is a ‘worldly fault’ (lokavajja). Because it arises only through the body-door, it is a ‘bodily action’ (kāyakamma). Here, the mind is merely a factor; the status of kamma is not obtained by the power of that mind.
194:
Because it is reached only with a mind of greed, it is an ‘unwholesome mind’ (akusala-citta). Because one who is endowed with either pleasant feeling or neutral feeling reaches it, it has ‘two feelings’ (dvi-vedana). Is it not that the origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so on belong to the offense and not to the training rule? Then why are the origins and so on of the training rule mentioned? To answer this, the sentence beginning with ‘These are the origins...’ was said. ‘They belong to the offense’ means they are the origins of the transgression (ajjhācāra).

Knowledge is called ‘muti’ because of repeated knowing; one who has that knowledge is ‘mutimā’, meaning one who possesses wisdom.

## The Commentary on the First Pārājika is Finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Second Pārājika

‘Here’ (ettha) means the decision should be known in these two words. The connection is that ‘all villages, categorized as single-hut villages and so on, should be understood as a village’. Therein, ‘categorized as single-hut villages and so on’ means a village where there is only one hut, one house, as in the Malaya country; this is called a ‘single-hut village’. By the word ‘and so on’ (ādi), it includes the categories mentioned as ‘a two-hut village, a three-hut village, a four-hut village’. However, a newly established single-hut village and so on does not count as a village as long as people have not yet entered and taken up residence. To show what kind of village it is, it is said, ‘whether enclosed’, and so on.

Therein, an ‘enclosed’ village means one surrounded by anything from a brick wall down to even thorn branches. The opposite of that is an ‘unenclosed’ village. A ‘non-human’ village means one that is possessed by yakkhas due to the total absence of humans, or a village from which humans have departed but intend to return for some business. However, a village from which they depart without any expectation of returning no longer counts as a village. To show that not only single-hut villages and so on are called villages, it is said, ‘even a...’, and so on. ‘Any caravan’ means any caravan among those such as a caravan of people on foot or a caravan of wagons. In this training rule, just as towns and cities are included by the term ‘village’, the precinct of a village (gāmūpacāra) is also included by the term ‘village’; thus it is said, ‘excepting the village and the precinct of the village’. Otherwise, the inclusion of the place of theft would not be complete according to the Matika, and the Buddhas do not prescribe a Pārājika that is incomplete.

‘Therein’ (tattha) means in those villages and village precincts. ‘At the door’ (dvāre) means inside the place where water falls from the eaves. ‘Inside the house’ (antogehe) means inside the front porch.
195:
"Enclosed" means having an enclosure or barrier made of walls, fences, and so forth. In describing this gharūpacāra (house precinct), the boundary such as the place where water falls [from the eaves] is mentioned with reference to an unenclosed house. It should be understood that the boundary is not only at the front of the house, but that same extent all around the house is called the gharūpacāra (the vicinity of the house). The word "in front of the house" and so on is used because people usually make enclosures only in front of the house. A man of average strength means a man of medium strength, neither weak nor very strong. By the words "as young people," it excludes the place where a stone falls when thrown by a woman who, wanting to scare away crows, raises her arm straight and throws a stone, or as when water is poured out. "Having rolled" means rolling along or turning over.

"If there are two threshold stones in that village" means if there are two thresholds in that enclosed village, like in the city of Anurādhapura. If a village has only one threshold, the area within a stone's throw of a person standing in the middle of the doorposts of that village is called the gāmūpacāra (the vicinity of the village). If there is no threshold stone in a village, the middle area between the doorposts of that village should be regarded as the threshold stone. If there are no doorposts either, the middle point between the ends of the fences or walls on both sides should be regarded as the threshold stone, as it is the place where a threshold stone would be. If a village was large in the past but later became a small village because the houses were destroyed, that village should be demarcated only by a stone's throw from the gharūpacāra. It should be understood that the former boundary of that village, whether enclosed or unenclosed, is no longer the measure. Does not the showing of this precinct of an unenclosed village seem to contradict the Padabhājana? For in that Padabhājana, it is said: "The gāmūpacāra is a stone's throw of a man of average strength standing at the threshold stone of an enclosed village," and "It is a stone's throw of a man of average strength standing in the gharūpacāra of an unenclosed village"—this much only was taught by the Blessed One. He did not teach that after defining that stone's throw as the village boundary, the area beyond that is the gāmūpacāra. Therefore, it is said: "In the Padabhājana also, the meaning should be understood in this very way."

## The intended meaning in this matter is:

In this context, a village is of two kinds: an enclosed village and an unenclosed village. Of these two, in an enclosed village, the enclosure itself is the boundary of the village. Therefore, without separately mentioning the boundary of that enclosed village, it is stated in the Pali: "The gāmūpacāra is a stone's throw of a man of average strength standing at the threshold stone of an enclosed village." In an unenclosed village, however, the boundary of the village must be stated. Therefore, to show the boundary of that unenclosed village, it is said: "Of an unenclosed village..."
196:
To show the boundary of that unenclosed village, it is stated (in Pārājika 92): "A stone's throw of a man of average strength standing in the gharūpacāra of an unenclosed village." Once the boundary of the village is shown, the characteristic of the village precinct (gāmūpacāra) can be known by the method already mentioned; therefore, it was not stated again as "a stone's throw of a man of average strength standing in that place." Nevertheless, it should be understood that the meaning regarding the precinct of that unenclosed village is also exactly as already stated. If someone were to say that only a stone's throw of one standing in the gharūpacāra is the "village precinct," then in his view, the gharūpacāra would fall into the error of becoming the "village" itself. If that were so, the distinction between house, gharūpacāra, village, and gāmūpacāra would become confused. In this matter, the decision should be understood without confusion. Therefore, by comparing the Pali and the Commentary, the village and the village precinct in this matter should be understood only by the method already mentioned.

The word "tattha" (therein) means "among those two kinds of precincts." The connection should be made as: "this precinct which is shown." In the phrase "entering a village at an improper time, etc.," the word "ādi" (etc.) includes entering a village without an outer robe (asaṅkaccika). The precinct of an enclosed village that was mentioned does not find application anywhere in the Vinaya Piṭaka. Rather, it was mentioned for the purpose of making it known that another stone's throw beyond the space where an enclosure should be made for an unenclosed village is called the "village precinct." When this is said, it should be understood: "If even a stone's throw of an enclosed village is called a precinct similar to a kappiya ground, how much more so should a stone's throw beyond the space where an enclosure should be made for an unenclosed village be called a precinct?" "To show the boundary of these" means it was stated in the Commentary to show the boundary of these villages and forests. "Pārājikavatthu" (the object of a Pārājika offense) refers to property worth one pāda (five māsakas). "To one who steals" means to one who takes.

"What is not given" (adinna) in the Dantapona Sikkhāpada refers to allowable food or drink that, although one's own property, has not yet been formally offered (appaṭiggahita). In this context (the second Pārājika), however, it refers to any article possessed by another and having an owner. Because that article has not been given by those owners either by body or by speech, it is called "adinna." To show the meaning that suffices for an act of theft, it is said: "the property of another human being." Since the word "saṅkhā" itself is expressed with the addition of the letter 'ta', it is said: "saṅkhā and saṅkhāta are the same in meaning." Therein, "the same in meaning" means they are identical in the sense of the word and there is no difference in meaning. This is a name for a portion or a group.
197:
A certain portion appears as a mass; therefore, this designation 'reckoning' (saṅkhā) is the name of that portion. Papañcasaṅkhā means that craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and wrong view (diṭṭhi) cause beings to delay in saṃsāra; therefore, these—craving, conceit, and wrong view—are called papañca (proliferations/impediments). Alternatively, whichever craving, conceit, or wrong view arises in a person, they manifest that person as 'one who is lustful,' 'one who is intoxicated,' or 'one who is established in wrong view'; therefore, they are called papañca. A portion is called saṅkhā. Since only the papañcas are the saṅkhās, it is called papañcasaṅkhā, meaning 'portions of proliferation'; this refers to craving, conceit, and wrong view.

Theyyacittasaṅkhāta means 'one who has a thieving mind.' 'A single set of mind' refers to a set of mind other than the non-thieving mind that occurs through the power of taking based on intimacy, temporary use, and so forth. 'By what is reckoned as thieving' (theyyasaṅkhātena) means by a set of mind that has the nature of thieving. If that is so, then why did the Blessed One state in the Vibhaṅga of this Matika term, 'one with a thieving mind, one with a mind to steal'? Because of this question, the sentence beginning with 'Yo ca' was spoken. 'By not taking the syllable' (byañjanaṃ anādiyitvā) means without paying regard to the syllables; it means without considering the literal sound. 'Only the meaning' (attham-eva) refers only to the essential meaning (bhāva-attha).

'Those thefts' refers to those twenty-five types of theft. This fivefold set has various goods by way of the animate and inanimate; therefore, that fivefold set is called 'the fivefold set of various goods' (nānābhaṇḍapañcaka). A collection of five thefts is called a pañcaka. Or, it is called a pañcaka because that various goods has a measure of five. Since the various goods itself is a fivefold set, it is called nānābhaṇḍapañcaka. This fivefold set has a single type of good by way of the animate; therefore, this fivefold set is called 'the fivefold set of a single good' (ekabhaṇḍapañcaka). The remaining terms follow the method already stated. Since the manual theft (sāhatthika) itself is a collection of five, it is called 'the fivefold set of manual theft' (sāhatthikapañcaka). This name arises through the power of the initial term, just as the triad beginning with 'wholesome' (kusala) is called the 'wholesome triad' (kusala-ttika). Therefore, it should be understood by its meaning as 'the fivefold set beginning with manual theft.' In the remaining two fivefold sets, it should be understood in this same way. 'Of this very [term]' (etassa-eva) refers only to this Matika term 'ādiyeyya' (should take). 'By the power of these terms' means by the power of these five terms. Herein, it should be understood that the first term is spoken by way of legal accusation, the second term by way of one who goes carrying another's goods, the third term by way of deposited goods, the fourth by way of animate beings, and the fifth by way of goods placed on land and so forth.

Now, to show the application of the meaning of those fivefold sets, the passage beginning with 'Tattha' was spoken. In that context, 'tattha' means among those two fivefold sets. 'The other' (itaraṃ) refers to the fivefold set of a single good. 'Park' (ārāma) refers to a flower park or a fruit park. 'Accuses' (abhiyuñjati) means he lies, saying of a park belonging to another, 'This is my own property,' and thus accuses, charges, or initiates a lawsuit. Although it is a conscious lie, it is stated that an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is incurred because it is a preliminary effort (pubba-payoga) for taking what is not given (adinnādāna).
198:
'There is an offense of wrongdoing' (āpatti dukkaṭassa) means an offense known as dukkaṭa would occur. Or, it means reaching a transgression known as dukkaṭa. In passages such as 'There is an offense of thullaccaya (grave offense),' it should be understood in this same way. 'He causes doubt in the owner' means he causes suspicion in the owner of the park, either due to his skill in legal decision-making or because he relies on powerful people. How? Seeing that the [litigating] monk is making such an effort in the legal decision, the owner thinks: 'Will I be able to make this park my own property, or will I not be able to?' When such doubt arises in the owner, it is said to be caused by that monk. 'He relinquishes the burden' (dhuraṃ nikkhipati) means when the owner thinks: 'This monk is very harsh and violent; he might even cause danger to my life or my holy life. I have no more use for this park now,' and thus he relinquishes the burden, stops his effort, and ceases to strive to make it his own property. If he (the litigating monk) has also relinquished the burden, the meaning is that an offense of defeat (pārājika) is incurred. Specifically, even if the owner has relinquished the burden, if the litigating monk has not yet relinquished the burden and still strives to give it back only after 'oppressing him well, showing my authority, and placing him in a state of being a servant who does whatever is commanded,' then for that duration, he is still free from the pārājika offense. If the litigating monk, after seizing it, relinquishes the burden thinking, 'I will not give this to him now,' but the owner has not yet relinquished the burden and is still striving to recover it by seeking allies, waiting for the right time, or thinking, 'I will first find a group of shameful people, then they will know,' then he is still free from the pārājika offense. When both relinquish the burden, the monk thinking 'I will not give it' and the owner thinking 'I will not get it,' then the pārājika offense is incurred by the litigating monk.

'One who carries another's goods' means one who carries another's goods either for wages or out of friendship. 'A burden on the head' means a burden placed on the head. Regarding the boundaries of the head: first, there is the throat-pit at the front of the neck; at the back of the neck, at the end of the hair, there is a whorl; on both sides of the neck, in some people, hair grows downwards, which are called 'ear-locks' (kaṇṇacūḷikā). The area below these ear-locks is the lower boundary. Above that is called the head. The burden placed within this area is what is meant. 'He lowers it to the shoulder' means: on both sides, below the ear-locks and above the elbows; below the nape-whorl and the throat-pit; and above the mid-back whorl and the chest-pit (the middle of the chest boundary)—this is called the shoulder. Lowering the burden to that shoulder is what is meant.
199:
