## 2. Kāya-saṃsagga-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

Regarding the word "otiṇṇo," it can be interpreted as either a passive (kamma-sādhana) or an active (kattu-sādhana) derivative. Wishing to show the meaning by way of both, it is said starting with "like beings overcome by demons (yakkha)," etc. "Asamapekkhitvā" means without reflecting according to reality; it means not seeing that objects such as visible forms, which cause delight, exist in the mode of impermanence, suffering, foulness, and non-self. "Pariṇatena" means changed or transformed. Therefore, the sentence starting with "as if transformed" is said. "Vuttarāgavasena" means by the power of the aforementioned lust for physical contact. ## 4. Explanation of the Training Rule on Serving One's Own Lusts

"Attakāmapāricariyāvasena" means [desiring] the service of sexual intercourse for one's own sake by the power of lust. In this training rule also, since only a woman capable of distinguishing between lewd and non-lewd speech is intended, the commentator said, "to a woman of the aforementioned types in the speaking of lewd words." In the term "attakāmapāricariyā", it is called "kāma" because it is desired; that is sexual intercourse. Serving or attending is "pāricariyā", which is the same as "pāricariyā". It means the desired service by the power of lust for sexual intercourse. Therefore, it is stated beginning with "known as the act of sexual intercourse" (methunadhamma-saṅkhātena). To show only the meaning without giving weight to the literal syllables, the word-by-word analysis (pāda-bhājana) states: "one's own desired sexual intercourse, one's own cause, one's own intention, one's own service." When it is said "one's own desired sexual intercourse, one's own cause, one's own service," the wise will understand, "By this much, service through sensual pleasure for one's own benefit is stated." It is called "Kalyāṇadhamma" (good quality) because of being endowed with good and auspicious qualities. Therefore, it is stated beginning with "tadubhayenāpi" (by both of those). Does not the request for sexual intercourse come in the training rule on lewd words (duṭṭhullavācā)? If so, why is this stated here? This is not a fault. "At that very moment" (tasmiṃyeva khaṇe) means at the very moment of speaking. A hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka), however, is not mentioned separately because of being in the same category as a paṇḍaka. Teachers say, "In these two training rules, as in the case of bodily contact (kāya-saṃsaggā), a grave offense (thullaccaya) is incurred for speaking lewd words and words for one's own sensual benefit to female yakkhas and female petas." "Tasmiṃyeva" means for a monk who perceives a paṇḍaka as a woman, a wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is incurred for praising the virtues of service through sensual pleasure for his own benefit. A wrongdoing is also incurred for speaking in a roundabout way, such as "Give the best gift, the act of sexual intercourse, to the monk who lives in your monastery." ## 5. Explanation of the Sañcaritta Training Rule

Wandering about is called sañcara; one who has this wandering is called sañcarī, or one is called sañcarī because of having the habit of wandering about. The state of being such a sañcarī is sañcaritta, meaning the act of wandering about. Since that sañcaritta is later taught as "the desire of a woman to a man," and so forth, it implies occurring between a woman and a man; thus it was said, "the state of wandering between a woman and a man." Among paṭiggaṇhana, vīmaṃsana, and paccāharaṇa: Paṭiggaṇhana (acceptance) means when a man, a woman, both of them, or their mothers and so forth say, "Venerable sir, please speak to such-and-such a woman (or man) in this way," one accepts their words by saying "Very well," "Let it be so," or "I will speak," either by breaking silence with words in any manner or by nodding the head and so forth. Vīmaṃsana (inquiry) means taking the message in the manner described and going to that woman or man, or to their parents, brothers, sisters, and so forth who will certainly inform them, and announcing that message. Paccāharaṇa (reporting) means when that monk has gone and announced it, whether that woman or man accepts it saying "Very well," or does not accept it, or remains silent out of shame, he comes back again and reports that occurrence to the [original] woman or man. Āpajjeyya means if he should practice.

"The desire of a woman to a man, or the desire of a man to a woman," in this context, it should be understood that the verb "should announce (āroceyya)" is elided. Therefore, it was said, "tattha" and so forth. Jāyābhāve means in the state of being a wife (to become a wife). Jārabhāve means in the state of being a husband (to become a husband). Here, the locative case is in the sense of cause (nimitta). Therefore, it means he announces for the sake of the state of being a wife, for the sake of the state of being a husband; because of the state of being a wife, because of the state of being a husband; by reason of the state of being a wife, by reason of the state of being a husband. This method also applies in places such as "he announces the state of being a wife." This statement, "either the state of being a wife or the state of being a husband," is spoken to show the purpose for which he announces their desire. Now, to show the meaning also by the method taught in the Padabhājana, it says "apica" and so forth. Although it is taught in the Padabhājana by way of the feminine gender, since the designation "either the state of being a wife or the state of being a husband" is common to both genders, it should also be applied and spoken by way of the masculine gender; with this intention, it says "by this very method" and so forth. Muhuttikā means a prostitute. This statement, "even to a prostitute who is consorted with for only a moment," is intended only as an illustration; with this intention, it says "by this very method" and so forth.
235:
In the phrase “excluding a woman who is nālaṃvacanīyā” (according to Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā 2.339-340), it refers to excluding a woman who has not been completely released by the local custom of giving betel, tea, leaves, etc. Some say that “nālaṃvacanīyā” refers to a woman with whom a monk should not speak for the purpose of sañcaritta (matchmaking).

A woman bought with wealth, whether little or much, is called “dhanakkītā.” Since she does not become a wife merely by being bought, but becomes a wife because she was bought for the purpose of cohabitation, it is stated in the definition (niddesa) of that term: “Having bought her with wealth, he makes her live with him” (Pārājika 304). “Chandavāsinī” refers to a woman who lives according to her own desire or will. Since she does not become a wife merely by her own desire, but only when accepted by the man, it is stated in the definition of that term: “A lover makes a lover live with him” (Pārājika 304).

By the word “ādi” (etc.), one should include these eight types: bhogavāsinī, paṭavāsinī, odapattakinī, obhaṭacumbaṭā, one who is both a slave and a wife, one who is both a worker and a wife, one captured under a flag (dhajāhaṭā), and one who cohabits for a moment (muhuttikā) (Pārājika 304). Just as there is no viśaṅketa (misunderstanding of the signal) for a monk who speaks by way of any of the terms such as “chandavāsinī,” even if not directly mentioned in the Pāḷi, there is no viśaṅketa for a monk who speaks by way of any words indicating cohabitation such as “Be the wife (bhariyā), spouse (jāyā), mistress of the children (pajāpati), mother of the children (puttamātā), housewife (gharaṇī), mistress of the house (gharasāminī), cook (bhattaraandhikā), obedient one (sussūsikā), or attendant (paricārikā) of such-and-named person” (Pārājika-aṭṭhakathā 2.305). If the three factors are fulfilled, an offense (āpatti) is indeed committed.

In the passage “māturakkhitaṃ brūhi” (speak to one guarded by the mother), “māturakkhitā” means a woman guarded by her mother so that she cannot cohabit with a man. Therefore, in the word-analysis (padabhājanī) of that term, it is stated: “The mother guards, protects, exercises authority, and makes her follow her will” (Pārājika 304). In the terms beginning with piturakkhitā, such as “piturakkhitā, mātāpiturakkhitā, bhāturakkhitā, bhaginirakkhitā, ñātirakkhitā, gottarakkhitā, dhammarakkhitā, sārakkhā, saparidaṇḍā” (Pārājika 303), the method should be understood in the same way as here.

In the passage “saṅghassa vā cetiyassa vā gilānassa vā kiccena gacchantassa” (for one going on business for the Saṅgha, a shrine, or the sick), it means when the uposatha hall (sīma building) or some other work of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha is unfinished. In that case, if a male lay follower sends a monk to a female lay follower, or a female lay follower sends a monk to a male lay follower for the purpose of providing meals or wages for the craftsmen, there is no offense (anāpatti) for the monk going on such Saṅgha business. The same method applies while shrine work (cetiyakamma) is being carried out.
236:
There is no offense for a monk who is sent by a male lay follower to a female lay follower, or by a female lay follower to a male lay follower, for the purpose of medicine for a sick person.

Although it is not directly stated here (as in the Sāratthadīpanī) that “a woman means a human woman, not a female yakkha, a female peta, or a female animal; a man means a human man, not a male yakkha,” nevertheless, since only human women and men are intended in this training rule, it is said: “their being of the human species.” “Nanalāṃvacanīyatā” means the state of not being one who should not be spoken to (i.e., one who has been released/given away as mentioned before). Here, the word “alaṃ” has the sense of prohibition. One who is not “alaṃvacanīyā” (not to be spoken to) is “nālaṃvacanīyā.” One who is not “nālaṃvacanīyā” is “nanalāṃvacanīyā.” The state of being “nanalāṃvacanīyā” is called “nanalāṃvacanīyatā.” It simply means “alaṃvacanīyatā” (the state of being fit to be spoken to).

“Paṇṇattiṃ” refers to this training rule. “Kāyavikārena” means by bodily gestures such as nodding the head. Likewise, for a monk who, after investigating by bodily gestures such as hand signals, returns and reports accordingly, or for a monk who says, “She will come to you for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma, etc.” (an offense occurs). “Kenaci vutte” means when spoken to by some man while the monk is sitting in a rest house (āsanasālā), etc.

If the parents of an Arahant have separated in anger and have become those who should not be spoken to (for matchmaking), and the father says to that monk who has come to the house, “Dear son, your mother has left me, an old man, and gone to her relatives' house; go and send her back to look after me.” If that monk goes and speaks to the mother, and then returns to the father and reports whether she will come or not, an offense arises for that monk through body and speech. Therefore, it is said: “But for one who does not know the regulation...” etc. By the word “pi” in “khīṇāsavassapi” (even for an Arahant), it indicates that for learners (sekha) and worldlings (puthujjana), it goes without saying (that an offense occurs). “Pituvacanena” means by the words of his own father. “Gantvā” means having gone near that mother. Even for one who does not know both the regulation (paṇṇatti) and the fact that she is a woman not to be spoken to, an offense arises through body and speech. “Tadubhayaṃ” means both the regulation and the fact that she is a woman not to be spoken to.

If a person, while knowing the regulation, commits the act of sañcaritta through these three methods, the offense arises through body and mind, through speech and mind, or through body, speech, and mind. It is said that these three are “sacittaka-samuṭṭhāna” (arising with consciousness/intention) because they occur with the mind that knows the regulation. That statement is inappropriate. This is because it is not fitting to say that an offense arises through sacittaka-samuṭṭhāna for one who, although knowing the regulation, thinks “this person is not one who should not be spoken to,” because the intention to transgress (vītikkkama-cetanā) cannot exist.

## The Explanation of the Sañcaritta Training Rule is Finished.
237:
## 6. Commentary on the Training Rule on Building a Hut (Kuṭikārasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā)

In the phrase beginning with 'Saññācikāya panāti', the word 'sayaṃ' is an indeclinable (nipāta) standing in the sense of the third case (instrumental) expressing the meaning of 'by oneself'. The word 'yācikā' is a verbal noun (bhāvasādhana) expressing the state of requesting. Between these two words, there is a compound where the middle word is elided (majjhepada-lopa-samāsa). The word 'pana' is merely an indeclinable. Therefore, the author of the Saṅgaha stated, 'It refers to a request initiated by oneself.' Since a request initiated by oneself is called one's own, it was said starting with 'tasmā' and so on.

Intending to address the question, 'Is it not the case that a hut cannot be built by request alone?', and to show its intended meaning, the phrase beginning with 'sayaṃ yācitakehi' was stated. In that context, 'sayaṃ yācitakehi' means with tools (upakaraṇa) requested by oneself, such as by saying, 'Give me an adze, give me an axe,' etc. 'Upakaraṇehi' refers to tools such as adzes and the like. Property that is guarded and protected by another owner without relinquishing it as 'This is mine' is called 'parapariggahitaka'. It means property belonging to another. 'Mūlachedavasena' means by way of cutting the root (paying the price), thereby releasing it from being another's property and making it one's own.

When requesting in this manner by way of 'mūlacheda', a monk who requests from a place of a non-relative or one who has not invited him commits a Dukkaṭa offense according to the training rule on requesting from non-relatives (Aññātakaviññatti). However, requesting to borrow temporarily (tāvakālika) is allowable. The statement 'saka-kammaṃ na yācitabbā' (one's own work should not be requested) is said for the purpose of protecting the training rule on taking life (Pāṇātipāta). One should not request manual labor without specifying the task. If requested in such a way, those hunters and others might say, 'Very well, Bhante,' send the monk away, and then kill deer and bring them. However, one should request by specifying, 'There is some work to be done at the monastery; please provide manual labor there.'

Because it is stated in the word-for-word analysis (Padabhājana), 'A hut may be plastered, or smeared, or both plastered and smeared,' it was said that 'a hut is any one of those such as ullitta, etc.' Therein, a hut smeared with the face turned upwards is called 'ullitta'. Those who smear the interior of a monastery smear in this way, facing upwards. A hut smeared with the face turned downwards is called 'avalitta'. Those who smear the exterior of a monastery smear in this way, facing downwards. Therefore, it was stated beginning with 'tatra ullittā nāma'. 'Piṭṭhasaṅghāṭo' refers to the doorposts (dvārabāhā). By the phrase 'sudhāya vā mattikāya vā' (with lime or with clay), it shows that apart from these two types of plastering, smearing with other things such as ash or cow dung is not considered 'alepa' (plastering).

Since one who builds a hut by requesting materials (saññācikā) must also practice according to the method stated here, it was said, 'whether building it oneself or causing it to be built by command.' Here, by the phrase 'whether building it oneself', the meaning is given according to capacity (sāmatthiya), but not according to the literal meaning of the word (padattha). By 'causing it to be built by command'...
238:
...the phrase 'kārāpentena' (by causing to be built) is according to the literal meaning of the word. Having done so, if one were to say 'by building or by causing to be built', the phrasing would be contradictory. For one who causes another to build is not called the one who builds; thus, such an objection is to be regarded as groundless. 

Because this hut has no owner, it is called 'asāmikā'; that 'asāmika' means having no master or person in control. Here, the absence of an owner is known by the absence of a donor who causes it to be built; therefore, it was said, 'devoid of a donor who causes it to be built.' 'Uddesa' refers to the person for whom it is intended.

'Tatra' is a locative case (bhummavibhat) in the sense of the owner, thus it says 'of that hut'. 'Dīghaso' is an ablative case (nissakkavibhat), thus it says 'by length'. 'Bahikuṭṭe' means outside the wall. A lump of clay mixed with chaff is called 'thusapiṇḍa'; the boundary of that clay lump is 'thusapiṇḍapariyanta'. It means by the boundary of that clay lump mixed with chaff. Whitewashing (setakamma) on top of the chaff-clay lump is, however, negligible (abbhohārika). That which exists inside is called 'abbhantarima'; it is measured by that internal part. 'Yattha' means in which hut. 'Pamāṇayutta' means the measurement of nine spans by the standard span (vidatthi). Because the maximum measurement was stated as 'seven spans in width' (tiriyaṃ sattantara), it was said, 'it shall not be four cubits (hattha) wide at the lower limit.'

'Having cleared' (sodhetvā) means making it like a level consecrated area (sīmāmaṇḍala). Requesting the Saṅgha three times according to the method stated in the Padabhājana means: 'Approaching the Saṅgha, placing the upper robe over one shoulder, bowing at the feet of the senior monks, sitting in a crouching position, joining the hands in reverence, one should say: "Venerable sirs, I wish to build a hut for myself, without an owner, by requesting materials myself. I, venerable sirs, request the Saṅgha to inspect the site for the hut."' Thus, requesting three times according to the method stated in the Padabhājana.

'Appointed by the Saṅgha' means monks appointed by the formal act of a motion and a second (ñattidutiya-kamma) as stated in the Padabhājana, or by way of the act of announcement (apalokana-kamma). 'Vatthu' means the site for the hut. 'Anārambha' means without danger or harm. Because one can walk around it, it is called 'parikkamana'; because it is with that surrounding space (upacāra), it is called 'saparikkamana', meaning having a surrounding space sufficient for walking around. Therefore, it was stated, 'by those monks' and so on.

In the phrase 'of ants and so on', ants refer to any kind of small insects such as red, black, or brown ones; 'of ants and so on' means starting with those. By the word 'ādi' (and so on), termites (upacikā) and others are included. 'Āsaya' means a permanent dwelling place; that dwelling place...
239:
The term 'āsayādi' (habitats and so forth) refers to habitats and similar places. In this context, the word 'ādi' (and so forth) includes insects and other creatures that dwell there. The phrase 'with sixteen types of dangers' means (the site must be free from) the sixteen types of dangers mentioned in the Pārājika Pali, such as: 'the habitat of ants, termites, mice, snakes, scorpions, centipedes, elephants, horses, lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, or any other kind of animal; or it is situated in crops, bean fields, a place of torture (abbhāghāta), a place of execution (āghātana), a cemetery, a garden, royal precincts, elephant stables, horse stables, a prison, a tavern, a slaughterhouse, a main road, a crossroad, a rest house, or a junction.' Among these, 'abbhāghāta' refers to a torture chamber. 'Āghātana' refers to a place where limbs and so forth are severed. 'Susāna' refers to a great cemetery. 'Saṃsaraṇa' refers to a junction or a road that does not lead through, where one must turn back after going.

'Āvijjhituṃ sakkuneyyatāya' means the ability to walk around the site because there are no cliffs or precipices. 'Tena bhikkhunā' (by that monk) refers to the monk who is building the hut. 'Yācitehi' (requested) refers to the monk who has requested (the site) three times, having placed his upper robe over one shoulder, paid homage at the feet of the senior monks, sat in a crouching position, and with joined palms said: 'Venerable sirs, I wish to build for myself a hut that is without an owner and for my own benefit. Venerable sirs, I request the Saṅgha for the designation of a site for the hut.' 'Ñattidutiyena kammena' (by a formal act with a motion as the second part) means:

'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so wishes to build for himself a hut that is without an owner and for his own benefit. He requests the Saṅgha for the designation of a site for the hut. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should designate a site for the hut for the monk named so-and-so. This is the motion. Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so wishes to build for himself a hut that is without an owner and for his own benefit. He requests the Saṅgha for the designation of a site for the hut. The Saṅgha designates a site for the hut for the monk named so-and-so. Let the venerable one who approves of the designation of the site for the hut for the monk named so-and-so remain silent. Let him who does not approve speak. The site for the hut has been designated by the Saṅgha for the monk named so-and-so. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I record it.' (This is the formal act...)
240:
By such a formal act with a motion as the second part as described in the word-for-word analysis (the Saṅgha should grant the site). The term 'Āḷavikā' refers to youths born in the Āḷavī region; even when they were ordained, they were known as 'Āḷavika'. Referring to those monks, it is said 'the Āḷavika monks'. 'When the plaster is applied and joined' means when the wall and the roof are joined together as one with the inner plaster, or when they are joined together with the outer plaster. There are two dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) offenses due to the presence of danger and the lack of an open space to walk around. 'Failing in both' means being devoid of both the designation (of the site) and the measurement; it means having a site that was not designated (to the Saṅgha) and exceeding the measurement. 'In that place' refers to either the door-frame or the window. 'The plaster does not join' means the previously applied plaster does not stick to the door-frame or the window and does not remain as one piece. The word 'that' refers to the door-frame or the window. 'At the very first' means because the work of applying plaster is finished, it is at the very moment the plastering is completed, before the door-frames and windows are installed.

Because it is stated in the word-for-word analysis: 'If a monk builds a hut on a designated site, of proper measurement, but with danger and without an open space, there is an offense of dukkaṭa. If a monk builds a hut on a designated site, of proper measurement, but without danger and without an open space, there is an offense of dukkaṭa,' it is therefore said 'merely because of the presence of danger' and so forth. 'Vippakata' refers to an unfinished hut. 'Even if giving to another' means there is no offense for a monk who gives it to another person or to the Saṅgha. A 'cave' (guhā) can be a brick cave, a stone cave, a wooden cave, or an earthen cave. A 'grass hut' (tiṇakuṭi) refers even to a seven-story mansion if it is roofed with grass. 'For another' means for a teacher, a preceptor, or for the Saṅgha. 'Except for a dwelling house' means excluding a house for one's own residence. In the phrase 'in Uposatha halls and so forth', the word 'and so forth' (ādi) includes steam baths (bathrooms), refectories, and fire rooms. 'The occurrence of the lower measurement' refers to being four cubits wide. 'One who builds without having the site designated' refers to a monk who builds either exceeding the measurement or within the measurement without having the site designated. In this context, not having the site designated is a non-action (akiriya). Building the hut is an action (kiriya).

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Building Huts is finished.
241:
## 7. Commentary on the Vihārakāra Training Rule

Because it takes on a large state, it is called 'Mahallaka'; that dwelling is called 'Mahallaka' (a large dwelling). Since a particular dwelling takes on a particular large state, and that large state belongs to that dwelling, it was said (by the sub-commentator), "Because this dwelling has a large state, it is called Mahallaka." To answer the question of how and from where that large state arises, it was said, "Because of having an owner," and so on. To show that this large state does not arise solely from having an owner (but also from exceeding measurements), it was said, "Because also," and so on. Since there is an objection as to why the Buddha taught only this much in the Padabhājanī, "A dwelling called Mahallaka is said to have an owner," it was said, "But because," and so on. Because they dwell here, it is called a 'Vihāra' (dwelling) or 'Āvāsa' (residence). In the Mātikā, the word 'vā' in the phrase "bhikkhū vā anabhineyya" has the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa), as in the passages such as "ayaṃ vā so mahānāgo" (this is indeed that great elephant).

'Kosambiyaṃ' means in the city of this name. It is said that in various places like the gardens and ponds of that city, Kosamba (trees) were abundant; therefore, it is known as 'Kosambī'. Some teachers, however, say, "Because it was established in a place not far from the hermitage of the sage named Kusumba." 'Channattheraṃ ārabbha' means concerning that Elder Channa who left with the Bodhisatta at the time of the Great Renunciation, and who was ordered by the Teacher to be given the Brahmadaṇḍa (Brahma-punishment) near the time of the Parinibbāna. 'Cetiyarukkhaṃ' means it is called 'Cetiya' because it is a place of honor; this name 'Cetiya' is a designation for shrines and celestial abodes worthy of worship. A tree designated as a cetiya is called a 'Cetiyarukkha' (shrine-tree). Because an offense is incurred by not showing the site for the dwelling, it is called "arising from mere non-action (akiriya)". By the word 'matta' (mere), arising from action (kiriya) is excluded. Some teachers, however, say, "Because it arises from both the non-action (akiriya) of not showing the site and the action (kiriya) of building the hut, it arises from both action and non-action." The only distinction is the absence of a fixed measurement.

## The Commentary on the Vihārakāra Training Rule is Finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Duṭṭhadosa Training Rule

It is called 'Duṭṭha' because it is corrupted; it is called 'Dosa' because it corrupts or destroys others. Therefore, it was said, "Dūsito ceva," and so on. Now, to explain "one who is both corrupted and a corrupter"...
242:
To explain in detail the meaning already stated in brief, he said the words beginning with "Uppanne hi dose". 'Pakatibhāvaṃ jahāpito' means having been made to abandon the natural state of calmness and clarity; it means being brought to a state of distortion.

'Ākāranānāttena' means by the distinct nature of these two aspects: the aspect of being corrupted and the aspect of being a corrupter. 'Nappatito' means not approached, not reached, or not attained by joy (pīti), happiness (sukha), and so on. Intending that whoever is not reached by joy, happiness, and so on, is said to be devoid of them, he said, "Pītisukhādīhi vivajjito". Intending that whoever is devoid of joy and happiness is said to be not pervaded by them, he said, "Na abhisaṭo", which means not suffused with joy, happiness, and so on.

Because the root of that Pārājika offense does not exist, it is called 'Amūlaka' (groundless). That groundlessness is intended only from the perspective of the accuser (codaka), not from the perspective of the accused (cuditaka); therefore, to show that meaning, the words beginning with "Yaṃ codakena" were said. In that passage, 'Yaṃ' refers to the Pārājika offense. 'Etaṃ' refers to the accused person's state of having committed or not committed the offense. 'Idha' means in this training rule.

Now, to clarify 'Diṭṭha' (seen) and so on, which he himself had mentioned, the words beginning with "Ettha ca" were said. By the word 'Tatheva', he points to the meaning: "either with a clear ear or with an ear like a divine eye". Suspicion (parisaṅkita) is of three types: suspicion from what is seen (diṭṭhapariသင်္ကိတ), suspicion from what is heard (sutapariသင်္ကိတ), and suspicion from what is sensed (mutapariသင်္ကိတ).

Among those three, seeing a monk and a woman in such a place and suspecting, "They have certainly done it," or "They will do it," is called 'suspicion from what is seen'. Hearing the voices of a monk and a woman in the dark or in a concealed place, and without knowing the presence of a second person, suspecting in the manner previously mentioned, is called 'suspicion from what is heard'. When scoundrels, together with women, have enjoyed flowers, scents, meat, liquor, and so on in a remote dwelling, a pavilion, or a hall, etc., and have left, a person investigating "Who did this?" might see the place; if a certain monk had made an offering there with scents and so on, or had drunk 'ariṭṭha' medicine for the sake of health, and the person smells that scent on him and suspects, "This must be the one," this is called 'suspicion from what is sensed'.

The absence of these three types of suspicion is called 'Aparisaṅkita'. Therefore, he said, "Not suspected by the mind through the power of seeing, hearing, or sensing." To show that such seeing, etc., is not only one's own, he said, "One's own or another's". Since an offense is incurred even for a monk who accuses with words such as "You are a paṇḍaka," it was said, "By one of the nineteen offenses suitable for a monk." If this is so, then why...
243:
In the word-by-word commentary (*Padabhājana*), the phrase "By a *pārājika* offense, that is, by any one of the four" (from the *Pārājika-pāḷi*) is referred to by the words "In the word-by-word commentary, however," and so forth. When prefixes (*upasagga*) and particles (*nipāta*) are used together with words that convey meaning, they function to illuminate that meaning; thus, it is said, "should destroy" (*dhaṃseyya*). Here, "destroying" means overpowering (or accusing). Therefore, it is said, "should overpower" (*abhibhaveyya*). The speech that occurs in the manner of "You have engaged in sexual intercourse," etc., is as follows: "You have engaged in sexual intercourse, you have taken what was not given, you have killed a human being, you have falsely claimed [attainments of jhāna, path, or fruit]."

In this accusation, some teachers say that one who has reached the ultimate matter (*antimavatthu*, i.e., a *pārājika* offense) should not be paid homage to, because the reason for not paying homage—"You are no longer a monk"—is not explicitly stated. This statement should not be accepted. This is because, among those who are not to be paid homage to, the Buddha did not mention the one who has reached the ultimate matter, and also because He taught, "A monk ordained later should pay homage to a monk ordained earlier" (*Parivāra* 468). This passage, however, is stated to show what the accuser (*codaka*) himself should say.

"In the vicinity" (*samīpe*) means in a place within the measure of twelve cubits. Indeed, only the rejection of the training (*sikkhāpaccakkhāna*) does not take effect through hand gestures; however, this accusation and the false reporting do take effect [through hand gestures]. Therefore, it is said, "or even by hand gestures."

*Brahmacariya* is so called because it is a noble (*brahma*), excellent, and praised practice. Alternatively, it is called *brahmacariya* because it is the practice of noble persons (*brahmas*) such as the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Disciples (*ariyasāvakas*), and of the Brahmas. [The text refers to falling away] from that *brahmacariya*. Therefore, it is called the "noble practice." "It would be good indeed" (*sādhu vata*) means it would be definitely good. The intention of one who accuses another of an offense, thinking, "We will perform the seven types of legal acts, such as the act of rebuke (*tajjaniyakamma*)," is called the intention for legal action (*kammādhippāya*). The desire to "make one rise from an offense" is called the intention for rehabilitation (*vuṭṭhānādhippāya*). The intention for investigation (*anuvijjanādhippāya*) means the desire to examine or scrutinize. An investigator (*anuvijjaka*) is a Vinaya expert who sits to decide a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) that has arisen in the midst of the Saṅgha. "What did you see?" means what was seen by you; it means, "Did you see him committing the first *pārājika*, or did you see him committing the second, third, or fourth *pārājika*?" By the word "etc." (*ādi*), this method is included: "How did you see? When did you see? Where did you see?"

It is called a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) because it must be dealt with (*adhikātabba*) by means of the settlements (*samatha*) which exist for the sake of pacification. Just as the state of being dealt with by the settlements exists in disputes (*vivāda*), etc., through the power of pacification, so too the state of being dealt with by those settlements exists for disputes, etc. Therefore, it is said, "Because of the state of being a matter to be settled by the settlements," and so forth. By this, the word *adhikaraṇa* is stated as a passive derivative (*kammasādhana*). A legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) is of four types: legal issues arising from disputes (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), legal issues arising from accusations (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*), legal issues arising from offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), and legal issues arising from duties (*kiccādhikaraṇa*). They pacify the legal issues such as disputes.
244:
The factors such as settlement in the presence (sammukhāvinaya) are called samatha because they pacify (legal issues). Alternatively, it is called adhikaraṇa because it is the place where [settlements] are applied. What are applied? The settlements (samathas). How are they applied? By way of pacification. It should also be understood here that samathas are so called because they pacify or settle the legal issue (adhikaraṇaṃ samenti vūpasamenti).

Since an accusation cannot be made with the other legal issues except for the legal issue arising from offenses (āpattādhikaraṇa), it is said: "In this context, only the legal issue arising from offenses known as pārājika is intended." An offense itself being a legal issue is āpattādhikaraṇa. A saṅghādisesa offense is incurred at the very moment of the groundless accusation; the meaning is that the accused monk knows [the accusation] at that very moment.

Mettiya-Bhummajaka refers to the monk Mettiya and the monk Bhummajaka. These were the leaders of the group of six monks (chabbaggiya). "Suddhaṃ vā" means one who has not committed a pārājika offense. By the words "If that monk knows at that very moment," the time of reflection is stated. Knowing at that very moment is difficult; however, if it is known after reflecting at [a later] time, it is indeed considered known. If he knows later, it does not reach the head (i.e., it does not become a pārājika).

The training rules regarding: renunciation of training, falsely claiming superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), lewd words (duṭṭhullavācā), serving one's own lusts (attakāmapāricariya), malicious intent (duṭṭhadosa), and truthfully claiming superhuman states—all these have the same limitation. Because a monk who speaks with any of the seven classes of offenses behind [another's] back incurs only an offense of wrongdoing (dukkhaṭa), it is said: "For a monk who accuses behind the back, it does not reach the head."

"Vuttanayāpattiyo" refers to the saṅghādisesa and dukkhaṭa offenses stated by the method of "for every word, for every word," and so forth. "Tatheva" means only for every word. "Vadantassa" refers to a monk speaking to an ordained monk in his presence with any of the seven classes of offenses. "Vuttanayeneva" means only for every word. Intending that a monk who speaks to an ordained monk in his presence after asking for permission incurs a pācittiya offense for every word, it is said: "For one who speaks after asking for permission, only a pācittiya is incurred." By the word "eva" (only), the dukkhaṭa offense is excluded. For one who speaks behind the back with any of the seven classes of offenses, a dukkhaṭa is incurred.

The seven types of formal acts are: the act of censure (tajjanīya), the act of subordination (niyassa), the act of banishment (pabbājanīya), the act of reconciliation (paṭisāraṇīya), and the three types of acts of suspension (ukkhepanīya).

In the statement that there is no formal act of asking for permission for one who prohibits the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā, even if it is prohibited before or after the Uposatha, it is not considered prohibited. However, if it is prohibited during the time (khetta) of prohibiting the Uposatha, it is considered prohibited. Therefore, in this kammavācā: "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs, today is the fifteenth day Uposatha; if it is the right time for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha," as long as one recites up to the syllable "re" [in kareyya], it must be prohibited; this is the time (khetta). If one prohibits after the syllable "yya" is spoken, it is called prohibiting afterwards...
245:
... it is. A monk who suspends [the Pavāraṇā] before 'Suṇātu me' is uttered (recited) is said to have suspended it beforehand. The suspension of Pavāraṇā is of two kinds: all-inclusive (sabbasaṅgāhika) and individual (puggalika). Among these two, in the all-inclusive suspension, in the motion (ñatti) text 'Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho... saṅgho tevācikaṃ pavāreyya', from the syllable 'Su' to the syllable 're', the Pavāraṇā is not yet finished; if one suspends it even with a single word during this interval, the Pavāraṇā is considered suspended. However, when the syllable 'yya' is reached, the Pavāraṇā is finished; therefore, if one suspends it from that 'yya' syllable onwards, it is not considered suspended.

In the individual suspension (puggalikaṭṭhapana), in the text 'Saṃghaṃ, bhante, pavāremi... tatiyampi bhante saṃghaṃ pavāremi diṭṭhena vā... passanto paṭi', from the syllable 'Saṃ' to the final syllable 'ṭi', the Pavāraṇā is not yet finished; if one suspends it even with a single word during this interval, the Pavāraṇā is considered suspended. However, when 'Karissāmi' is uttered, it is finished; therefore, if one suspends it upon reaching this word 'Karissāmi', it is not considered suspended. In this same manner, it should be understood for the two-fold (dvevācika), one-fold (ekavācika), and same-seniority (samānavassika) Pavāraṇās. Indeed, in those Pavāraṇās as well, only up to the end of the syllable 'ṭi' is the period for suspension. Therefore, the [Saṅgaha] teacher said, 'The period for suspension should be known.'

'Osaṭe vatthusmiṃ' means when the matter spoken by the accuser himself is brought forth in the midst of the Saṅgha. 'Does this and that' means he commits the act of taking life (pāṇātipāta), the act of taking what is not given (adinnādāna), and accepts gold and silver (jātarūparajata). For one who speaks behind the back with the intent to insult, saying 'Such and such a person is not a good monk, not a lay follower (upāsaka)', an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is incurred; if spoken in the presence, it is only an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Therefore, it was said, 'If, having specified and determined,' and so on. 'Saṅkhyūpagamana' means reaching the state of conventional designation (vohāra/paññatti).

## The Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Corrupt Intent (Duṭṭhadosasikkhāpada) is Finished.

## 9. Aññabhāgiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

'Aññabhāgassa' means of another portion or category; it means of a category other than the one the accuser wishes to charge, such as the category of animal birth and so on. By the neuter designation 'idaṃ', it points to a male goat (chagalaka) and the like; it means 'this male goat and so on'. Or, the neuter designation is made in consideration of the word 'adhikaraṇa' (legal case); it means 'this case (adhikaraṇa) known as a male goat and so on'. 'Aññabhāgo vā' means another portion or category consisting of animal birth and so on. 'Assa' means...
246:
...of the male goat and so on. (Aññabhāgiya means) a male goat and so on that belongs to a different category. Here, 'that which is connected to a different category is aññabhāgiya' is the meaning of the first grammatical analysis (viggaha). 'That which possesses a different category is aññabhāgiya' is the meaning of the second grammatical analysis. In truth, setting aside animal birth and so on, although there is no separate male goat etc. in the ultimate sense (paramattha), just as in 'the body of an image' and so on, even though there is no distinction, it is stated by way of conventional usage (lokavohāra) through the conceptualization of distinction as 'this belongs to a different category' or 'a different category exists in this'. It is called 'adhikaraṇa' because [the name-designation] is placed here. Therefore, it is said, 'It should be known as the support (ādhāra)'. It is called 'ādhāra' (support/basis) because [the name-designation] is established upon it. Therefore, it is said, 'It means the basis or foundation (vatthu adhiṭṭhāna)'.

Now, wishing to analyze the meaning briefly stated as 'belonging to a different category' etc., by taking the meaning that appears in the originating incident (aṭṭhuppatti) solely for the purpose of showing the method, the teacher said 'Yo hi so' and so on. By saying so, it should be understood that this training rule was laid down for the purpose of closing the opportunity for wicked monks who might make such accusations in the future, and not for the sake of Mettiya and Bhummajaka. Since they were the first offenders (ādikammika), no offense was incurred; therefore, the meaning should be analyzed in a general sense. It should be understood that such an objection—that it should not be analyzed specifically as 'He who is Dabba Mallaputta appearing in the originating incident' and so on—is groundless. The word 'hi' is a particle indicating cause; it means 'because'. 'Aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ' means the arising of the matter is 'atthuppatti', and 'atthuppatti' itself is 'aṭṭhuppatti'; it means in that originating incident (in the prologue of the training rule). 'Chagalako' means a white male goat. The word 'so' (that) is connected with the word 'hoti' (is). 'Aññassa...pe... chagalakabhāvassa ca' means of the other portion or category (group) known as 'being of animal birth and being a male goat'.

If it is asked, 'From what is this other, since it is said
247:
It means that for that person, there is (that part); therefore, (he is called 'belonging to another part'—*aññabhāgiya*). In this context of "*Aññabhāgiyasaṅkhyaṃ labhati*," only the word "*so*" should be brought from the rule "*so yvāyaṃ*" and connected as "that person receives the name of having another part." Alternatively, the word "*so*" should be understood as an elliptical part of the text. The word "*ca*" has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). That word "*ca*" should be placed after the word "*adhikaraṇa*" and understood as "*adhikaraṇañca*." "*Tesaṃ*" refers to the monks Mettiya and Bhummajaka. It refers to those monks who, upon seeing a he-goat behaving improperly with a she-goat, said, "Friends, let us name this he-goat Dabba Mallaputta."

"*Nāmakaraṇasaññāya*" means by the perception known as naming. Here too, bringing in "*yo so*" etc., it should be connected thus: because that goat—which was the object of that perception of naming and was called "the goat named Dabba Mallaputta" in the account of the occasion (*atthuppatti*)—is the support (*ādhāra*), the basis (*vatthu*), and the foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

Now, regarding the question of how it is known that "*adhikaraṇa*" here should be understood as the support (*ādhāra*) and not as one of the four legal issues such as *vivādādhikaraṇa* (legal issues arising from disputes), the phrase beginning with "*tañhi sandhāya*" is stated. There, with the word "*taṃ*," it refers back to the goat which is the foundation of that naming. It should be connected as: it is not said with reference to any one of the *vivādādhikaraṇa*, etc. To the question "*kasmā*" (why?), the reason is given as "*asambhavato*" (because it is impossible). Now, to make that impossibility clear, the phrase beginning with "*na hi*" is stated. It should be connected as "*na hi upādiyiṃsu*" (indeed, they did not take). "*Upādiyiṃsu*" means they took. To the inquiry of whether there is a pretext (*lesa*) even in the four legal issues and if it is said because of that, the phrase beginning with "*na ca catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ*" is stated. Now, to support that very point, the phrase beginning with "*jātilesādayo hi*" is stated. There, because birth itself is a pretext, it is called *jātilesa*. By the word "*ādi*," pretexts of name (*nāmalesa*), etc., are included.

There is a verse here:
"Pretexts are ten: by way of birth, name, clan, appearance (gender), and offense;
And by way of bowl, robe, preceptor, teacher, and lodging."

What is called *āpattilesa* (pretext of an offense) is seeing someone committing a common (minor) offense. If one accuses that person with a *pārājika* offense, saying, "You are not a monk, you are not a son of the Sakyan," then for every word spoken, a *saṅghādisesa* offense is committed. Thus, because *āpattilesa* is also spoken of by attributing it only to a person, (the Buddha said) "only the pretexts of persons are mentioned."
248:
The monks Mettiya and Bhummajaka gave the name "Dabba Mallaputta" to the he-goat; that name "Dabba Mallaputta" has been mentioned (in the Commentary). Having thus shown the impossibility, the phrase beginning with "*ettha ca*" is now stated to explain the meanings of the words *desa* and *lesa* through this very context. "*Ettha*" means in these two, *desa* and *lesa*.

*Desa* is a designation (name) consisting of various aspects such as birth, etc. Therefore, it is said "*jātiādīsu*," etc. "*Aññampi vatthuṃ*" means leaving aside the basis that is the support and referring to another basis as well. As to how it adheres, it is said "*vohāramatteneva*," etc. The meaning is that it adheres merely by designation, but not in actual fact. By the phrase "it adheres slightly," it is shown that the word "*lesa*" is a form derived from the root "*lis*" in the sense of adhering. Although there is a difference between *desa* and *lesa* in terms of syllables (*byañjana*) according to the method mentioned, there is no difference in meaning; therefore, it is said: "This is a designation for any one part of birth, etc."

If it is said "of an *aññabhāgiya* legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*)" with reference to the he-goat which is the support of the naming, then why in the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājana*) is that legal issue not distinguished, and instead it is said, "'Of an *aññabhāgiya* legal issue' means it is either *āpattaññabhāgiya* or *adhikaraṇaññabhāgiya*," etc.? To this, the phrase beginning with "but in the *padabhājana*" is stated. "*Taṃ*" refers to the legal issue known as the support. "*Āvibhūtaṃ*" means becoming clear. "*Atthuddhāravasena*" means by way of extracting the meanings expressed by that word *adhikaraṇa*.

Is it not said that "words are established only in relation to a single meaning," and thus many meanings cannot be expressed by a single word? This statement is true if one considers specific words; however, this analysis (*vicāra*), which is stated by taking the common nature of various meanings being expressible by the word *adhikaraṇa*, is called the extraction of meaning (*atthuddhāra*) of the word *adhikaraṇa*. Therefore, it is said: "The four legal issues which have arisen by way of extracting the meaning through the commonality of the term (*vacanasāmañña*) 'adhikaraṇa'."

*Aññabhāgiyatā* means the state of belonging to another part or group. *Tabbhāgiyatā* means the state of belonging to that part or group. These are not clear except in the places shown in the *padabhājana*. At the end, the accusation by way of *āpattaññabhāgiya* and the accusation such as "A monk is seen committing a *saṅghādisesa* offense, he has the perception of *saṅghādisesa* in a *saṅghādisesa*, and one accuses that monk of a *pārājika*" are referred to as "*adhikaraṇaññabhāgiya*." Each legal issue, because of the difference in the nature of the subject matter (*vatthu*), belongs to another part, another group, or another category of each of the remaining three legal issues.
249:
## Commentary on the Aññabhāgiya Training Rule

By the word "ādi" (etc.), the word-by-word analysis beginning with "How is one legal issue a part of another legal issue?" is included.

In this context, regarding the phrase "based on a mere pretext of some cause," since the explanation of its impossibility has already been stated below in connection with showing it, it is said: "The remaining analytical discourse is just the same as what was stated in the eighth training rule." In that statement, "the remaining analytical discourse" refers to the analytical discourse beginning with: "By a Pārājika means by any one of the nineteen Pārājikas suitable for a monk" (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Aṭṭhakathā, Commentary on the Duṭṭhadosa Training Rule). Regarding the phrase "is just the same as what was stated," the discourse stated in this training rule is intended to be "just the same as what was stated" only in terms of what is common with that eighth training rule, but not what is uncommon, because a new explanation is intended. Therefore, it says: "But this discourse..." and so on. Since there is no offense for one who perceives it as such in the previous training rule as well, it is said: "In this case too." "One who perceives it as such" means even one who perceives: "This monk has indeed fallen into a Pārājika."

The word "iti" has the meaning of "beginning" or "manner." Because of this meaning of the word "iti," if a certain monk sees another monk of the noble (Khattiya) caste committing a Pārājika offense, and then, seeing another monk of the noble caste who is his enemy, he takes that pretext of being of the noble caste and accuses him: "I saw a noble (Khattiya) committing a Pārājika offense; you are a noble, therefore you have committed a Pārājika offense; or rather, you are indeed the noble one, no other, and you have committed a Pārājika offense; you are no longer a recluse; you are no longer a son of the Sakyans; there is no Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, or Saṅgha act with you"—for every word spoken, there is a Saṅghādisesa offense. In this accusation, the state of being "another part" (aññabhāgiya) should be understood through the differences between those nobles, such as height and so on, or through the fact of being seen and so on. The state of being a "legal issue" (adhikaraṇa) should be understood through the basis of the designation "noble" (Khattiya). This method should also be understood in the case of pretexts such as names and so on.

Regarding the pretext of an offense (āpattilesa), if a certain monk sees another monk committing a minor offense, and he accuses that monk of a Pārājika, for every word spoken, there is a Saṅghādisesa offense. If that is so, how is it a legal issue of another part? The minor offense that the monk has fallen into is the "legal issue of another part" relative to the Pārājika. The so-called "pretext" of that legal issue of another part is the general nature of being an "offense" common to all offenses, just as the state of being a noble is common to all nobles. By this aforementioned method...
250:
By this aforementioned method, it includes the specific distinction beginning with: "A certain monk sees another monk committing a Saṅghādisesa offense."

If a monk does not learn the Aññabhāgiya training rule
According to the literal meaning and scriptural logic,
He would only reach the state of being "another part" (alienated)
Among those who are experts in the Vinaya.

## The Commentary on the Aññabhāgiya Training Rule is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Saṅghabheda Training Rule

"Sahitassa" means of one who is united by body and mind. Therefore, it is said: "The meaning is of one who is not separated from both mind and body." "Assa" is the meaning of the word "samaggassa" (of the harmonious). "Samānasamvāsako" means one who has a common communion, such as sharing the same Uposatha and so on; thus he is called "one of common communion." It refers to a Saṅgha that is free from different communions, whether by view (laddhi) or by legal act (kamma). "Kāyasamaggidānato" means by the body, or by giving the unity of the body; it means by approaching within the forearm's length (hatthapāsa) in various acts of the Saṅgha.

"How might this Saṅgha be split?" means by what means could this Saṅgha become a divided group? "Vāyameyya" means he should strive, he should seek a faction, he should form a group. It is called "karaṇa" because it brings about one's own result. It refers to any cause. It is called "adhikaraṇa" because it is an "excessive cause" (adhika-karaṇa). It refers to a specific cause. Since the specific cause of the schism in the Saṅgha is the "adhikaraṇa," the words "bhedanassa" (of the breaking) and so on are stated. There are eighteen grounds that cause schism:

"Upāli, here in this Dispensation, monks explain non-Dhamma as Dhamma, and they explain Dhamma as non-Dhamma. They explain non-Vinaya as Vinaya, and they explain Vinaya as non-Vinaya. They explain what was not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata as spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata. They explain what was spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata as not spoken or uttered. They explain what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as practiced by the Tathāgata. They explain what was practiced by the Tathāgata as not practiced. They explain what was not prescribed by the Tathāgata as prescribed by the Tathāgata. They explain what was prescribed by the Tathāgata as..."
251:
They represent what was not prescribed by the Tathāgata as 'prescribed by the Tathāgata'. They represent what is not an offense as 'an offense', and what is an offense as 'not an offense'. They represent a light offense as 'a grave offense', and a grave offense as 'a light offense'. They represent an offense with a remainder as 'an offense without a remainder', and an offense without a remainder as 'an offense with a remainder'. They represent a gross offense as 'not a gross offense', and an offense that is not gross as 'a gross offense'. (Cūḷavagga, 352).

In this way, there are eighteen kinds by way of the eighteen grounds for causing schism taught in the Kammakhandhaka. Because the effect exists in connection with that cause, the cause is here called 'basis' (vatthu). Regarding this matter, there are also summary verses:

"Dhamma, Vinaya, what was spoken, practice, and prescriptions—these are the pairs; offenses, lightness, grossness, and having a remainder—these are the pairs.

These eighteen are called 'the bases for causing schism'; they are held with perverted views and are dependent on the root of contention."

'Paggayha' means that which is upheld, raised up, or made manifest. 'Tiṭṭheyya' means to remain acting exactly as one has undertaken or upheld. Because a monk who thus upholds and stands by [his view] both manifests that cause and does not relinquish it, it is said: "He should both manifest it and not relinquish it." To the question of how far away monks might hear [of the schism] and yet incur a dukkaṭa offense for not going to speak out, it is said: "By the lowest limit," and so on. In this context, although the word "pi" is used in an unusual position, it should be understood in connection with the phrase "about half a yojana." In that sentence, the phrase "about half a yojana" indicates that if it occurs within a single monastery, there is no need even to mention it (as it is obvious). By the word "having gone," it indicates that for a monk who speaks by sending a messenger or a letter, there is no release from the offense; rather, he must go in person and prevent it, saying: "Friend, schism in the Saṅgha is very serious; do not strive for schism in the Saṅgha."

'Samāgacchatu' means let them become united. Since unity occurs by way of having the same doctrine, it is said: "Let him be one of the same doctrine." 'Ekaladdhika' means one who has the same doctrine or the same view. 'Aññamaññasampattiyā' means by the fulfillment of having mutual views and thoughts that are the same. Some say, "By the attainment of each other's virtues such as morality..."
252:
Some [teachers] say "by way of attainment (sampatti)." Indeed, a discordant Saṅgha recites the Pātimokkha separately, either outside the boundary (sīmā) or in each individual cell (pariveṇa); thus, it is not a unified recitation. Therefore, [the author of the Vinayasaṅgaha] said: "It has the meaning of the recitation of the Pātimokkha proceeding in unity." The phrase "a dukkaṭa offense for not relinquishing" means that a dukkaṭa offense is incurred according to the number of monks who individually speak and admonish him. "A formal act of admonition (samanubhāsana-kamma) should be performed" means that the formal act of admonition should be performed up to three times. By the words "with three proclamations of a formal act consisting of a motion and four parts (ñatticatuttha-kamma) as stated in the Word-Analysis (Padabhājana), beginning with 'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me; this monk named so-and-so is striving for the schism of the unified Saṅgha' (Pārājika, 413)," it is meant that the act should be performed. Because it is stated separately as "should he strive for schism," it should be understood that the formal act of admonition should be performed for a monk who strives for schism by seeking a faction and so on, even before he takes up and upholds the legal issue that leads to schism. Because there is no offense for a monk who relinquishes [his view], it is said: "There is safety (well-being) for that monk."

Although a bhikkhunī cannot actually split the Saṅgha, because she can strive for schism, it is called a "common prescription" (sādhāraṇa-paññatti). For a monk who is committing a saṅghādisesa offense, the dukkaṭa offense from the motion (ñatti) and the thullaccaya offenses from the two proclamations (kammavācā) are subsided; therefore, "samanubhāsanakamme" and so on were said. That the dukkaṭa and thullaccaya offenses subside means that the dukkaṭa incurred at the end of the motion and the thullaccayas incurred by the two proclamations—these three offenses subside just as uncommon offenses subside due to a change of gender. However, if at the conclusion of the motion, a sense of shame (lajji-dhamma) enters him, restraint arises, and he relinquishes that schism, he is released after confessing the dukkaṭa incurred by the motion. But if he does not relinquish it and continues to strive for schism, taking up and persisting in the legal issue that leads to schism, the dukkaṭa of the motion subsides and he stands in the thullaccaya offense at the first proclamation. This same method should be understood for the remaining proclamations. As long as he has not yet been admonished by the formal act of admonition, even if he does not relinquish it, he does not yet incur a saṅghādisesa offense. Also, for a monk who relinquishes, if he relinquishes before the motion, at the moment of the motion, at the conclusion of the motion, or during the first, second, or third proclamations before reaching the syllable "ya," he does not incur a saṅghādisesa offense. Therefore, "asamanubhāsiyamānassa ca" and so on were said.

In this training rule, however, because it is stated in the Parivāra, "Devadatta strove for the schism of the unified Saṅgha; in that matter [it was prescribed]" (Parivāra, 17), Devadatta is the first doer (ādikammika). And that Devadatta...
253:
Devadatta only strove for a schism in the Saṅgha; he was not one who did not give up his view. This is because that [formal] act [of exhortation] was not performed against that Devadatta. How is this to be known? It is known through the Suttas (canonical texts). For it is stated in the Parivāra: "The monk Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture-killer lineage, did not give up that matter despite being exhorted three times regarding his evil wrong view." Thus it is known that the act was performed against Ariṭṭha, but it is not evident that it was so for Devadatta.

If someone were to say out of their own preference, "The act should have been performed against that Devadatta as well," even if they said so, there is no offense for the originator (ādikammika) in not giving up the view. This is because there is no such thing as being free from an offense for one who transgresses a prescribed training rule, except for cases specifically allowed. The writing of "ādikammikassa" (for the originator) in the section on non-offense (anāpatti-vāra) in the word-analysis (padabhājana) of the Ariṭṭha training rule in some books is merely a scribal error (pamādalikhita). That it is a scribal error is known because the imposition of an offense is shown in the Kammakkhandhaka as follows: "First, the monk Ariṭṭha should be reproved; having been reproved, he should be made to remember the fault; having been made to remember, the offense should be imposed."

In this training rule [on schism], regarding the striving for a schism, since that [formal] act was not performed against Devadatta, who was the originator, the offense itself had not yet arisen for him. However, because the training rule was prescribed with reference to Devadatta, he is called the "originator" (ādikammika). Thus, it is because of the absence of an offense that it is said there was no offense (anāpatti) for him. Although this non-offense is established by the phrase "asamannubhāsiyamānassa" (for one who has not yet been exhorted), the term "asamannubhāsiyamāna" refers to one for whom the exhortation is simply not performed, not the originator. This Devadatta is indeed the originator. Therefore, it is said "ādikammikassa." By this same method, the decision in all [rules involving] exhortation (samannubhāsana) should be understood, excluding the Ariṭṭha training rule.

There is the origin of exhortation (samannubhāsana-samuṭṭhāna) because it arises from body, speech, and mind. It is a non-action (akiriya) because the offense is incurred by one who does not perform any bodily movement or verbal utterance saying, "I give it up." It is a release through perception (saññāvimokkha) because one is freed from the offense in the absence of the perception "I do not give it up." It is with intention (sacittaka) because it occurs only with the mind that knows "I do not give it up."

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Schism in the Saṅgha is finished.
254:
## 11. Commentary on the Training Rule on Following the Schismatic

'Tasseva' means only of the one striving for schism. 'Kho' is merely a particle. 'Pana' is a particle used in a distinctive sense. The words that cause discord, which divide even a harmonious group into fragments, are here called 'vagga'; thus it is said, "they speak words siding with a divided group." 'Asāmaggi-pakkhiyā' means those who exist in a side of disharmony, the makers of discord; their speech is 'asāmaggi-pakkhiya-vacana'. Alternatively, speech that exists in a side of disharmony is 'asāmaggi-pakkhiya-vacana'. The statement "The Saṅgha does not perform a [legal] act against the Saṅgha" is said with reference to an act performed by way of punishment; however, acts such as Ubbāhikā (referral to a committee) are indeed suitable to be performed even by many monks. 'Dhamma-vādī' means a speaker of what is real. 'Vinaya-vādī' means a speaker of settlement. In the phrase 'jānāti no', the words 'desire and preference' (chanda and ruci) should be brought in and connected. Therefore, it is said, "he knows our desires and so forth." In the word 'bhāsati', the word 'no' is joined by changing the grammatical case. Therefore, it is said, "he speaks with us, saying 'let us act in this way'." By the word 'etaṃ', that monk's action is referred back to; thus it is said, "whatever act he performs," and so on. 'So' refers to that monk striving for a schism in the Saṅgha. In the phrase 'sametāyasmantānaṃ', the word 'cittaṃ' (mind) should be supplied; thus it is said, "may the minds of the venerable ones be in agreement." The phrase 'vuttasadisāyeva' means that what should be said here is the same as what was already said below in the commentary on the Aññabhāgiya training rule.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Following the Schismatic is finished.

## 12. Commentary on the Training Rule on Being Difficult to Speak to

One who is difficult to speak to, whose nature is such that he cannot be instructed or admonished, is 'dubbaca-jātika', one of a contrary nature. Therefore, it is said, "of a nature difficult to speak to," and so on. 'Unable to be spoken to' means unable to be admonished because of intolerance when something is being said. 'Uddesīyati' refers to the recitation, the Pātimokkha; those [rules] included or contained within that recitation are 'uddesa-pariyāpanna'. It means "among those included in the recitation." Therefore, it is said, "in the recitation," and so on. Now, if one asks how all training rules are included in the Pātimokkha recitation, it is said, "Because they are collected thus: 'If there be an offense, let him disclose it'." By this statement, "If there be an offense," all offenses are indeed collected in the recitation. This meaning should be understood in the context of the Vinaya training rules which are the cause for obtaining the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā).
255: By this statement, all offenses are included in the Nidānuddesa. "In the training rules" means in the Vinaya regulations which are the means for attaining the higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā). Because this point is very clear, it was not mentioned in the Commentary. "With the five fellow-dhamma practitioners" refers to monks, nuns, male novices, female novices, and female trainees (sikkhamānā). "Because they should be practiced" means practiced according to one's ability. In fact, they practice only the training rules relevant to them, not all. "Prescribed by the Buddha" means established or ordained by the Buddha. Alternatively, it should be understood here as 'spoken with reason and Dhamma'. In the word "for the purpose of speaking" (vacanāya), the dative case is taken in the sense of the ablative, meaning "because of that speech of mine". ## The Explanation of the Dubbaca Sikkhāpada is finished. ## 13. Explanation of the Kuladūsaka Sikkhāpada. Since a city is a specific type of village, by taking "village" in this training rule, "city" is also included; thus it is said, "a city is also comprised within a village." Alternatively, it is taken by the word "vā" (or) which has the sense of an unstated alternative. Here, the distinction between these three should be noted: a place with a market but without a surrounding wall is a market town (nigama); a place with both a wall and a market is a city (nagara); and a place different from these two is a village (gāma). "Corrupts families" means causing the four types of families—Khattiya, Brāhmaṇa, Vessa, and Sudda—to fall into corruption. In corrupting them, it is not with impurities or mud, but rather destroying their faith through one's own bad conduct. Therefore, it is said, "by giving flowers, etc." In that context, giving flowers belonging to oneself to any person who has come to one, either by bringing them oneself, having them brought, calling them oneself, or having them called, for the sake of currying favor with families, is called "giving flowers". "Giving flowers, etc." refers to those things beginning with giving flowers. By the word "etc.", one should include giving fruits, aromatic powder, clay, tooth-sticks, bamboo, providing medical treatment, and acting as a messenger on foot. "Destroys faith" means causing people to lose confidence in or not want to see other virtuous monks who do not perform such acts like giving flowers. Because of the favors done through giving flowers and so on, those people envy other virtuous monks who do not do so and do not associate with them. Thus, it should be understood that such a monk destroys the people's faith. "Evil habits" means those that are low because they are loathed by the Buddha...
256:
...evil habits. Since those habits, such as planting young flowering plants for the sake of gaining favor with families, are intended here, it is said, "planting young flowering plants, etc." However, for the benefit of the monastery (ārāma), etc., planting through allowable expressions (kappiya-vohāra), etc., is permissible.

In that context, "young flowering plant" (mālāvaccha) refers to a young flower tree. Both young flower trees and flower bushes are called "mālāvaccha." Planting such a young flowering plant is mālāvaccharopana. Those acts beginning with such planting are called mālāvaccharopanādayo. Here, the word "etc." (ādi) includes having them planted, watering them oneself, having them watered, picking flowers oneself, having them picked, stringing them into garlands oneself, and having them strung.

In the Mātikā, "are seen" means they are seen by those who see them directly. "Are heard" means they are heard and noted through the ear-door by those who hear from others. "Dūṭṭhāni" means corrupted (spoiled in conduct). "Enough of your staying here" (alaṃ te idha vāsena) means your staying in this monastery is not suitable; let your staying here not happen. Here, the word "alaṃ" has the sense of prohibition.

"One who has been subjected to the act of banishment" (pabbājanīyakammakata) refers to a monk upon whom the act of banishment has been performed by a formal act with a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatutthakammavācā) as stated in the word-analysis (padabhājana), beginning with "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs, these Assaji and Punabbhasuka...", after having reproved him, made him remember the offense, and charged him with the offense. "In whatever monastery he lives" refers to a monastery located outside the village.

"In that village... not allowed to roam" means even if the village or market town is up to twelve yojanas in extent, and the monastery is up to three yojanas in extent, just as he is not allowed to roam for alms in that village or market town, he is also not allowed to stay in that monastery. One staying in that monastery must not roam for alms even in a nearby village; one staying in a nearby monastery must not roam for alms in that village. However, it is permissible for one staying in a nearby monastery to roam for alms in a nearby village.

"Offenses to be incurred" (āpajjitabbā āpattiyo) are: a dukkaṭa offense for giving one's own property to gain favor with families; a thullaccaya offense for giving the Saṅgha's property by exercising authority; and a pārājika offense for giving by force. In the Mātikā, the phrase "since he departs" is spoken in terms of the duties of a monk who has undergone the act of banishment. At the beginning, however, it should be understood in terms of the act of banishment itself. "Assajipunabbhasuke" refers to the monk Assaji and the monk Punabbhasuka.

## The explanation of the Kuladūsaka-sikkhāpada is finished.
257:
## Commentary on the Conclusion of Saṅghādisesa

In the term "Paṭhamāpattikā," although the analysis is done by its individual parts, the meaning of the compound as a whole is obtained. Therefore, the author stated, "The first of these offenses is called Paṭhamāpattikā." The phrase "only at the moment of transgression" means it occurs only at the moment of transgressing the basis (vatthu). By the word "only" (eva), the moment of performing the formal act of admonition (samanubhāsana) is excluded. The duration of days is called "yāvatīhaṃ." Therefore, the author stated, "as many days as there are." It should be understood that "ahāni" means days.

"By way of the basis" means by way of the mere transgression such as the emission of semen. "This" refers to this transgression. "By way of the name only" means by way of the name, such as "an offense of such-and-such a name" or "this is an offense called Saṅghādisesa," excluding the basis. Here, the word "matta" (mere/only) excludes the basis. Although some palm-leaf manuscripts write "nāmagottavasena" (by way of name and lineage), such writing is not good because it has already been stated as "an offense of such-and-such a name." The connection should be made as: "Now I will not tell this offense to anyone." "Relinquishing the burden" means giving up the effort to report it. It should be understood that it is not only the offense of one who conceals it while being mindful of it as an offense by way of basis and name that is concealed; rather, even for one who does not know [the basis and name] but conceals it with the mere perception of an offense, thinking "I will conceal the offense," it is also considered concealed.

However, if in this offense one perceives it as a non-offense, or perceives it as a different class of offense, or is in doubt, and with the desire to conceal it, relinquishing the burden, lets the dawn rise, it should be applied as being "not concealed" (acchannā). As for a non-offense, whether one conceals it perceiving it as an offense or perceiving it as a non-offense, it remains not concealed. If one conceals a light offense as heavy, or a heavy offense as light, he stands on the side of the shameless (alajjī). However, the offense is not concealed. If one confesses a heavy offense thinking it is light, it is neither confessed nor concealed.

One is called "Pakatatta" because he has a self (virtue) that is in its natural state. The meaning is one whose self is not altered by legal acts (kamma). Therefore, the author stated, "one who is not suspended and is of equal communion." "Only by the aforementioned method" means only by the method already stated, such as "Now I will not tell this offense to anyone." If one conceals it perceiving himself as not being a pakatatta, thinking "A legal act has been performed against me by the Saṅgha," it is not concealed. Whether one who is not a pakatatta perceives himself as a pakatatta, or one who is a pakatatta perceives himself as not being a pakatatta, if they conceal it, it is not concealed. And this has also been said:

Whoever has reached a Saṅghādisesa offense,
And conceals it out of disrespect.
Who that person is should be considered by the wise.
This question was spoken by a suspended monk.

I have already mentioned below the words to be spoken regarding the ten dangers. If a monk is of a fearful nature and conceals it in the dark because he perceives a danger from ghosts or wild beasts, that monk's offense is not concealed.
258:
“Whoever reaches a remaining heavy offense (Saṅghādisesa), and conceals it out of disrespect; he is not a nun, nor does he touch the fault; this question is considered by the wise who are skilled in the Vinaya.” (Parivāra 481).

This question was spoken by a person who has been suspended (ukkhittaka) by the Saṅgha. The explanation regarding the ten dangers has already been stated in the introduction (Nidāna). If a monk, being of a fearful nature, conceals an offense in the dark because he perceives danger from ghosts or fierce wild beasts, it is not considered concealed. For a monk living in a mountain monastery who must cross a gorge or a river to report an offense, if there are dangers such as fierce wild beasts or ghosts on the way, or if pythons are lying on the path, or if the river is in flood—if he conceals it while perceiving such dangers, it is not considered concealed. For one who has a real danger, whether he perceives it as a danger or as a non-danger, if he conceals it, it is not considered concealed.

“Bhikkhuno” refers to a monk of the same category (sabhāga). If there is a small boil in that monk's mouth, or if he suffers from lockjaw, or has a toothache, or has received very little alms-food, he is not actually unable to speak or travel due to such reasons. However, if he perceives, “I am unable,” he is called one who perceives himself as unable while being able. Even if this monk conceals it, it is not considered concealed. For a monk who is truly unable to speak or travel, whether he perceives himself as able or unable, if he conceals it, it is not considered concealed.

In the statement, “These two factors have a clear meaning,” if a monk relinquishes the burden thinking, “I will conceal it,” and enters into a state of shame in the morning, afternoon, or the first watch of the night, but reports it before dawn, he is said to be one who desires to conceal but does not actually conceal.

If a monk living in a place where there are no other monks commits an offense and, while waiting for the arrival of a monk of the same category or while traveling to find one, a half-month or a month passes, he is said to be one who conceals it even though he does not desire to conceal it. This offense is also not considered concealed.
259:
If a monk, immediately upon committing an offense, departs quickly like a man who has stepped on fire, goes to where a fellow monk (sabhāga) is, and discloses it, he is said not to conceal it, as he has no desire to conceal. "Sabhāga-matta-meva pamāṇaṃ" means that the standard is simply being a fellow monk who is not an enemy. This is because the disclosure should be made only in the presence of a fellow monk who is not an enemy. If a monk is one who is not on good terms (visabhāga) and has a desire to disparage or blame upon hearing it, the disclosure should not be made to such a person, even if he is one's own preceptor (upajjhāya). In such a case of committing an offense, whether it occurs in the morning, evening, day, or night, it must be disclosed before the dawn rises. If the dawn rises, it is considered concealed, and due to that concealment, one incurs a dukkaṭa offense. "Saṅkhepato" means in brief. In detail, it should be understood as stated in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary.

"Akāmā parivatthabbaṃ" means that if an offense is left without remedy, it becomes an obstacle to heaven and liberation (sagga-mokkha); therefore, one must undergo probation (parivāsa) even if one does not wish to. Thus, it is said "na kāmena," and so forth. "Parivāsaṃ samādāya" means undertaking the duties of probation in the midst of the Saṅgha. Although there are four types of probation—appaṭicchanna-parivāsa, paṭicchanna-parivāsa, suddhanta-parivāsa, and samodhāna-parivāsa—here, since appaṭicchanna-parivāsa is not intended, only three types are mentioned: "tattha paṭicchanna... tividho parivāso." "Tattha" refers to that sentence. Probation given when there is a concealed offense is called paṭicchanna-parivāsa because it pertains to concealment. Probation given starting from the end of the period of purification is called suddhanta-parivāsa. Probation given by combining (offenses) is called samodhāna-parivāsa.

Now, to show those three types of probation by way of their specific forms, the text says "tattha," and so forth. "Hi" means "because."
