An offense concealed for a whole day is called "ekāha-paṭicchanna." "Vutta-nayena" means according to the method already mentioned, such as "āpatti ca hoti," and so forth. In this context of "ekāha-paṭicchannaṃ," the word "iti" carries the meaning of "and so forth" (ādi-attha), as in the usage "iti vā, iti evarūpā..." By this word "iti" meaning "and so forth," the remaining Pali text should be included: "Venerable Sir, I, for that one offense of intentional emission of semen (sañcetanika sukka-vissaṭṭhi) concealed for one day, request one day of probation from the Saṅgha." After having him request probation three times in this manner, "according to the method found in the Khandhaka" means according to the method described in the Samuccaya-khandhaka. "Tato" means...
260:
Starting from a fortnight (pakkha), which is half a month. "Atireka-pakkha-paṭicchanna" means an offense concealed for a period exceeding one fortnight. "Tato" means starting from the thirtieth day. "Māsa-paṭicchanna" means an offense concealed for thirty days and nights, called "māsa" (month) because it seems to encompass or bring an end to the life of beings. "Saṃvacchere puṇṇe" means when a period of twelve months, called "saṃvacchara" (year), is completed, which occurs in accordance with the existence of various beings and the occurrence of the Dhamma.

"Vatthu-kittana-vasena vā" means by way of mentioning the substance (vatthu) along with the name. Therefore, it should be understood that the word "matta" (only) is used above in "nāma-matta-vasena vā." "Nāma-matta-vasena" means by way of the name only, without mentioning the substance. Since there are two kinds of names, and the name "āpatti" (offense) is a general name applicable to all, the text says "tasmā." "Sukka-vissaṭṭhi" is the name of this offense. Here, the word "iti" indicates the meaning to be spoken. This is merely an illustration, as terms like "kāya-saṃsaggi" (physical contact) and others are also desired as the substance (vatthu), and so forth. It is called "vatthu" because it is a transgression, and it is called "gotta" (lineage) because it is not shared with other offenses. "Gotta" is so called because it protects wisdom and speech. It means it protects wisdom and speech by not allowing them to go from its own kind to other offenses such as physical contact (kāya-saṃsaggi). This offense is named "saṅghādisesa." Here, the word "iti" indicates the combination of the word and the thing named. Therefore, it is said "nāmañceva āpatti ca" (both the name and the offense). It is called "nāma" because it is a name common to its own kind, and it is called "āpatti" because it is to be reached through that particular transgression. This too is merely an illustration, as the term "āpattiyo" is also desired as a name, and so forth. Alternatively, the word "iti" has the meaning of "and so forth." By doing so, phrases such as "kāya-saṃsagganti ādi vacanenāpi" are also established.

With reference to the inquiry as to which word in the formal act (kammavācā) this action is taken by, the text says "tattha," and so forth. Because "āpatti" is a general name common to all and is reached through transgression, it is both a name and an offense; thus it is said "āpattiyoti vacanenāpi." Because it is proper to perform this Vinaya act of probation, etc., by way of the substance (vatthu), the lineage (gotta), the name (nāma), and the offense (āpatti), the text says "tasmā." "Etesu" means in those substances, etc., or in sukka-vissaṭṭhi, etc. "Vattaṃ samādātabbaṃ" means it should be undertaken by even one of the two aforementioned terms. However, if undertaken by both, it is very well undertaken. Therefore, it will be said later: "In the case of undertaking (samādāna), the method is the same."
261: "Ārocetvā" (having informed) means:— "Venerable sirs, I have committed one offense of intentional emission of semen (sukka-vissaṭṭhi) and concealed it for one day. I requested the Saṅgha for one day of probation (parivāsa) for that one offense of intentional emission of semen concealed for one day. The Saṅgha granted me one day of probation for that offense. I am now undergoing that probation. Venerable sirs, I inform you (of my probation). May the Saṅgha recognize me as one who informs."—having informed in accordance with the respective grammatical construction (yojanā) in this manner. Taking this meaning, it is also permissible to inform in any language. "The person who informs monks as they arrive" is said with reference to visiting monks (āgantuka). In this context, if informing a single monk, one should say at the end: "May the venerable one recognize me as one who informs." If informing two: "May the venerable ones recognize me as one who informs." If informing three: "May the venerable ones recognize me as one who informs." Without breaking the duties and without the interruption of the night means:—"Monks, a monk on probation should not consent to the salutation or the rising from the seat of regular monks (pakatatta)," etc. It means without breaking the ninety-four duties mentioned in the Parivāsika-khandhaka, and without the "interruption of the night" (ratticcheda) mentioned as: "Upāli, there are three interruptions of the night for a monk on probation: living together, living apart, and not informing." The decision here is: If visiting monks pass through the middle of the monastery, whether they rest for a moment or not, they must be informed. If they leave while the monk (on probation) is unaware, and he finds out after they have gone, he must go and inform them. If he is unable to reach them, only the interruption of the night occurs, not the dukkaṭa offense of breaking the duty. Even if they do not enter the monastery but pass through the precinct (upacāra-sīmā), if he knows they are visitors just by hearing the sound of an umbrella, a cough, or a sneeze, he must go and inform them. Even one who finds out after they have gone must follow and inform them. If he is unable to reach them, only the interruption of the night occurs, not the dukkaṭa offense of breaking the duty. One who comes during the night and leaves during the night also causes the interruption of the night for that monk on probation.
262:
There is no *dukkaṭa* offense for breaking the duties due to ignorance. If one performs the rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) without knowing [of an interruption], it is as if it were not performed; so it is stated in the *Kurundī* Commentary. Therefore, one should perform it by taking extra nights. This is the “unmistaken practice” (*apaṇṇaka-paṭipadā*).

If one sees a monk traveling by boat on a river or the like, or standing on the opposite bank, or traveling through the air, or at a distance at the foot of a mountain or in a forest, etc., and can identify him as a monk, one must inform him by going by boat, or by making a loud sound, or by following quickly. If one does not inform, there is both an interruption of the night and a *dukkaṭa* offense for breaking the duties. If, despite making an effort, one is unable to catch up or make oneself heard, it is only an interruption of the night; there is no *dukkaṭa* offense for breaking the duties.

When going to any other monastery, one must also inform the monks. If one sees all of them in one place, one should inform them while they are there. If they are in various places, such as under trees, one must go to those respective places and inform them. If one intentionally fails to inform, there is both an interruption of the night and a *dukkaṭa* offense. If, while searching, one does not see some of them, it is only an interruption of the night; there is no *dukkaṭa* offense. However, if one intentionally fails to inform, there is both an interruption of the night and a *dukkaṭa* offense.

“In that very place” means only within the *māḷaka* precinct. When monks leave the *māḷaka*, it is permissible to deposit (*nikkhipitုံ*) the duties in the presence of even a single monk. A monk who remembers after leaving the *māḷaka* must deposit the duties in the presence of a monk traveling with him. Therefore, it is said: “or in the presence of a single person.” If that traveling companion also departs, one must inform and deposit the duties with another monk who was not informed at the *māḷaka*.

“The place where regular monks (*pakatatta*) are” refers to a place suitable for performing *Saṅghakamma*. “Beyond two stone-throws” is said for the purpose of leaving the vicinity (*upacāra*) where the sound of monks reciting can be heard. “Turning away from the main road” is said for the purpose of leaving the vicinity of monks traveling on the road. “In a place concealed by a thicket or a fence” is said for the purpose of leaving the vicinity of sight.

“One must inform after undertaking the duties” means that one must undertake the duties and inform about the probation (*parivāsa*) in the manner already described. “One must inform” is stated in a general sense. When informing, if the other is junior, one should say “Friend (*āvuso*)”. If the other is senior, one should say “Venerable Sir (*bhante*)”. If another monk comes to that place for some business...
263:
If this monk undergoing probation (parivāsa) sees the monk (who has arrived for some business) or hears his voice, he must inform him. For a monk who does not inform, there is both an interruption of the night (ratticcheda) and a breach of duty (vattabheda). Therefore, the author of the Saṅgaha stated: "Whichever other monk he sees, he must inform that monk as well." If this monk undergoing probation enters the precinct (upacāra) of twelve cubits and goes without knowing, there is only an interruption of the night (ratticcheda), but no breach of duty (vattabheda).

"Uṭṭhite" means when the sun has risen. "Yaṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ bhikkhuṃ" refers to whichever other monk is seen first among all monks, whether it be a monk leaving the monastery or a visiting monk. The statement that he must inform that monk means that for a monk who does not inform, there would be an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa); the author of the Saṅgaha said this with reference to that dukkaṭa offense, not with reference to the interruption of the night (ratticcheda). Otherwise (if it were intended for the interruption of the night), the author of the Saṅgaha would have said, "having informed all the monks belonging to the monastery boundary (sīmā)."

"Yāva rattiyo pūrenti" means that for as many nights as the offense was concealed, he must undergo probation until those many nights are fulfilled. However, in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary, it is stated: "In this way, for as many days as the offense was concealed, he undergoes probation for that many days, or for more days than that, in order to dispel remorse (kukkucca)." "Vitthāro" means elaboration (papañca).

"Itaresu pana dvīsu" means in the midst of the two types of probation: Suddhantaparivāsa and Samodhānaparivāsa. "Khandhake" means in the Samuccayakkhandhaka of the Cūḷavagga. Regarding the terms Cūḷasuddhanta and Mahāsuddhanta (I shall state the Vinaya decision): Whichever monk, from the time he became a monk in direct order, or from the day he reported the offense in reverse order, is asked, "Do you know your state of purity for this many named days, fortnights, months, or years?" and he says, "Yes, Bhante, I know; I have been pure for this much time," the Suddhantaparivāsa given to that monk is called "Cūḷasuddhanta."

A monk undergoing that Cūḷasuddhanta probation should subtract the amount of time he knows his state of purity and undergo probation for the remaining one month or two months. If he took the probation marking it as "I have been impure for only one month," and while undergoing probation he remembers another month, he must undergo probation for that remembered month as well; there is no need for the act of giving probation again. If he took the probation marking it as "I have been impure for two months," and while undergoing probation he decides "I have been impure for only one month," he needs to undergo probation for only one month; there is no need for the act of giving probation again. For this Suddhantaparivāsa goes up (increases) and also comes down (decreases); this is its characteristic. Whichever monk, though questioned by way of the aforementioned direct and reverse order, does not know the limit of the nights, does not remember, or has doubt regarding the limit of the nights, the Suddhantaparivāsa given to him is called "Mahāsuddhanta."
264:
Whichever monk, though questioned by way of the aforementioned direct and reverse order, does not know the limit of the nights, does not remember, or has doubt regarding the limit of the nights, the Suddhantaparivāsa given to him is called "Mahāsuddhanta." Having taken that Mahāsuddhanta probation, he must count the nights from the day it was taken back to the day of his higher ordination (upasampadā) and undergo probation. This Mahāsuddhanta does not go up, but it does come down. Therefore, if while undergoing probation he makes a decision regarding the limit of the nights, thinking "My offense was for one month or one year," he must undergo probation for that month or year. In this matter, although Cūḷasuddhanta is given to one who says "I have been pure for this much time," it is said that "both of these should be given" because there is not always certain knowledge. The statement that the procedure for giving that Suddhantaparivāsa appears in the Khandhaka means that the procedure for giving both types of Suddhanta appears in the Samuccayakkhandhaka of the Cūḷavagga, beginning with "Therefore, monks, that monk should approach the Saṅgha... and should speak thus." Therefore, the meaning is that it should be understood according to the method stated there. This method of decision is stated in detail in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary.

Combining by shaking off and abandoning is called Odhānasamodhāna. Combining by the value of offenses concealed for a long time is called Agghasamodhāna. Combining mixed offenses is called Missakasamodhāna. Now, to show those three types of Samodhānaparivāsa in brief, he said the words beginning with "Tattha." "Antarāpattiṃ āpajjitvā paṭicchādentassa" refers to a monk who, having taken probation and undergoing it without having laid down the duties (vatta), commits another Saṅghādisesa offense in the interval before the probation is completed and conceals it. "Parivutthadivase" is a term for close marking; by that term, the meaning "also on the days when Mānatta is being practiced" is also stated. "Makkhetvā" means clearing by way of returning to the beginning (mūlāya paṭikassana) through a formal act with one motion and three proclamations (ñatticatuttha kamma). "Samodahitvā" means placing at the position of the original offense, or including it. "Dātabbaparivāso" refers to the probation given by a formal act with one motion and three proclamations beginning with "Bhante, let the Saṅgha listen to me." The intended meaning is this: Whichever monk, having taken probation for a concealed offense, while undergoing it, or while being worthy of Mānatta, or while practicing Mānatta, or while being worthy of Abbhāna, without having laid down the duties, commits another offense that is equal to or less than the previous offense...
265:
If a monk has concealed the nights, he is returned to the beginning (mūlāya paṭikassana). By doing so, the days already spent in probation and the days already spent in manatta are all discarded and rendered as non-days; then, the newly committed offense is combined with the original offense, and probation (parivāsa) is granted.

If, however, an intervening offense (antarāpatti) has been concealed for a longer period than the original offense (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 102), that intervening offense is made the base, the other offense is combined with it, and probation is granted. If the intervening offense is unconcealed, one should continue with the previously undertaken probation without returning to the beginning.

"Ya ekā vā...pe... sabbacirappaṭicchannāyo" means either a single offense that has been concealed longer than all other offenses, or two, three, or many offenses that have been concealed longer than all others. "Tāsaṃ" refers to those longest-concealed offenses. The procedure for granting these should be understood according to the method taught in the (Cūḷavagga) Samuccayakkhandhaka.

Suppose a monk has one hundred offenses concealed for ten days each, another hundred offenses concealed for ten days each, and another hundred offenses concealed for ten days each. By doing this ten times, there are one thousand offenses concealed for one hundred days. What should that monk do? He should combine all offenses and observe probation for ten days. In this way, by a single ten-day period, the one hundred days are considered observed. Concerning this, it is stated:

"A monk undergoing probation, having concealed
A thousand offenses for a hundred nights,
By living for ten nights (of probation),
May be released from those offenses."

This is called combination by value (agghasamodhāna).

Now, to describe mixed combination (missakasamodhāna), the text begins with "Missakasamodhāno nāma." The method to be understood therein is as follows:

(The monk should state:) "Venerable sirs, I have committed many Saṅghādisesa offenses: one sukka-vissaṭṭhi offense, one kāya-saṃsagga offense, one duṭṭhullavācā offense, one attakāma offense, one sañcaritta offense, one kuṭikāra offense, one vihārakāra offense, one duṭṭhadosa offense, one aññabhāgiya offense, one saṅghabheda offense, one bhedānuvattaka offense, one dubbaca offense, and one kuladūsaka offense. Venerable sirs, I request the Sangha for combined probation (samodhāna-parivāsa) for those offenses."
266:
After making him request three times, probation should be granted with a formal act (kammavācā) appropriate to that request. In this context, it is suitable to perform the formal act by combining the offenses according to the subject matter, lineage, name, or the nature of the offense as previously mentioned, such as "I have committed many Saṅghādisesa offenses of various grounds" or "I have committed Saṅghādisesa offenses." This is mixed combination (missakasamodhāna). At the end of all formal acts for probation, the discussion on laying down or not laying down the duties (vatta) should be understood according to the previous method. Because only the general meaning of all three types of combined probation (samodhāna-parivāsa) is stated, and because the detailed decisions (vinicchaya) are not touched upon, it is said, "This is a brief summary of all three types of combined probation." Since the investigation of combination (samodhāna) is a very vast subject, where could one find that investigation without omission? Intending this, it is said, "As for the details..." and so forth.

"Chārattā" (six nights) means: the time when sound is cut off or becomes silent is called "ratti" (night). It means the time when the sounds of beings are stilled. Because six nights are gathered together, or because it is a collection of six nights, it is called "charatta." "Charatta" is the same as "chārattā." Since there can be no whole without its parts (individual nights), the meaning is stated as "six nights."

"Granting only manatta without giving probation" means: because the offense was not concealed, and because he becomes worthy of manatta immediately upon committing the offense, only manatta is granted without giving probation. To show that the manatta given to a monk who has already completed probation for a concealed offense is called "concealed manatta" (paṭicchanna-mānatta), it is said, "For whom there is a concealed offense..." and so forth. "This" refers to concealed manatta. "Herein" refers to this sentence. Since one might ask how the procedure for granting and the decision regarding both types of manatta should be understood, it is said, "Of both..." and so forth.

"This" (ayaṃ) refers to the words that will be spoken later. According to the method stated under probation, "region" (padesa) refers to a place two stone-throws away from the enclosure of a monastery that has an enclosure, or from the place where an enclosure should be for a monastery without one, turning away from the main road and being hidden by a thicket or a fence. "Having undertaken" means having undertaken within the time before dawn (aruṇa). "Having announced" means:

"Venerable sirs, I have committed one sukka-vissaṭṭhi offense involving intention, which was not concealed. Venerable sirs, I request the Sangha for the six-night manatta to be observed for that one unconcealed sukka-vissaṭṭhi offense committed with intention."
267:
“I have requested; to me, the Saṅgha has granted six nights of Mānatta (penance) to be practiced for a single Saṅghādisesa offense of intentional emission of semen, which was not concealed. I am practicing that Mānatta. Venerable sirs, I inform you; let the Saṅgha recognize me as one who is informing,” and so forth (Cullavagga Aṭṭhakathā 97). Having informed according to the days of the offense, and taking this meaning, it is permissible to inform in any language. From the time of informing, except for one monk, the remaining monks may go if they have duties to attend to. At dawn, the duties (vatta) should be laid down in the presence of that monk. If that monk also leaves before dawn for some business, the duties should be laid down after informing the first monk encountered, whether he is leaving the monastery or arriving as a guest. Because this monk stays after informing the Saṅgha and noting the presence of the monks, he does not incur the fault of practicing in a deficient group (caraṇadosa) or the fault of being away (vippavāsa). If no monk is found, he should go to the monastery and lay down the duties after informing the first monk he meets. Therefore, the author of the Saṅgaha says, “Beyond that, whether those monks go or do not come, one should practice according to the previous method.”

“Yattha siyā” means in a Samanasaṃvāsaka Sīmā where there is a Bhikkhu Saṅgha numbering twenty. “Avhātabbo” means he should be called by the power of the act of rehabilitation (Abbhāna kamma). To know how the Abbhāna kamma is understood, it is said, “Abbhāna kammaṃ pana,” etc. “Pāḷivasena” means by the power of the Pāḷi text, “Suṇātu me bhante saṅgho,” etc. “Vinicchayavasena” means by the power of the decision: “Monks who wish to be rehabilitated should first perform what is worthy of rehabilitation. Since this monk has laid down his duties, he stands in the position of a regular monk (pakatatta); it is not proper to rehabilitate a regular monk, therefore he should be made to undertake the duties. Only after undertaking the duties is he worthy of rehabilitation. That monk also, having undertaken the duties and informed, should request rehabilitation. For a monk who has not laid down his duties, there is no need to undertake them; he becomes worthy of rehabilitation simply by the passing of six nights,” and so forth (Cullavagga Aṭṭhakathā 97). All these acts, such as the practice of Parivāsa, are easily understood through the Pāḷi and the Commentaries; therefore, for fear of excessive length, they are not detailed here. Those who desire them should take them from that source (Khandhaka).
268:
However, because this Abbhāna act must be performed by a group of twenty, if it is performed by a Saṅgha of fewer than twenty, it is invalid (not firm). Therefore, the author of the Saṅgaha stated, “Ekenāpi ce...pe... anabbhito.” “Ayaṃ” refers to this aforementioned practice (paṭipadā). “Sāmīcī” refers to the conduct (vatta).

## Thus ends the Explanation of Saṅghādisesa
## in the Līnatthappakāsanī Ṭīkā, named Vinayatthamañjūsā,
## in the Commentary on the Pātimokkha, Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī.
269:
## Section on Indefinite (Aniyata) Offenses
## 1. Explanation of the First Aniyata Training Rule
After saying “mātugāmena” (with a woman), it is said again “ekāya” (with one); therefore, it means “with a single woman known as a mātugāma.” A place that is not public is called secluded (raho). Since it is not in the presence of one who would make it a non-offense, the state of being non-public is called secluded. Therefore, it is called “seclusion from the eye.”

“Seclusion means seclusion from the eye and seclusion from the ear. Seclusion from the eye is a place where one cannot be seen even if eyes are blinking, eyebrows are raised, or the head is lifted. Seclusion from the ear is a place where ordinary speech cannot be heard.” Although seclusion from the ear is also shown in the Padabhājana Pāḷi, why is it not mentioned, and only “seclusion from the eye” is stated? This is answered starting with “Kiñcāpi.” By this, it is shown that the words “seclusion from the ear” in the Pāḷi are stated by way of extracting the meaning.

Then how is it known that “only seclusion from the eye is intended here” in this first Aniyata training rule? It is known because of the statement “in a concealed seat” and because it is said “it is possible to indulge in sexual intercourse.” Therefore, the sentence starting with “Sacepi” is said. By the words “for one who has closed the door-leaf,” it is shown that seclusion from the eye is possible due to being concealed. A person sitting at the door of a room where the door is not closed makes it a non-offense. It should be understood that not only one sitting at the door of a room with an unclosed door, but also one sitting within a space of twelve cubits inside the door, makes it a non-offense. Therefore, the sentence starting with “Yattha pana sakkā daṭṭhuṃ” is said.

A person who is dozing while sitting, like a monkey's sleep (kapimiddha), opens his eyes for a short time and closes them for a short time, and does not fall into a deep sleep; therefore, it is said, “even one who is dozing makes it a non-offense.” For one who is dozing while lying down, it is not so; therefore, it is said, “one who is dozing while lying down does not make it a non-offense.” This means he does not make it a non-offense.

In the act of sexual intercourse, a woman is not considered a second companion (witness). This is because women tend to conceal each other's faults. Therefore, in the Great Forest (Mahāvana) at Vesālī, while a monk was lying down with the door open, many women did as they pleased and then left. Therefore, it is said, “even if there are a hundred women, they do not make (a companion).” “That act” refers to the act of misconduct (ajjhācārakamma). Since one only sleeps after sitting...
270:
Therefore, including lying down within the scope of sitting, the author of the Saṅgaha said "one should perform the act of sitting" to show this. "In this matter also" etc. was said. The phrase "should be decided by one of the three rules" means that for a monk who admits to sitting, the application of one of the three rules indeed occurs. Only a monk who admits to sitting in that manner should be decided upon by the Pārājika, Saṅghādisesa, or Pācittiya offenses. One who does not admit should not be decided upon. This means that one who does not admit to sitting should not be decided upon by one of the three rules. Even for a shameless person (alajjī), a decision of an offense is made only upon admission. As long as there is no admission, it should be said "he is neither pure nor impure," but he should be dealt with according to the sequence of the conduct (vattānusandhi). For it has been said:

"Admission is made among the modest (lajjī); such admission does not exist among the shameless (alajjī). Even if the shameless speaks much, one should deal with him according to the sequence of the conduct."

Not only in the accusation by one of the three rules should a decision be made by admission, but also in the accusation together with the manner of sitting etc., a decision should be made by admission. To show this meaning, it was said: "In whatever manner that trustworthy female lay follower (upāsikā) should speak, in that manner that monk should be decided upon." Therefore, it was said "in the manners of sitting etc." etc. Here, although "one who admits" was not explicitly stated by the Buddha, because it is the subject (adhikāra), the author of the Saṅgaha said "only the one who admits should be decided upon in that manner." Since there is no deviation in the words of such a female lay follower, the phrase "what is seen is indeed so, or it is otherwise" shows the possibility of it being otherwise in seeing. Because it is not fixed due to being uncertain, it is called "Aniyata" (Indefinite). Therefore, it was said "of the three offenses" etc.

If, due to the enjoyment of sitting in private, one desiring to go near a woman applies eye-salve, a dukkaṭa offense is committed. If he puts on the undergarment, ties the belt, or puts on the robe, a dukkaṭa offense is committed for every effort. If he goes, a dukkaṭa offense is committed for every step. Having gone, if he sits, it is only a dukkaṭa. Therefore, it was said "known as defilement associated with sexual intercourse" etc. Here, even if there is no sexual lust in the enjoyment of sitting in private, because it is a defilement connected to that intercourse, it is called "defilement associated with sexual intercourse." That is why the word "associated" (sannissita) was used. "Due to the enjoyment of privacy" means the enjoyment arising from the thought: "I shall sit in private with such-and-such a woman and engage in laughing, talking, etc."
271:
It is because of the cause of the enjoyment that has arisen that the sitting occurs. If there is no wise man who is not blind, is intelligent, is not sleeping while lying down, and is within the vicinity (upacāra) of 12 cubits, a Pācittiya offense is committed for sitting; this is the meaning of the words "nisajjāya pācittiyaṃ."

If that woman, for some reason, repeatedly gets up and sits down, a Pācittiya offense is committed for every sitting. If, having gone intending to see a certain woman, he does not see her, but another woman comes and sits, and enjoyment arises, a Pācittiya offense is committed. If many women come, Pācittiya offenses are committed according to the number of women. If those women repeatedly get up and sit down, Pācittiya offenses are also committed according to the number of sittings.

For a monk who goes and sits with the thought "I will enjoy sitting in private with whatever woman I see" without specifying, the offenses should be known according to the aforementioned method, based on the women who come and based on the repeated sittings.

"A man of the aforementioned manner" means a man who is not blind and is intelligent. "Being in the vicinity" means being within 12 cubits. If a monk who has gone and sat with a pure mind experiences the desire for the enjoyment of privacy when a woman comes and sits near him, there is no offense for such a monk.

## The Explanation of the First Aniyata Training Rule is Finished.

## 2. The Explanation of the Second Aniyata Training Rule

In the words "na heva kho pana paṭicchannaṃ," it should be understood that courtyards, balconies, etc., which are enclosed from the outside but open inside, are also included within the category of non-secluded places (appaṭicchanna-ṭṭhāna). It was said in the Mahāpaccariya: "Such a place is taken only as a non-secluded place." "Saṅghādisesena vā" means by the Saṅghādisesa offense known as physical contact (kāyasaṃsarga) or lewd speech (duṭṭhullābhāsana). That is why in the Word-for-Word Analysis (Padabhājana), the Buddha said: "If that female lay follower should say: 'Venerable Sir, I saw you sitting and engaging in physical contact with a woman,'" etc.

This training rule comes by way of lewd speech. Having heard lewd speech, even a woman does not conceal it. This is true; in the training rule on lewd speech, those women who were modest left the monastery and caused the monks to be criticized; therefore, in this training rule, it is intended that "even a woman" can make it so that there is no offense. Alternatively, in this training rule, because it is a non-secluded place, even one woman can make it so there is no offense; however, in the first training rule, because it is a secluded place, even a hundred women cannot make it so there is no offense; this is how the meaning should be understood. In the words "anandho abadhiro" (not blind, not deaf), "not blind" is said by way of physical contact, and "not deaf" is said by way of lewd speech.
272:
Regarding the origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth, this training rule has three origins: it arises from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It involves action (kiriya), release by perception (saññāvimokkha), is with consciousness (sacittaka), is a worldly fault (lokavajja), and consists of bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome consciousness, and is associated with two feelings: pleasant and neutral. Therefore, [the author of the Saṅgaha] stated: "In this rule, the origins and so forth are just like those of the Adinnādāna training rule." In this training rule, one who reaches physical contact also speaks coarse words, and while speaking coarse words, he remains seated. Thus, it is said to "arise from body, speech, and mind." Alternatively, it should be understood as referring specifically to the coarse words.

## The Commentary on the Second Aniyata Training Rule is Finished.

"This Aniyata recitation (uddesa) is stated for the purpose of showing the characteristics of whether an offense should be imposed or not; an offense should be dealt with only when the matter is admitted in an accusation based on seeing and so forth, and not otherwise," so say the teachers.

## Thus, in the commentary on the Pātimokkha called Kaṅkhāvitaranī,
## in the work called Vinayatthamañjūsā, which clarifies the hidden meanings (Līnatthappakāsanī),
## the Commentary on the Aniyata is finished.
273:
## Nissaggiya Section
## 1. Robe Chapter (Cīvaravagga)
## 1. Commentary on the Kathina Training Rule

In the phrase 'niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ', it is called 'niṭṭhitacīvara' because it is a robe that is finished. It means when the robe which is the basis for the benefits and the robe that is expected are finished. However, since that robe can reach completion through making it or through destruction and so forth, it is stated: "by the conclusion of the sewing work," and so forth.

In that context, the conclusion of the work of making loops and button-strips that should be done with a needle is called 'sūcikamma-pariyosāna' (conclusion of the sewing work). 'Naṭṭhaṃ' means taken away by thieves and so forth. Such being stolen is also called 'finished' (niṭṭhita) because the concern regarding its making (karanapalibodha) has ended. 'Vinatṭhaṃ' means eaten by termites and so forth. 'Daḍḍhaṃ' means burnt by fire.

'Cīvarāsā upacchinnā' means the expectation that has arisen, thinking 'I will receive a robe from such and such a family,' is cut off. Because the concern regarding making is finished due to these destructions and so forth, it should be known as the 'state of being finished' (niṭṭhitabhāva). Therefore, it is stated: "or by these reasons," and so forth. By this, the absence of concern (palibodha) for the robe is meant. Thus, it is said: "it means when the concern regarding the making of the robe is cut off."

How is this known? It is stated: 'atthatakathinassa hi', and so forth. It is called 'Kathina' because of the sense of collecting the five benefits without letting them go elsewhere; it means 'firm' (thira). A monk who has spread the Kathina is called 'atthatakathina'. The word 'hi' is a particle indicating a reason. In the phrase "he receives that many Kathina benefits," it should be understood by adding "that monk who has spread the Kathina." It means he receives the Kathina benefits such as traveling without taking leave (anāmantacāra) and so forth. Alternatively, the phrase 'atthatakathinassa bhikkhuno' should be connected by changing the case ending to 'atthatakathino bhikkhu'.

The meaning is this: there are two types of concerns (palibodha)—robe concern (cīvarapalibodha) and residence concern (āvāsapalibodha). As long as one of these two concerns exists, one receives the benefits such as traveling without taking leave; if they do not exist, one does not receive them. Why? Because by the term 'niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ', this meaning—that the concern regarding the making of the robe is cut off—is understood.

'Saṅghassa' means by the Saṅgha (saṅghena). Here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (kattar). 'Ubbhate' means when it has been removed by any one of the eight grounds (mātikā) or by internal removal (antarubbhāra).
274:
In that Pali, 'tatra' means in that Kathina. 'Ubbhāro' means removal (cancellation). Regarding the approximately thirty monks from Pāveyya who had completed the first rainy season retreat (purimavassa), the Blessed One allowed the Kathina in the Kathinakkhandhaka (Mahāvagga 306), saying: 'Monks, I allow monks who have completed the rainy season retreat to spread the Kathina.' Thus it is said, 'This spreading of the Kathina is allowed.'

In that context, 'purimavassa-vuṭṭhānaṃ' means for monks who have resided for the first rainy season retreat without any breach. By this term, it is shown that only those monks who entered the first retreat (purimikā) obtain the benefits of spreading the Kathina, and not those who entered the second retreat (pacchimikā). Let it be so regarding the completion of the retreat; as for the number, how many monks are required to obtain the spreading of the Kathina? It is said starting with 'so'. 'So' refers to that spreading of the Kathina. 'Sabbantimena paricchedena' means by the minimum limit in terms of number. It is valid if there are five persons. This means it is valid if there are five persons: four donors of the Kathina cloth and one recipient as the minimum limit.

Some teachers say, 'It is valid for five persons because it is a five-fold act (pañcavaggakaraṇīya),' but that is merely their opinion. This is because it is stated in the Campeyyakkhhandhaka (Mahāvagga 388): 'Monks, a group of four monks (catuvagga), excluding three acts—Ordination (Upasampadā), Pavāraṇā, and Abbhāna—[can perform other acts].'

Therefore, it is said so because it is allowed for those who completed the first retreat and because it is valid with a minimum of five persons. 'Yattha' means in that monastery. 'Ānisaṃse' refers to the Kathina benefits such as anāmantacāra (traveling without informing), etc.

However, if four monks have entered the retreat and one novice who has completed the retreat is ordained during the second retreat (pacchimikā), he completes the required number and also receives the benefits. The same method applies in cases of three monks and two novices, two monks and three novices, or one monk and four novices.

The Ñattidutiya-kammavācā (formal act with one motion) stated in the Khandhaka [for giving the Kathina cloth] is as follows:

'Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This Kathina cloth has arisen for the Saṅgha. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give this Kathina cloth to the monk named so-and-so for the purpose of spreading the Kathina. This is the motion (ñatti). Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This Kathina cloth has arisen for the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha gives this Kathina cloth to the monk named so-and-so for the purpose of spreading the Kathina. Whichever venerable one approves of giving this Kathina cloth to the monk named so-and-so for the purpose of spreading the Kathina, let him be silent. Whichever venerable one does not approve, let him speak. This Kathina cloth has been given by the Saṅgha...'
275:
"...to the monk named so-and-so for the purpose of spreading the Kathina. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent. Thus I understand it." (Mahāvagga 307).

Thus, by this Ñattidutiya-kammavācā stated in the Kathinakkhandhaka [the cloth is given]. 'Kathinattharāraha' means one who is worthy of spreading the Kathina. That monk should be understood as one endowed with the eight factors, such as knowing the preliminary duties (pubbakaraṇa), etc. It is indeed stated in the Vinayavinicchaya: 'A monk who is expert in the eight things is worthy of spreading the Kathina.' It is also stated in the Parivāra (Pari 409):

'A person endowed with eight factors is capable of spreading the Kathina. With which eight factors is a person endowed capable of spreading the Kathina? He knows the preliminary duties (pubbakaraṇa), he knows the relinquishing (paccuddhāra), he knows the determination (adhiṭṭhāna), he knows the spreading (atthāra), he knows the grounds (mātikā), he knows the impediments (palibodha), he knows the removal (uddhāra), and he knows the benefits (ānisaṃsa). A person endowed with these eight factors is capable of spreading the Kathina.'

Herein, 'pubbakaraṇa' means performing washing, inspecting, cutting, tacking, sewing, dyeing, and marking (kappakaraṇa). 'Paccuddhāra' means relinquishing the old outer robe (saṅghāṭi), etc. 'Adhiṭṭhāna' means the determination of the Kathina robe. 'Atthāra' means the spreading of the Kathina. 'Mātikā' means the eight grounds [for removal]. 'Palibodha' means the two impediments: the impediment of residence (āvāsapalibodha) and the impediment of the robe (cīvarapalibodha). 'Uddhāra' means the removals such as that ending with departure (pakkamanantikā), etc. 'Ānisaṃsa' means the five benefits [of Kathina].

As for what is stated in the Samantapāsādikā (Mahāvagga Commentary 306): 'By whom should the Kathina be spread? By the one to whom the Saṅgha gives the Kathina robe. To whom should the Saṅgha give it? To the one whose robe is worn out. If many have worn-out robes, it should be given to the senior monk. Among the seniors, it should be given to the one who has a large following and is able to make and spread the robe on that very day. If the senior is unable but a junior is able, it should be given to him. Nevertheless, it is proper for the Saṅgha to show favor to the Great Elder (Mahāthera); therefore, it should be said, "Venerable Sir, please accept it; we will make it and offer it to you."' This statement should also be taken as giving it only after considering the worthiness to spread the Kathina.

The Saṅgha that gives [the Kathina cloth] gives it for whichever of the three robes [is worn out]. Normally, for a monk who has a double-layer robe (dupaṭṭa), the Kathina cloth is given for the sake of a double-layer robe. If that monk's single-layer robe is thick and the Kathina cloth is thin, then for the sake of suitability, the Kathina cloth of double-layer measurement is given. To a monk who says, 'If I get a double-layer measurement [cloth] for suitability, I will wear it as a single-layer robe,' it is also proper to give a Kathina cloth of double-layer measurement. Furthermore, to one who is greedy by nature, desiring gains...
276:
If the robe is worn out and tattered, the Kathina cloth is given specifically for the purpose of replacing that worn-out robe. For a monk who normally uses a double-layered robe, it is given for the purpose of a double-layered robe. Even if that monk's single-layered robe is thick and the Kathina cloth is thin, it should still be given in an amount sufficient for a double-layered robe for the sake of suitability. It is also permissible to give a double-layered Kathina cloth to a monk who says, "If I do not get enough for a double-layered robe, I will wear only a single-layered one." However, it should not be given to a monk who is naturally greedy. Such a monk must not take the cloth with the intention of spreading the Kathina and then later sewing it, thinking, "I will make two robes."

"Tena" refers to the monk who spreads the Kathina (atthāraka). "Tadaheva" means on that very day. "Cutting into five or more sections (khanda)" means: among the three robes such as the outer robe (saṅghāṭi) which have five sections, etc., one should cut it into five sections or more than five, such as seven sections, by means of large circles (maṇḍala) and small circles (aḍḍhamaṇḍala) sufficient for any one of those robes. While that Kathina robe is being made, no monk should refrain from participating by thinking, "I am a senior elder (thera)" or "I am very learned (bahussuta)." A monk who does not participate out of disrespect commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Therefore, all monks must assemble and complete the tasks of washing, cutting, sewing, and dyeing. Thus, the author of the Compendium (Saṅgaha) said, "The remaining monks must also be assistants to that monk who spreads the Kathina."

"Katacīvarameva" refers to the Kathina cloth for which the preliminary work has been completed. At the very least, even the inner robe (antaravāsaka) must be made by cutting; otherwise, the spreading is invalid (atthāravipatti). As the Blessed One said:

"Monks, how is the Kathina not spread? It is not spread by merely marking... it is not spread except with a robe that has five sections or more than five sections, which has been properly cut on that very day."

For this reason, it is said, "A robe that is not cut and not sewn is not suitable." "Tena bhikkhunā" refers to the monk who spreads the Kathina. "Attharitabbaṃ" means the spreading must be performed. That spreading should be understood as the act of making the formal verbal declaration. As the Blessed One said:

"If one wishes to spread the Kathina with the outer robe (saṅghāṭi), the old outer robe must be relinquished, the new outer robe must be determined (adhiṭṭhāna), and the verbal declaration must be made: 'I spread the Kathina with this outer robe.'"

This is the detailed explanation. Regarding the variation in verbal expressions such as "Venerable Sir," "Friend," "Do you all rejoice," and "Rejoice," it is said, "And to the elders," and so forth.
277:
Having thus shown the method to be followed by the monk who spreads the Kathina (atthāraka), the text now says "Tehipipi" and so forth to show the method to be followed by those who rejoice (anumodaka). The word "Anumodāma" (We rejoice) is spoken in the plural as a mark of self-respect. Although it is said this way, teachers say that a single monk should not say "Anumodāma" but should say "Anumodāmi" (I rejoice); this point should be accepted after careful consideration.

Now, to show the benefits of the Kathina (āniśaṃsa), the text says "Purimavassaṃvuṭṭhesupi" and so forth, examining the basis. In that context, "tesaṃyeva" means only for the monk who spreads the Kathina and the monks who rejoice. It is indeed said in the Parivāra: "The Kathina is spread for two persons: the one who spreads it and the one who rejoices in it." "Te" refers to that spreader and the rejoicer. "Tato paṭṭhāya" means starting from the spreading and the rejoicing. "Yāva kathiinuubbhāra" means the five benefits are obtained not only during the one month of the robe-season (cīvaramāsa), but until the Kathina is removed by any one of the eight grounds (mātikā) or by the interim removal (antarubbhāra). The meaning is that once it is removed, those benefits are no longer obtained.

Now, to show those five benefits in detail, the text says "Anāmantacāro" and so forth. Therein, "anāmantacāra" means the wandering into families by a monk who has been invited to one of the five types of meals, without informing an existing monk. "Asamādānacāra" means wandering without taking the robe that has been determined by name; it means staying away from any one of the three determined robes at dawn. "Yāvadatthacīvara" means keeping an undetermined and unassigned robe for as long as needed, even beyond ten days. "Gaṇabhojana" means the collective eating of any of the five types of meals, such as cooked rice, obtained by request or invitation by four or more monks. "Yo ca tattha cīvaruppādo" means whatever communal robe arises within that Kathina territory—whether it be the robe of a deceased monk, a robe offered to the Sangha, or a robe acquired through communal property—it will belong to those monks who have spread the Kathina. Therefore, it is said, "And the robe that arises for the Sangha in that monastery."

"Whatever bowl or other requisites arise for the Sangha in that monastery belong to all monks. However, the cloth purchased with items such as rice that arise in that monastery belongs only to the monks who have spread the Kathina. Regarding rice and other items [purchased] with cloth..."
278:
It is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada that when items such as rice are caused to be purchased, those items reach all the monks. This statement should also be understood as well-said, because the arising of robes does not occur from the time of purchase. Monks who have not spread the Kathina robe receive four of the five benefits, excluding the practice of traveling without taking the robes (asāmādānacāra) during the robe-season. If they were to receive the benefit of traveling without taking the robes as well, the monks of the Pāveyya country, upon completing the rainy season residence, would not have approached the Blessed One with water-soaked robes. Because they did not receive that benefit, they approached the Blessed One only after taking the three robes even during the robe-season.

Having thus shown the spreading of the Kathina, the author now says 'Taṃ panetaṃ kathiṇaṃ' etc., wishing to show the removal of the Kathina. In that context, mātikā means 'mother' or 'progenitress'. Indeed, these eight mātikā cause the removal of the Kathina. Among those eight, it is called pakkamanantikā because it ends with departure. The remaining terms should be understood in the same way. Among those removals of Kathina (kathiṇuddhāra), if a certain monk, having spread the Kathina, takes the Kathina robe and departs from that monastery without concern, thinking 'I shall not return,' the removal of his Kathina occurs just by crossing the boundary (sīmā). This is to be known as pakkamanantika kathiṇuddhāra.

If a monk takes the robe of benefit and departs, and upon reaching outside the boundary, he thinks, 'I will make this robe right here; I will not go back to that monastery,' and without concern for that monastery, he completes the making of that robe, the removal of that monk's Kathina is called niṭṭhānantika kathiṇuddhāra.

If a monk, taking the robe that is the source of benefit, reaches outside the boundary and decides, 'I will not make this robe, nor will I go back to that monastery,' then the removal of that monk's Kathina is called sanniṭṭhānantika kathiṇuddhāra.

If, having received and taken that same robe of benefit and gone outside the boundary, while thinking 'I will make this robe right here; I will not go back,' that robe is lost, destroyed, or burnt, it is nāsanantika kathiṇuddhāra.

If, having received the robe of benefit, he reaches outside the boundary while still having the concern to return to that monastery, but hears that 'The monks at the monastery have removed the Kathina,' the removal of that monk's Kathina is savanantika kathiṇuddhāra.

Because the cutting off of expectation (āsā) is the end of this mātikā, it is called āsāvacchedikā. If a monk, having been told by someone 'I will give you a robe,' has an expectation for that robe and reaches outside the boundary, abandoning concern for the monastery, and then that person says 'I am no longer able to give it,' the expectation is cut off. The removal of that monk's Kathina is called āsāvacchedika kathiṇuddhāra.

If a monk, while having the concern to return to the monastery where he spent the rainy season from another monastery, goes and returns, and while on the way...
279:
...when it is said 'I will give,' he cuts off the expectation for that robe; the removal of that monk's Kathina is called āsāvacchedika kathiṇuddhāra. If a monk, while having the concern to return to the monastery where he spent the rainy season from another monastery, goes and returns, and while on the way, he passes [the full moon day of Phagguna, which is the limit of the Kathina period], the removal of that monk's Kathina is called sīmātikkamanantika kathiṇuddhāra. It is called sahubbhāra because it occurs together with the removal by other monks. The removal of the Kathina of a monk who, taking the robe of benefit and having the concern to return, goes outside and reaches the time of the removal of the Kathina [the full moon day of Phagguna], is to be known as sahubbhāra kathiṇuddhāra.

'In this pakkamanantika removal of Kathina, first the robe-impediment (cīvarapalibodha) is cut off,' etc. Because the decision regarding the cutting off of the robe-impediment and so forth is stated in detail in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary, the author of the Saṅgaha says, 'There is a detailed decision in that Commentary.' Or, it should be understood that this is said because the detailed decision on the removal of the spreading (atthāra) alone appears in that Commentary. The absence of the remaining impediment means the absence of the monastery-impediment (āvāsapalibodha) which remains after the robe-impediment. 'Assa' refers to the time. The phrase 'dasāhaparamam' is in the accusative case in the sense of continuous duration, thus it says 'that period of ten days at most.' 'Atirekaṃ' means an extra robe; that state of being extra is in relation to robes that have been determined (adhiṭṭhita) or assigned (vikappita), hence it says 'adhiṭṭhitavikappitesu' etc.

A robe woven with linen threads is called khoma. The remaining types like koseyya (silk) and so on are the same. A cloth woven with hair other than human hair and the hair of beasts of prey is called kambala (wool). A cloth made of hemp fibers is called sāṇa. A cloth made by mixing five kinds of threads such as linen is called bhaṅga. Some also say 'it is made of fiber alone.'

'Tadanulomānaṃ' refers to one of the six kinds of robes that are substitutes for those such as linen: dukūla, pattuṇṇa, somārapaṭṭa, cīnapaṭṭa, iddhija, and devadinna. Among those substitutes, the dukūla robe is a substitute for the hemp robe (sāṇa) because it is made of fiber. Cloth produced from silkworms in the Pattuṇṇa region is called pattuṇṇa. Cloth produced in the Somāra region is called somārapaṭṭa. Likewise, cloth produced in the Cīna region is called cīnapaṭṭa. These three are substitutes for silk (koseyya) because they are made of threads produced by silkworms. Robes that arise for 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks through the power of their merit are called iddhija. Since that iddhija robe is one of the types such as linen, it is a substitute for them. A robe given by devas is called devadinna; that robe is produced from a wish-fulfilling tree (kapparukkha) and is similar to the cloth given by the goddess Jālinī to the Elder Anuruddha.
280:
Being similar to the cloth offered to the Elder Anuruddha, that robe produced by psychic power also conforms to linen and other such materials, as it belongs to one of those categories.

An extra robe (atireka-cīvara) that is one carpenter's cubit in length and half a cubit in width is the minimum size suitable for assignment (vikappanā). In the phrase "eight finger-breadths by the Sugata's finger-breadth," a Sugata finger-breadth is currently equivalent to three finger-breadths of a man of medium height. Thus, "eight finger-breadths by the Sugata's finger-breadth" means the measure of one carpenter's cubit. In the phrase "four finger-breadths in width," the meaning should be understood according to the same method mentioned. Because there is no formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) or assignment (vikappanā), and because it is not included among those robes that have been determined or assigned, this robe is called an "extra robe" (atireka-cīvara).

To show the manner in which this determination and assignment should be known, the passage beginning with "Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ" was undertaken. In that context, "Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ" means "that which was said by us: 'because it is not included among those robes that have been determined or assigned'" to indicate the extra robe. "To determine the triple robe" means to determine it by pronouncing its name (such as saṅghāṭi). "Not to assign" means that I do not authorize assignment by names such as saṅghāṭi. However, it is indeed allowable to assign it by saying, "I assign this robe (imaṃ cīvaraṃ vikappemi)." The general statement regarding the authorization to determine the triple robe serves to show that the triple robe must definitely be assigned, as there is no distinction in terms of time, unlike the itch-cloth (kaṇḍupaṭicchādi) and the rainy-season cloth (vassikasāṭikā). It should be understood that this is not for the purpose of prohibiting assignment in every way.

Indeed, this is true: because of the teaching to withdraw the old robe (paccuddharitvā) and determine the new one, and because of the teaching such as "there is no offense if one determines or assigns," the opportunity for assignment is also given for the triple robe. This method is the same for all robes. A monk wishing to determine the triple robe and others should determine them by pronouncing their respective names, such as "I determine this saṅghāṭi." However, a monk wishing to assign should not take the specific name of the robe like "this saṅghāṭi," but should assign it by saying, "I assign this robe to you." Whether it is the triple robe or another robe, if one assigns it by taking its specific name, it does not count as assigned and remains in the status of an extra robe.

"To assign after that" means to assign after the four months of the rainy season by saying, "I assign this robe." It is also authorized to use a robe assigned in this way. Some teachers say, "It is authorized to keep it until the four months of the rainy season of the coming year after assigning it when those four months have passed." "After that" means after recovery from illness. Because the use of these rainy-season cloths and itch-cloths is authorized after assigning them when those four months have passed or after recovery from illness...
281:
In the Gaṇṭhipadas (glossaries), it is stated: "A robe assigned in such a way should be determined with another name and used." "The state of being determined or assigned should be known" means that the acts of determination and assignment should be understood.

It is called "pañcaka" (a five) because it is five cubits in length; a length of five cubits measured by a fist-clenched cubit is called "muṭṭhi-pañcaka." This method also applies to "muṭṭhi-ttika" (three-fist-clenched cubits). Since the navel can be covered even by wearing it, it is said: "A robe of two cubits is also allowable." The word "pi" (also) should be understood to mean that not only a robe of three cubits (aḍḍhateyya) is allowable, but a robe of two cubits is also allowable. "Extra" (atireka) refers to a robe that is the size of the Sugata's robe or even larger than that. "Paccuddharāmi" means "I set aside" or "I relinquish." It is also allowable to say, "I determine this robe as a double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi)." "By performing a bodily gesture" means by touching the robe with the hand or other parts, or by moving it. This determination is not valid for one who does not touch it with some part of the body.

"Twofold" means twofold by way of being in the presence (sammukha) and in the absence (parammukha). "Vācā bhinditabbā" means the words must be uttered. "Inside a room, etc." (antogabbhādīsu) means inside a chamber or on the upper floor of a mansion. "In a neighboring monastery" (sāmanta-vihāre) means in a nearby monastery where one can go and return on the same day. This is merely the head of the teaching (a general guideline); therefore, teachers say that a robe located far away should also be determined. By the words "having noted the place where it is kept," the marking of the robe is meant. This is because there is no benefit in merely noting the place where the robe is kept.

"With cloths that have been determined and kept" refers to cloths kept after being determined as a bedspread (paccattharaṇa), a face towel (mukhapuñchanacoḷa), or an accessory cloth (parikkhāracoḷa). Since the names such as saṅghāṭi do not exist before determination, the procedure for separately relinquishing (paccuddharaṇa) the bedspread, etc., is shown by saying, "I relinquish this cloth." Since they are determined by names such as "bedspread," there is no fault even if one says, "I relinquish this bedspread," etc. "They should be determined again" means they should be determined by names such as saṅghāṭi. For a monk who has an accessory cloth, if a saṅghāṭi or similar robe is made from cloths determined and kept as accessory cloths, there is no need to relinquish and redetermine. The determination made previously is the determination itself. However, if one sews a larger second layer or a piece together with that determined robe, it should be determined; if one sews a piece of equal or smaller size, there is no need for determination.

"For the sake of using comfortably" means that because there is no fault of being away from the robes (vippavāsa), one may leave it in some place and go elsewhere for duties such as listening to the Dhamma, and after the dawn has risen elsewhere, return and relinquish it...
282:
It is for the sake of comfortable use, because one can wear and use the robe without having to forfeit it (nissajjanaṃ) by returning to where the robe is after having spent the dawn in another place for matters such as listening to the Dhamma, having left the determined robe in an unspecified place where there is no fault in being away for a night. “Pari kkhāracolaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ” means to determine it after making it into an accessory cloth.

“Anati rittapamāṇā” means having a size not exceeding the measurement stated as “six spans in length and two and a half spans in width by the Sugata span.” “Paccuddhari tvā vikappetabbā” means it should be assigned after being withdrawn from its status as a rain-cloth. This means that within ten days starting from the first day of the cold season (the day after the full moon of Kattika), it should be withdrawn from being a rain-cloth and assigned in the manner beginning with, “I assign this robe to you.” Otherwise, as it will be stated later that “a rain-cloth relinquishes its determination by the passing of the rainy season months, and an itch-covering cloth by the recovery from the illness,” if there is no determination after the rainy season months have passed, what would there be to withdraw? In that case, the word “having withdrawn (paccuddhari tvā)” would be inappropriate.

Some teachers, however, say: “Just as a robe arising within the Kathina month becomes nissaggiya if the Kathina month passes, so too this rain-cloth becomes nissaggiya when the rainy season months pass. Therefore, it should be withdrawn on the full moon day of Kattika and assigned on the first day of the cold season thereafter; the word construction should be understood as ‘having withdrawn, it should be assigned thereafter.’” That is not correct. For a robe arising in the Kathina month stands in the position of an extra robe (atirekacīvara); thus, if it is not determined on the final day, it becomes nissaggiya upon the passing of the Kathina month. This rain-cloth, however, is not like that because it has been kept under determination. Therefore, how could it become nissaggiya when the rainy season passes? Only a robe that is neither determined nor assigned becomes nissaggiya when the time limit passes. Therefore, even in the cold season, the rain-cloth receives a ten-day period of grace without determination or assignment.

Similarly, the itch-covering cloth (kaṇḍupaṭicchādi) also receives a ten-day grace period after the determination is relinquished. However, it should be assigned without exceeding ten days. Since it is permitted for the purpose of bathing, it is allowable even if it is dyed only enough to discolor it. The statement “two are not allowable” is said because both cannot be determined. They say that if another rain-cloth is obtained during the rainy season, the previous one should be withdrawn and assigned, and then the new one should be determined.

“Pamāṇayuttaṃ” means being endowed with this measurement: “two spans in length and one and a half spans in width.” “Pamāṇikā” means being four spans in length and two spans in width. This refers to the statement made in this text, “paccuddhari tvā vikappetabbā.”
283: It is a (rainy-season robe) endowed with the measurement stated as: "four spans long and two spans wide by the Sugata span." What should be said regarding the phrase "paccuddharitvā vikappetabbā" has already been stated above. Since the Buddha allowed the determination of requisite cloths (parikkhāracola) for items such as bowl bags and water filters by saying, "Bhikkhus, I allow a requisite cloth," when the three robes are complete and there is a need for water filters etc., it is said that "there is no count for requisite cloths." The Blessed One, out of compassion, allowed that whatever items the monks receive, they may determine them according to this procedure and then, "whenever there is a need for a water filter etc., let them make and take those items." For this very reason, it was said "a bag also," and so on. By the word "ādi" (and so on), it also includes determination in absence (asambhukhādhiṦṦhāna) such as "I determine these robes as requisite cloths." By the phrase "and in a coverlet given for the purpose of lodging requisites," he excludes one's own upper coverlet. Some teachers say: "A coverlet that is used only by spreading it on the five types of benches without wearing or draping it is allowable even if it is one's own and not determined." That statement is inappropriate because the coverlet is specifically qualified as "given for the purpose of lodging requisites." It should be understood that for sitting mats, pillows, upper covers, and rugs, there is no requirement for formal determination as they are merely lodging requisites. ## Regarding how the determination is lost for a monk using this determined robe, it was said "and all these," and so on. Therein, "by being snatched away" means being snatched and taken by thieves and the like. "By returning to the lower life" means returning to the state of a layman, which means disrobing; it refers to wearing white clothes with the thought, "I will become a layman while remaining virtuous." Some say: "For one who has committed an ultimate offense (pārājika), wearing white clothes or discarding the saffron robe is called returning to the lower life." Others say: "By the phrase 'returning to the lower life,' only the loss of determination for a bhikkhunī is taken. This is because when she disrobes, she is no longer a bhikkhunī. A bhikkhu, however, even if disrobing, remains a bhikkhu as long as he has not renounced the training, and thus his determination is not yet lost." "By renouncing the training" means renouncing the training while still remaining in the monk's outward form. If a monk renounces the training while remaining in the monk's form, even the robe clinging to his body loses its determination. "By death" means by passing away. "By change of sex" means the change of the male faculty or female faculty; it refers to the appearance of the female faculty in a male, or the appearance of the male faculty in a female.
284:
By the phrase "kaniṭṭhaṅgulinakhapiṭṭhippamāṇena" (the size of the back of the nail of the little finger), the minimum limit is shown. "Orato" means from within. If a monk first places an upper layer (or outer layer) over a worn and thin spot (as a patch) and later cuts away and removes the worn part, the determination (adhiṭṭhāna) is not broken. The same principle applies when exchanging circular patches (maṇḍala). In the case of a double-layered robe (dupaṭṭa), if a hole occurs in one layer or if it rots and falls away, the determination is not broken. Whether one makes a small robe large or a large robe small, the determination is not broken.

A monk who wishes to place both ends in the middle—if he first cuts and then joins them together, the determination is broken. However, if he first joins them and then cuts, the determination is not broken. For a monk who has the robe washed by laundrymen to make it white, the determination remains as it was.

In the phrase "vassānamāsātikkamenāpi" (even by the passing of the month of the rainy season), the word "pi" (also/even) has the sense of inclusion. Because of that word "pi," it should be understood that the rainy-season robe (vassikasāṭika) loses its determination not only through the eight causes previously mentioned, such as giving it away, but also through the passing of the month of the rainy season. In the phrase "ābādhavūpasamenāpi" (even by the recovery from illness), the meaning should be understood in the same way. "Vikappanasikkhāpade" refers to the ninth training rule of the Surāpāna Vagga in the Pācittiya Pali.

In the phrase "taṃ atikkāmayato," the word "taṃ" refers either to the robe or to the time. Therefore, it is said, "taṃ yathāvuttajātippamāṇaṃ," etc. "Assa" means of the monk. "Tassa yo aruṇo" refers to the dawn that has passed after the day the robe was obtained. "Cīvaruppādadivasena saddhiṃ" means together with the dawn of the day the robe was obtained. Here, by the word "divasa" (day), the dawn associated with that day is meant.

Now, to show to whom it should be forfeited and in what manner it should be forfeited, the phrase "taṃ gahetvā" (taking it), etc., is stated. "Tatrāyaṃ nayo" means this is the procedure for that forfeiture. "Aññathāpi" means in another language or in any common language. "Paṭibalena" means by one who is capable of speaking. "Āyatiṃ saṃvareyyāsi" means you should achieve restraint in the future; you should be one who has the doors of body and speech restrained.

These words, beginning with "passasi" (Do you see?), are the words to be spoken in order by the monk who receives the confession and the monk who confesses the offense. Specifically, "passasi" is the word to be spoken by the receiver of the confession. "Āma passāmi" (Yes, I see) is the word to be spoken by the confessor. "Āyatiṃ saṃvareyyāsi" (You should practice restraint in the future) is the word to be spoken by the receiver. "Sādhu suṭṭhu saṃvarissāmi" (Very well, I will restrain myself properly) is the word to be spoken by the confessor. By this phrase "sādhu suṭṭhu saṃvarissāmi," he shows his establishment in future restraint. In the case of two offenses or many offenses, the distinction in grammatical number (singular/plural) should be made according to the previous method. In the phrase "ñattiyaṃ āpattiṃ sarati vivarati"...
285:
The grammatical number should be distinguished by saying "two offenses" (dve āpattiyo) or "many offenses" (sambahulā āpattiyo). The statement that the grammatical number should be distinguished for two or many offenses means that the distinction in number should be made according to the objects, such as "Venerable sirs, these robes" (imāni cīvarāni).

Having thus shown the procedure for forfeiture to the Saṅgha, to show the procedure for forfeiture to a group (gaṇa), the text says, "gaṇassa pana nissajjantena" (but by one forfeiting to a group), etc. In that passage, "the remaining procedure is the same as previously mentioned" means that in forfeiting the robe, receiving the confession, and returning the forfeited robe, except for the distinction in grammatical number such as "to the venerable ones" (āyasmantānaṃ), the rest is identical to what was said regarding forfeiture to the Saṅgha.

Now, to show the procedure for forfeiture to an individual (puggala), the text says, "puggalassa pana" (but to an individual), etc. In that passage, "in two or three" refers to two or three offenses and also to the robes to be given. Just as in forfeiture to a group, the Pali for forfeiture to two individuals should be understood. If there were a specific difference, the Pali would have been stated separately here, just as the Buddha stated the pārisuddhi-uposatha for three monks separately—saying, "Monks, I allow the pārisuddhi-uposatha to be performed by three; and thus, monks, it should be performed: a competent monk should inform those monks with a motion (ñatti)"—and then stated the pārisuddhi-uposatha for two monks separately, saying, "Monks, I allow the pārisuddhi-uposatha to be performed by two; and thus, monks, it should be performed: the senior monk, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder..."

However, since there is no such distinction, He passed over it without stating it separately; thus, the Pali stated for a group is the Pali for this case as well. But in receiving the confession of the offense, there is this distinction: when an offense is being confessed after forfeiting to a group, the monk receiving the confession sets forth a motion (ñatti); but here, without setting forth a motion, one of the two monks should receive the confession just as a single individual does. Indeed, there is no such thing as setting forth a motion for two monks. If there were, He would not have stated the pārisuddhi-uposatha for two monks separately.

In returning the forfeited robe also, just as a single person says, "I give this robe to the venerable one," it is proper to say, "We give this robe to the venerable one." There are commentaries stating that even formal acts involving a motion and a second proclamation (ñattidutiya-kamma), which are weightier than this giving of a forfeited robe, should be performed after consultation (apalokana); those statements are consistent with this matter. Therefore, it is said, "but for two monks" (dvinnaṃ pana), etc. The forfeited robe must certainly be given back; it is not permissible not to give it. This is because this forfeiture is merely a Vinaya procedure (vinayakamma). By such forfeiture, that robe does not actually become given to the Saṅgha, the group, or the individual. Therefore, it is said, "the forfeited object" (nissatṭhavatthu), etc.
286:
For a monk who uses a robe that should have been forfeited without having forfeited it, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). This means that whether it is an inner robe (antaravāsaka) worn once or an upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) donned once, if he wanders for the whole day without removing it from his body, there is only one offense of wrongdoing. If he removes it and then puts it on or dons it again, there is an offense of wrongdoing for each effort. There is no offense for a monk who adjusts an inner robe or an upper robe that was poorly worn. There is also no offense if another person uses that robe. In this regard, the statement beginning with "He uses it after receiving back the robe made by another" serves as evidence.

In the case of a monk who perceives that ten days have passed when they have not, or who is in doubt, an offense of wrongdoing is incurred; here too, the phrase "for the monk who uses it" should be brought in and connected. A monk who perceives that ten days have not passed when they have actually passed refers to a monk who, regarding a robe for which ten days have passed, perceives, "This robe has not yet exceeded ten days," or when ten days have passed, he perceives, "Ten days have not yet passed."

Now, wishing to show the section on offenses (āpattivāra) collectively, beginning with "If one perceives it as determined when it is not determined, it is a nissaggiya," the author says "Tathā" (In the same way) and so on. "Tathā" means that just as there is a triad of pācittiya (tika-pācittiya) due to a difference in perception regarding a robe that has exceeded ten days, so too there is a triad of pācittiya due to a difference in perception such as perceiving it as determined in the seven cases such as not being determined.

In that context, "a monk who perceives it as relinquished when it is not relinquished" refers to a monk who, regarding a robe that has not yet been given or relinquished to anyone, perceives, "I have already given it, I have already relinquished it." "A monk who perceives it as lost when it is not lost" refers to a monk who, when many robes belonging to others are kept together with his own robe and thieves take those robes, perceives his own robe as lost even though it is not lost. The same method should be understood for cases such as perceiving it as destroyed when it is not destroyed. In the phrase "not plundered," it should be understood as a robe that has not been plundered by way of a forceful robbery after breaking into a room.

"Vissajjite" means regarding a robe given to another. How is it given, and how is it received? If one says, "I give this to you, I am giving, I bestow, I dedicate, I relinquish, I give up, I hand over," or if one says, "I give to such-and-one... I hand over," it is considered given whether in the presence or absence of the recipient. When it is said, "Take it for yourself," and the other says, "I take it for myself," it is well-given and well-received. When it is said, "Make it your property, let it be your property, you shall make it your property," and the other says, "I shall make it my property, let it be my property, I will make it my property," it is poorly given and poorly received. This is because the giver does not know the act of giving, and the receiver does not know the act of receiving. However, if when it is said, "Make it your property," the other takes it saying, "Very well, Bhante, I take it for myself," it is well-received. If one says, "Take it," but the other says, "I do not take it," and then the first person says, "It is given..."
287:
"I have given it to you; take it." The other person also says, "I have no need for this robe." Then, the first monk, thinking "I have given it," lets ten days pass. The latter monk also, thinking "I have rejected it," lets ten days pass. In such a case, which monk incurs an offense? No offense is incurred by either monk. Whichever monk wishes to use it should determine (adhiṭṭhāna) it and use it. What should a monk who is in doubt about the determination do? He should inform others of his doubt and say, "If this robe is not yet determined, let it be a robe allowable (kappiya) for me," and then relinquish it according to the method already mentioned. For a monk who performs the disciplinary act (vinayakamma) after informing others in this way, there is no offense of lying (musāvāda).

Just as this training rule on wearing an extra robe is a failure in conduct (ācāra-vipatti), so too the training rules following this are also failures in conduct. Therefore, it is said, "In both Pātimokkhas," and so on. However, due to failure in livelihood (ājīva-vipatti), six classes of offenses have been laid down, excluding wrong speech (dubbhāsita):

"For the sake of livelihood, by reason of livelihood, being of evil desire and overcome by ambition, if one falsely and untruthfully claims a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), there is an offense of defeat (pārājika). For the sake of livelihood, by reason of livelihood, if one practices matchmaking (sañcaritta), there is an offense involving a community (saṅghādisesa). For the sake of livelihood, by reason of livelihood, if one says, 'That monk who lives in your monastery is an Arahant,' and the listener understands, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya). For the sake of livelihood, by reason of livelihood, if a monk who is not ill requests fine food for his own sake and eats it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
