For the sake of livelihood, by reason of livelihood, if a nun who is not ill requests fine food for her own sake and eats it, there is an offense to be confessed (pāṭidesanīya). For the sake of livelihood, by reason of livelihood, if a monk who is not ill requests curry or rice for his own sake and eats it, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa)."

Thus, by way of Pārājika and so on, six classes of offenses are laid down due to failure in livelihood, excluding dubbhāsita. Due to failure in view (diṭṭhi-vipatti), two classes of offenses, pācittiya and dukkaṭa, are laid down. In the case of not relinquishing a harmful view, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) due to the motion (ñatti), and an offense of expiation (pācittiya) at the end of the formal announcement (kammavācā). Thus...
288:
Due to the cause of failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti), two groups of offenses are prescribed by way of Pācittiya and Dukkaṭa. "Herein" refers to the discussions on failures (vipattikathā).

"Reaching the count" (gaṇanupagata) means the state of entering the count of days. Even if a robe is given into the hands of another with the words, "I give this robe to such-and-such a person," it does not yet enter the count of days as long as it has not reached the [monk's] hand, as stated in the Cammakkhandhaka: "It does not enter the count as long as it does not reach the hand." Therefore, as long as it has not been brought and given, or as long as one has not been informed by a messenger saying, "Venerable sir, a robe has arisen for you," it does not enter the count of days, and it is permissible to keep it without formal determination (anadhiṭṭhita). However, from the time it is brought and given, or from the time one hears that it has "arisen," it enters the count, and must be formally determined within ten days.

It is called "Kathina-origination" (kathinasamuṭṭhāna) because its origin is named after the Kathina. This means there are two origins by way of the third and sixth origins. It is said to originate from body and speech because of the failure to perform the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) and assignment (vikappanā) that should be done by body and speech; and from body, speech, and mind if there is intention. It is a "non-action" (akiriya) because the offense is incurred through the non-performance of determination and assignment. It is "not released by perception" (nosannāvimokkha) because one incurs the offense even if unaware. It is a bodily act and a verbal act because of the failure to do what should be done through the bodily door and the verbal door.

## The Explanation of the Kathina Training Rule is Finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Udossita Training Rule

"By the monk" (bhikkhunā) means "of the monk"; here the instrumental case is used in the sense of the possessive (sāmī). Therefore, it is said, "As in the previous training rule," and so on. Why then is the meaning not taken in the instrumental sense but in the possessive sense? To this, it says, "For by way of the instrumental..." and so on. The word "hi" is a particle indicating cause. "One whose obstacles are severed" (chinnapalibodha) means one whose obstacles regarding robes and residence are severed. "One night" (ekarattaṃ) means only one night. "Triple robe" (ticīvaraṃ) is a collective term for the three robes. "With that triple robe" (tena ticīvarena) means with those three robes. Even if one is separated from one robe, it is called being separated from the triple robe, either because it is part of the prohibited set or because the term for the whole is applied to the part. Therefore, it is said, "By the method of determination of the triple robe," and so on.

To define the characteristic of separation (vippavāsa), it says, "A village is of one precinct" (gāmo ekūcāro), and so on. In that context, the name "dwelling" (nivesana) is a name for a specific location not made by way of udossita and so on. It is also called "udavasita." A place where goods such as grain are kept is called an "udossita" (storehouse). An "atta" is a specific building with thick walls made of bricks, four or five stories high, to ward off enemy kings. Some say an "atta" is a house with thick walls and a brick roof without rafters. Others say it is a building constructed in the shape of a court.

A "māḷhikā" is a square mansion with a single peak. Or some say a "māḷhikā" is a building with many corners or a monastery built in a circular shape. A "pāsāda" is a long mansion or any mansion excluding the "aḍḍhayoga" (half-roofed dwelling) and so on. A "hammiya" is a mansion with a truncated roof. Or some say a "hammiya" is a monastery with a balcony. A "nāvā" (boat) refers to both boats on land and boats in water. A "sattha" is a group of caravan traders. A "khala" is a threshing floor. An "ārāma" is a flower garden or an orchard. Some teachers say a "vihāra" refers to all monastery compounds or all houses, whether fenced or unfenced.

Among these fifteen places for keeping robes, "nivesana" and others should be understood as being located outside the village. (Alternatively) Here, fourteen places starting with "nivesana" are taken. If taken by way of "nivesana" and others located within the village, they should be noted as being only within the village precinct (upacāra). Some teachers, however, say that six places starting with "nivesana" are located outside the village.

In the phrase "transgressing the hatthapāsa" (hatthapāsatikkama), a perimeter of three cubits is called a "hatthapāsa." To go beyond that perimeter is to transgress the hatthapāsa. It is proper to stay within the hatthapāsa. If a monk of great psychic power is in the sky beyond that hatthapāsa when dawn rises, the robe is forfeited (nissaggiya).

The decision in this training rule is: if a village is under one king or one village-head and is enclosed by a wall, making it a single precinct, a monk may stay anywhere he likes within the village, depending on the house. If it is not enclosed, he must stay in the house where the robes are kept, or within the hatthapāsa surrounding that house. In the case of a village belonging to many kings or many city-chiefs, such as the cities of Vesālī and Kusinārā, if it is enclosed by a wall, he should stay in the house where the robes are kept or within the hatthapāsa of that house. If the house is on a road, then surrounding that house...
289:
Now, to define the characteristic of vippavāsa (living apart from the robe), the phrase "A village is a single precinct" (gāmo ekūpacāro) and so forth is stated. In that context, nivesana is a name for various types of houses that are not constructed as udosito (sheds or stables) and the like. Udosito refers to a hall (shed) for storing goods such as vehicles. This udosito is also called "udavasito". Aṭṭo is a special type of house with thick walls made of bricks, having four or five stories, built to ward off enemy kings and others. Other teachers say, "Aṭṭo is a house with thick walls where the roof is made only of bricks without using rafters." Some also say, "It is made in the form of a platform." Māḷo is either a square mansion joined by a single peak or a special type of house with many corners joined by a single peak. Other teachers say, "Māḷo is a dwelling made in a circular shape." Pāsādo refers to either a long mansion or any mansion other than aṭṭo, māḷo, and hammiya, including varieties like aḍḍhayoga. Hammiya is a mansion with a flat roof (a top-truncated mansion). Other teachers say, "It is a mansion equipped with a moon-terrace." Nāvā (boat) is of two types: those stationed on land and those stationed in water. Sattho (caravan) is either a group of travelers on foot or a caravan of carts. Dhannyakaraṇa refers to a threshing floor. Ārāmo is either a flower garden or a fruit orchard. Vihāro is an entire dwelling place, whether enclosed or unenclosed. Some teachers say, "A house is also called a vihāro." In this context, nivesana and the like are taken as things situated outside the village. As for those situated inside the village, since they are already included under the name "village", the village regulations apply. Other teachers say, "The items from nivesana to hammiya are situated outside the village enclosure (fence)."

In the term hatthapāsātikkame, hatthapāsa is an area measuring two and a half cubits; exceeding that hatthapāsa is called hatthapāsātikkama. In such an instance of exceeding the hatthapāsa [an offense occurs]. However, staying within the hatthapāsa is allowable. If a monk possessing psychic power causes the dawn to rise while he is in the sky beyond that measure, it is still a nissaggiya (an offense of forfeiture).

The decision in this training rule is as follows: If a village belongs to a single person, whether by the power of a king or a village headman, and it is a single precinct because it is enclosed by walls and so forth, then having placed the robe in such a village, one may stay anywhere one wishes within that village. If it is an unenclosed village, one must stay in the house where the robe is placed, or one must not leave the hatthapāsa around that house.
290:
If the village belongs to various kings or various village headmen, like the cities of Vesālī and Kusinārā, and it is enclosed as described, then in such a village, one must stay in the house where the robe is placed, or one must not leave the hatthapāsa of that house. If there is a house on a certain street, one must stay in the rest house (sabhā) in front of that house on that street, or at the door of the house; one must not leave the hatthapāsa of those rest house doors or house doors. If that village is unenclosed, one must stay in the house where the robe is placed or within its hatthapāsa. Regarding a compound (nivesana), if it belongs to a single family and is enclosed, one may place the robe inside the compound and stay within the compound. If it is unenclosed, one must stay in the room where the robe is placed, or one must not leave the hatthapāsa of that room. If the compound belongs to various families and is enclosed, one must stay in the room where the robe is placed, or one must stay at the common main door or within the hatthapāsa of those room doors. If it is unenclosed, one must stay in the room where the robe is placed, or one must not leave the hatthapāsa of that room. This same method applies to sheds (udosito) and the like.

As for a caravan (sattho), whether it is a group on foot or a caravan of carts: if the caravan belongs to a single group, having placed the robe within the caravan, one must not leave within seven abbhantara from the front or the back, and one must not leave within one abbhantara from the sides. If a traveling caravan stands spanning across a village or a river, being connected with the part that has entered inside and spreading across this bank and the other bank, then only the caravan regulations (satthaparihāra) are obtained. However, if the part that has entered inside is comprised within the village or the river, then both the village regulations and the river regulations are obtained. If [the caravan] stands exceeding the monastery boundary (sīmā) and the robe is within the boundary, one must go to the monastery and stay there. If the robe is outside the boundary, one must stay near the caravan itself. If, while traveling, the caravan is broken in the middle because a cart is broken or an ox is lost, one must stay in the section where the robe is placed. In a field (khetta) as well, if the field belongs to a single family and is enclosed, one may place the robe within the field and stay within the field. If it is unenclosed...
291:
One should not be separated from the robe beyond a forearm's length (hatthapāsa). If it is a field belonging to various families and is fenced, one should place the robe inside the field and stay at the gate of the field or within a forearm's length of that robe. If it is not fenced, one should not be separated from the robe beyond a forearm's length. This method is the same for both threshing floors and enclosures (gardens). Regarding the monastery, the decision is the same as what was said regarding the house (nivesana).

At the foot of a tree, one should place the robe in a place where the shadow falls all around at midday, in a dense area within that shaded space. If one places the robe in a sunny spot of a tree with sparse branches, and at dawn that monk is not within a forearm's length of the robe but is in the shadow of that tree in another spot (not where the robe is), it is a nissaggiya offence. If the tree belongs to various families, one must not be separated from the robe beyond a forearm's length.

In an open space, in forests such as the Viñjhā forest, or on small islands in the middle of the ocean where fishermen do not come, one may place the robe and stay anywhere within seven abbhantaras (sattabbhantara) around that robe. A monk staying beyond these seven abbhantaras is considered to be separated from the robe.

Since this detail is not mentioned in this text but is mentioned in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary, it is said: "Here, this is the summary," and so on. "Here" refers to the phrase "should be separated from the three robes" (ticīvarena vippavaseyya). "Summary" refers to the summary explanation (saṅkhepa-vaṇṇanā). In this Pāḷi text, although the headings are laid down without distinction such as "a village has one precinct or various precincts," the status of having one precinct or various precincts for villages, houses, storehouses (udosita), fields, threshing floors, enclosures, and monasteries is analyzed by way of being fenced or unfenced, such as "a village is called having one precinct if it belongs to a single family and is either fenced or unfenced," and so on. However, for watchtowers, sheds, mansions, flat-roofed houses, boats, caravans (carts), the foot of a tree, and open spaces, it is not said in that way, but rather by way of belonging to one family or various families, such as "it is a watchtower of one family, it is a watchtower of various families," and so on. Finally, it is analyzed as having one precinct or various precincts as: "In an open space, in a forest that is not a village, the area within seven abbhantaras all around is one precinct; beyond that is various precincts." Therefore, in villages and so on, a fenced area is one precinct...
292:
An unfenced village and so on should be understood as 'various precincts' (nānūpacāra). Among watchtowers and so on, if it is the property of one family, it is 'one precinct' (ekūpacāra); if it is the property of various families, it is 'various precincts'. In an open space, it should be understood according to the method already mentioned. Indeed, in phrases like "a village has one precinct or various precincts," the gate is considered the 'precinct' (upacāra). However, in the Pāḷi "an open space is one precinct," other teachers say that the 'precinct' refers to the area measured as seven abbhantaras all around.

'Except by the monk's formal permission' (aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā) means the permission given to a monk by the Saṅgha; it means excluding that permission. Therefore, the author of the Saṅgaha said, "What the Saṅgha..." and so on. 'Gives the permission for non-separation' (avippavāsa-sammutiṃ deti) is the permission for not being separated, or permission for the sake of non-separation; it means giving that permission through a formal act with a motion and a second (ñattidutiya-kammavācā).

In the term 'santaruttarena', 'antara' refers to the undergarment (antaravāsaka), and 'uttara' refers to the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga). The upper robe together with the undergarment is called 'santaruttara'. Therefore, it means with the upper robe together with the undergarment. 'Relinquished within dawn' (anto aruṇe paccuddhaṭe) means that a monk who is unable to return (to where the robes are) and reach them before dawn, stays where he has arrived and relinquishes the determination (of the robes) before dawn. 'Should return' (paccāgantabbaṃ) means that when returning to the place where the robes were kept, one should come in a way that does not aggravate the illness.

In fact, from the moment one starts searching for a companion or makes the resolution "I will go," staying (without relinquishing the robes) is permissible. However, one who gives up the effort (to go), thinking "I will not go now," should relinquish the determination, thinking "This robe will remain as an extra robe (atireka-cīvara)." Therefore, it was said: "One should relinquish the determination while staying in that very place." 'He' (so) refers to the illness for which the permission was given. It means that there is no further need for the act of giving permission; the monk simply possesses the allowed state.

'The state of determined robes' (adhiṭṭhita-cīvaratā) is the state of robes determined according to the method of determining the three robes. 'Separation' (vippavāsa) means, if the robe is within a bound boundary (baddha-sīmā), letting dawn rise outside that boundary. If it is an unbound boundary (abaddha-sīmā), it is letting dawn rise beyond the forearm's length (hatthapāsa) outside the aforementioned villages and so on. In a bound boundary, however, it is permissible to leave the robe anywhere and stay anywhere else within the boundary. In this training rule, not relinquishing the determination is connected as 'non-action' (akiriyā).

## The explanation of the Udosita Training Rule is finished.
